llm-sft and imagenet versions are directly selectable for training. A raw COCO upload is converted for the trainer automatically (a data.yaml is generated); YOLO produced by an annotation export needs no conversion at all.

A sharegpt line looks like this and feeds the LLM/VLM trainers directly:

{"conversations": [{"from": "human", "value": "Describe this image."},
                   {"from": "gpt", "value": "A blue circle on a red background."}]}

docs.title: Create and upload
docs.text:
1. On the Datasets page, create a dataset with a name, description and format.
  2. Upload individual images or a ZIP archive. Images may sit at the archive root or in an images/ subdirectory.
  3. The archive is extracted and ingested asynchronously — follow progress in the version list. Each successful ingest becomes a new retained version.
  4. Pre-staged corpora (for example an LLM-SFT JSONL plus an images/ directory already placed in object storage) can be registered from their S3 prefix without a browser upload.

Accepted image types are jpg / jpeg / png. Bulk bytes go to the S3-compatible object store; the workbench and trainers receive short-lived presigned URLs instead of file copies.

docs.title: Versioning rules
docs.text:
• Every upload increments the version; old versions are retained and remain selectable. Versions are never mutated.
  • An annotation export (COCO/YOLO for vision, JSONL for text) is itself a new dataset version, so a model is always traceable to the exact labels it learned from.
  • Switch between versions when creating a job; the rest of the pipeline does not change.
  • The version records its file counts (images and annotation files), format, size and origin (upload, export, S3 reconciliation).

docs.title: How versions feed the factory
docs.text:
upload images ──► v1 (raw)
annotate + export ──► v2 (YOLO / JSONL, training-ready) ──► training
new field images ──► v3 ──► annotate gaps ──► v4 ──► retrain

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
How do I prepare labeled training data?

Label the images in the annotation workbench, then use Export. Vision projects export COCO/YOLO; text-classification exports plain JSONL; generation/chat projects export sharegpt JSONL. The result is a new dataset version the training page can select immediately.

How are version numbers incremented?

Automatically, once per finalized upload or export. You cannot overwrite a version.

Can a dataset mix images and text?

VLM corpora do exactly that: an llm-sft JSONL references files in an accompanying images/ directory. For pure vision use COCO/YOLO/ImageNet; for pure text use JSONL/LLM-SFT without images.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Label the data on the Annotations page, or
  • Start a Training run directly on a training-ready version.
  • Set up pre-labeling first? See ML Backend.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Evaluation scores a model version against a labeled dataset with a real inference pass, so you can decide whether a version is good enough to deploy — or needs more data, retraining or a different optimization target. It also gives the FP32-vs-quantized comparison that makes an optimization result trustworthy rather than just faster.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
For computer-vision models Forge reports the standard detection/classification metrics plus end-to-end latency:

Metric Meaning mAP50 Mean Average Precision at IoU 0.50 — the headline detection score mAP50-95 mAP averaged over IoU 0.50–0.95 — rewards tight, accurate boxes Precision Of the predicted boxes, the fraction that are correct Recall Of the real objects, the fraction that were found F1 Harmonic mean of precision and recall Latency Measured per-image inference time on the evaluation runtime

For optimized (ONNX/int8) versions, compare against the source FP32 version: the accuracy drop (for example the mAP50 delta) is the number the optimization quality gate uses, alongside latency and size.

docs.title: Run an evaluation
docs.text:
1. On the Evaluation page, choose a model version and a dataset.
  2. Set the parameters:
Parameter Default Notes Confidence threshold 0.25 Detections below it are ignored; lower it when a model under-predicts Maximum images 0 0 means the whole dataset; cap it for a quick check Task type from the model Detection / segmentation / classification
  1. Submit. The dataset is converted to the layout the evaluator needs automatically.
  2. Read the metrics table and, for an optimized version, the drop relative to its FP32 source.

docs.title: Which data to evaluate on
docs.text:
• By default evaluation uses the val split produced at training time. This prevents accidentally scoring on the training images (data leakage) and makes different versions directly comparable.
  • You can point the job at any other dataset version instead — for example a newly collected field batch — to measure real-world behavior. Keep that dataset separate from training if you want an honest number.

docs.title: Interpreting the result
docs.text:
• mAP high, latency high → keep accuracy, deploy on stronger hardware or optimize more aggressively.
  • Large quantized drop → revisit calibration data or keep FP16/FP32 for that target.
  • Low recall (objects missed) → add examples of those scenes to the next dataset version and retrain.
  • Low precision (false boxes) → raise the confidence threshold or add hard-negative images.

docs.title: Quick sanity check without a job
docs.text: On the Models page, Try with image runs one uploaded image through any version directly — drawing detected boxes (or showing classification top-5 and timing) without creating a KServe deployment. The Grad-CAM overlay on PyTorch versions visualizes where a detector/classifier is looking. It is an interactive check, not a replacement for dataset-level metrics.

docs.title: LLM / VLM versions
docs.text: The benchmark metrics above are the computer-vision evaluation. For fine-tuned LLM/VLM versions, use the training run's loss / eval-loss curves and step-level history to confirm convergence, and validate behavior on your own prompt/reference set with the trial-inference path before serving.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Why is precision 0?

Either the model has not converged, or the confidence threshold is too high so almost no boxes survive. Lower the threshold (0.25 is the usual starting point) and rerun; also check that the evaluation dataset's classes match the model's classes.

Which dataset is used by default?

The validation split generated during training, so training data is not reused for the score.

The model needs an ONNX artifact?

Evaluation runs on the available model artifact; conversion is handled by the pipeline. If a version has no runnable artifact, train or upload one first.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Accept the version and deploy it: Models.
  • Improve speed/size again: Optimization.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
NereidForge (Forge) is the privatized model factory of the NereidAI suite: one production line that turns your own data into field-ready models — prepare data, annotate, train, optimize, evaluate, register and deploy, all running on-premises and fully offline. Data never leaves your network, and every dataset, model version and evaluation report is retained as an organizational asset. See the product page for the full capability overview.

Forge covers two model families on the same production line:

Track Typical models Output Computer vision (CNN) YOLO / RT-DETR (detection), SAM (segmentation), timm/TorchVision (classification) ONNX / quantized runtimes for CPU, Intel, NVIDIA, AMD LLM / VLM Qwen / LLaMA-family text and vision-language models LoRA / QLoRA adapters and merged checkpoints, served via vLLM-compatible runtimes

docs.title: The production line
docs.text:
datasets ──► annotations ──► training ──► optimization ──► evaluation
            (versions)   (pre-label)   (CV | LLM/VLM)   (ONNX/int8)     (metrics)
                                                                        │
                                                                        ▼
                                                  model registry ──► deployment (KServe)
                                                                        │
◄──────────────────────── field data / new images feed a new round ─────┘

Every stage writes an immutable, versioned artifact, so any model can be traced back to the exact dataset version and base model that produced it.

docs.title: The pages in this manual
docs.text: Stage Page What you do there 1 Datasets Create datasets, upload images/ZIP or text corpora, manage immutable versions 2 Annotations Label in Label Studio / CVAT, run ML-assisted pre-labeling, export 3 ML Backend Register the pre-labeling service that predicts boxes/labels for annotators 4 Training Run CV or LLM/VLM training on CPU/GPU from multiple vendors 5 Optimization ONNX graph optimization and int8 quantization per target device 6 Evaluation Score mAP / Precision / Recall / F1 and latency, compare to the baseline 7 Models Browse versions, try a model on an image, deploy with KServe

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Dataset version — every upload or annotation export is a new, immutable version. Training always references one fixed version, so a run is reproducible.
  • Base model — a starting point from the model pool: a YOLO checkpoint for CV, or a pretrained LLM/VLM (for example a Qwen model) for fine-tuning.
  • Job — one asynchronous pipeline run (training, optimization, evaluation, export). The cluster schedules CPU/GPU automatically; progress, logs and curves are available on the job detail page.
  • Model version — the output registered in the model library. Trained, optimized and manually uploaded artifacts all become versions of one model, keeping their lineage and metrics.
  • Artifact storage — images, checkpoints and reports are stored in the on-premises S3-compatible store (SeaweedFS); the database and message plane never carry the bulk bytes.

docs.title: Your first CV model (15-minute tour)
docs.text:
1. Prepare data — on the Datasets page, create a dataset (COCO/YOLO) and upload jpg/png images or a ZIP (images at the archive root or in an images/ folder). Ingestion is asynchronous; the upload becomes version 1.
  2. Annotate — on the Annotations page, create a project (detection, segmentation or classification), open the embedded Label Studio workbench, and draw a few labels. Optionally choose a registered model in the project header and run Semi-automated annotation, then correct the suggestions.
  3. Export — export to YOLO. The export is registered as a new, training-ready dataset version.
  4. Train — on the Training page, pick the exported version, a base model (YOLOv8n is a safe start), and accept the suggested hyperparameters (epochs 100, imgsz 640, batch 16, train/val 0.8). Forge splits train/val and runs a real Kubeflow Pipelines run.
  5. Optimize — on the Optimization page, select the trained version and a target device (CPU / Intel OpenVINO / NVIDIA TensorRT / AMD / Ascend). Each target independently runs ONNX optimization and int8 quantization and reports measured speedup, size and latency.
  6. Evaluate — on the Evaluation page, score a version against the val subset. Review mAP50 / Precision / Recall / F1, and the accuracy_drop of a quantized version. If precision is 0, lower the confidence threshold to 0.25 and retry.
  7. Deploy — on the Models page, select a version, choose a serving runtime (OpenVINO on CPU, Triton on GPU), and create the KServe service. Forge creates the InferenceService and Ingress and returns the endpoint domain.

docs.title: Your first LLM / VLM
docs.text:
The same loop applies, with two differences:

  • Data — create a dataset of format LLM-SFT: a sharegpt-style JSONL corpus (one conversation per line), plus an images/ folder for VLM. Text projects in the annotation workbench export directly to this format.
  • Training — choose an LLM/VLM base model. NVIDIA and AMD runs use the LLaMA-Factory trainer; Intel Arc uses the native transformers + PEFT route (LoRA/QLoRA). Pick the accelerator that matches your node on the training form; without a GPU the form falls back to CPU.

The loop repeats

Field data starts the next round: upload it as a new dataset version, annotate the gaps, retrain, optimize and re-evaluate. Every model version keeps its data, metrics and deployment history — the factory gets faster the more it runs.

docs.title: ML Backend
docs.text:
The ML Backend is the service behind semi-automated annotation: when an annotator requests pre-labeling, it predicts boxes, masks or labels on the unlabeled tasks and writes them into the workbench as editable predictions. People then review and correct instead of drawing every label from scratch — this is the "machine first, human review" step of the factory's flywheel.

It implements the standard Label Studio ML Backend protocol, so it plugs into the embedded Label Studio directly, and the same inference also serves CVAT pre-annotation and the model trial feature.

docs.title: What it is — and is not
docs.text:
• It is a model-agnostic routing layer, not one fixed model. Per request it loads the model version the project selected and routes by family:
/predict
   ├── CNN (detection / segmentation / classification) ──► ONNX Runtime / Triton
  └── LLM / VLM (vision-language or text) ───────────────► vLLM-compatible OpenAI endpoint
  • The image ships no bundled weights. All models live in the platform's S3-compatible store and are loaded on demand into bounded in-memory caches, so one shared service serves every model version you upload; idle memory stays small and unused models are evicted automatically.
  • It is a backend for the annotation workbench, not the production serving path — field inference of approved models uses KServe deployments from the Models page.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text: Endpoint Purpose GET /health Health probe (the console's reachability check requires status UP) GET /setup Model information, supported labels and version POST /predict Batch prediction used to pre-fill annotations POST /train Optional trigger for interactive training POST /try/predict Single-image trial used by Try with image (boxes / top-5 / timing) SAM segment route Click-to-segment in the CVAT video editor with an uploaded sam model

docs.title: Register the backend
docs.text:
1. On the ML Backend page, register the service with a name and its URL.
  2. Use the shared in-cluster service address provided by the platform install. Do not invent a host name or use an external/host address: the workbench pod runs inside the cluster and cannot resolve host domains, and the shared service has no external ingress by design.
  3. The console performs a real GET /health probe; a reachable service reports healthy.

The normal flow does not require a per-model backend: keep the shared service, and choose the concrete model version in each annotation project's header. A separately deployed, dedicated backend is only needed for advanced isolation — it can be created from a registered model through the custom backend deployment (a per-model Kubernetes Deployment + Service).

docs.title: Choose the pre-labeling model per project
docs.text:
In the annotation project header (both Label Studio and CVAT), select a model and version for pre-labeling. The choice is stored on the project and applied to batch and single-image pre-labeling:

  • Only detection/segmentation models with weights are offered (SAM appears in the video editor separately).
  • With no model selected, the semi-automated button is disabled with an explanatory tooltip — there is no silent built-in fallback.
  • A model you just trained can be selected immediately, so each iteration pre-labels the next batch better.

Requests are batched to stay within the service timeout; predictions return in input order and are mapped back to the images automatically.

docs.title: Model support
docs.text:
• Detection: YOLO family / RT-DETR (PyTorch or ONNX, including legacy YOLOv5/v6/v7 via their ONNX artifacts).
  • Segmentation: SAM-family models for click-to-segment (upload a version with task type sam; the checkpoint must keep an official SAM-compatible file name).
  • Classification: PyTorch/ONNX classifiers, top-5 output.
  • VLM/LLM: Qwen-VL / Florence-2 style models through the vLLM route for label/box suggestions and text annotation.
  • Ultralytics applies its own default confidence (0.25); the project's configured threshold is passed through, so tune it in the project rather than assuming a later filter has an effect.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The backend shows unreachable / unhealthy?

Verify the registered URL is the shared in-cluster service address from the install guide. A browser/host URL fails DNS from the workbench pod, and the old namespace address from a previous install is invalid after migration. GET /health must return status UP.

Pre-labels are empty or labels do not match?

The selected model's classes must match the project's label schema, and the model version must have weights. Weak or low-confidence predictions (below threshold) are intentionally not inserted — lower the threshold or pick a stronger/newly trained model.

A newly selected model seems ignored?

The service loads weights on demand and caches per artifact. After re-uploading weights to the same storage key, restart/roll the backend to drop the cached copy; prefer uploading a new version/key instead.

Where are large images cached?

Downloaded images use a dedicated scratch directory with an LRU cap (separate from the weights directory); weights and media never pollute each other and the service logs evictions and every predict call.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Use it in the workbench: Annotations.
  • Train a model, then loop it back as the pre-labeler: Training.
  • One-off checks of a version: Models → Try with image.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: The model library is the registry at the center of the factory: every trained, optimized or imported version lands here with its lineage, metrics and deployment history. From this page you compare versions, sanity-check a model on an image, and publish it as a live inference service.

docs.title: Model and versions
docs.text:
• A model groups versions of the same solution; a version is one immutable artifact.
  • Versions arrive three ways:
  • Training — registered automatically on success (weights + ONNX for CV; adapters/tokenizer for LLM/VLM).
  • Optimization — registered under the source model as {source-version}-onnx-{dtype}, carrying target device, speedup, size and accuracy-drop metrics.
  • Manual upload — import .pt / .pth / .onnx / .safetensors (and related checkpoints); the framework is inferred from the suffix.
  • Each version stores its framework (pytorch / onnx / …), task (detection / segmentation / classification / llm / vlm), source job, metrics and artifact URIs.

docs.title: Compare and select
docs.text: The version table shows task, framework, target device and the measured speedup/size for optimized versions. When several int8 targets exist, pick by the latency/accuracy point you need rather than by name. Keep both the FP32 source and the quantized versions until the optimized one passes evaluation.

docs.title: Try a version on an image
docs.text:
Before deploying, use Try with image on a version row:

  • Upload one image and set a confidence threshold; Forge runs it through the shared ML Backend using that exact version — no KServe deployment needed.
  • Detection draws boxes with labels and scores; classification returns the top-5; elapsed inference time is reported.
  • PyTorch (.pt) versions additionally support a Grad-CAM heatmap that shows the regions driving the prediction (ONNX has no gradients, so the toggle is unavailable there).
  • Legacy checkpoints that modern Ultralytics cannot load directly are served transparently via their sibling ONNX artifact (the UI marks this); the original .pt is never modified.

docs.title: Deploy with KServe
docs.text:
1. Select a version and open Deploy.
  2. Choose a serving runtime. The list comes from the KServe ClusterServingRuntime definitions installed in the cluster — for example OpenVINO (CPU, the validated default) or NVIDIA Triton (GPU); vLLM-compatible runtimes for LLM/VLM appear when the cluster provides them.
  3. Choose the accelerator/domain as the form requires and confirm.
  4. Forge submits a pipeline that creates the KServe InferenceService and an Ingress, then records the service name, runtime and domain on the version.

By default the endpoint follows <model>-<version>.inference.<platform-domain>; point DNS for that domain at the cluster ingress. Deployments are asynchronous (typically 1–3 minutes) — the Deployments list refreshes automatically and shows deploying / ready / failed state straight from KServe.

Undeploy removes the InferenceService and Ingress; the model versions and artifacts remain in the library and can be redeployed at any time.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• For manual import, provide a supported checkpoint/ONNX file.
  • The runtime you choose must exist as a ClusterServingRuntime, and GPU/NPU runtimes need the corresponding device available on a node.
  • The deployment domain must resolve in DNS to the cluster ingress address.
  • KServe and its service account / ingress bindings are provisioned by cluster operations as part of the platform install.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
How do I reach a deployed model?

The deployment response and the Deployments list show the endpoint domain. The Ingress is created automatically; DNS just needs to point at the cluster ingress IP.

OpenVINO or Triton?

OpenVINO for CPU inference (validated end-to-end); Triton for NVIDIA GPU serving. For LLM/VLM use the vLLM-compatible runtime installed on the cluster. Pick the runtime that matches where the model will actually run.

Try works but deployment fails?

Trial uses the shared ML Backend and does not need KServe; deployment additionally requires a matching serving runtime, node resources and DNS. Check the deployment state/message and cluster provisioning first.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Serve and integrate the endpoint; retrain later from field data — the loop starts again at Datasets.
  • Improve a deployed model with Optimization and Evaluation.

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text:
A trained model is usually too large or too slow for a field device. Optimization compiles the model to ONNX, applies graph optimization and int8 quantization for a chosen target silicon, and benchmarks the result on that target — so you trade a controlled, measured accuracy drop for latency, throughput and storage gains.

Each (source version × target device) combination is an independent job and produces its own model version. Selecting several targets fans out into several runs in one submission.

docs.title: Target devices
docs.text:
Targets are vendor-first: selecting a vendor maps to the runtime/export path the optimizer uses.

Selection Optimizer target Typical runtime in the field CPU cpu ONNX Runtime (CPU) Intel openvino OpenVINO NVIDIA tensorrt TensorRT / Triton AMD onnx-rocm ONNX Runtime (ROCm) Huawei Ascend ascend Ascend runtime

Legacy values (cpu, openvino, tensorrt, …) are accepted as-is. A target whose toolchain or hardware is absent from the cluster stays pending rather than failing silently — run it on a node that has that accelerator.

docs.title: What the pipeline does
docs.text:
1. Take the source version's ONNX artifact (training emits one; a manually uploaded .onnx works too).
  2. Run ONNX graph optimization for the target.
  3. Quantize weights/activations to int8 with a calibration set.
  4. Benchmark source vs. optimized with ONNX Runtime on the target — this is a real measurement, not an estimate.
  5. Register the result as a new version with measured metrics and a gate verdict.

The optimized artifact lands in object storage (SeaweedFS) and is registered under the source model with a name like {source-version}-onnx-{dtype-suffix}, so every optimized version keeps its lineage to the trained model.

docs.title: Metrics and quality gates
docs.text:
Each optimized version records:

  • Speedup — optimized vs. source latency on the same target.
  • Size reduction — artifact bytes before vs. after.
  • Latency — measured inference latency (the optimization sweep can search parameter combinations, minimizing latency subject to a hard mAP-drop bound).
  • Accuracy drop — evaluation metrics of the quantized model against the FP32 source (for example mAP50 delta).

The gate separates what must never regress from what an operator may accept:

  • Hard gate — task-accuracy drop and numerical safety (NaN/Inf). A failed hard gate blocks automatic registration.
  • Soft gate — performance targets such as latency/throughput; a miss is flagged (YELLOW) and can be reviewed and manually released with the gate recorded, rather than hidden.

Always confirm the int8 model's accuracy on the Evaluation page before deploying it; quantization is hardware- and data-dependent.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The source version must have an ONNX artifact. Train it in Forge (the CV trainer exports ONNX) or upload an .onnx manually to the model library.
  • The matching hardware/toolchain for GPU/NPU targets must exist in the cluster; otherwise the task stays pending.
  • Use a representative calibration set — quantization quality follows the data it calibrates on.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Where does the speedup number come from?

From a real benchmark (optimize.py via ONNX Runtime) comparing the source and optimized models on the target, not from a table of estimates.

Can I optimize for several chips at once?

Yes — select multiple targets in one task; Forge creates one independent job and one output version per target, then compares them in the model library.

The int8 model lost too much accuracy.

Re-run with a more representative calibration set; if the drop still exceeds the gate, keep the FP32/FP16 version for that target or choose a less aggressive path. Review accuracy_drop in evaluation.

Does this optimize LLM/VLM models?

This page describes the CV ONNX/int8 line. LLM/VLM serving efficiency is handled primarily through LoRA/QLoRA adapters at training time and the chosen serving runtime; a single-page CV quantizer is not applied to large language checkpoints.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Verify the optimized version: Evaluation.
  • Pick the winning target and deploy: Models.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
Training runs a real pipeline job on the cluster from a fixed dataset version and registers the result as a new model version. It is not a mock: a trainer container runs on CPU or GPU, emits live loss curves and logs, and uploads artifacts into object storage on completion.

Forge schedules the work through Kubeflow Pipelines; you only fill the training form. Two training routes share the same job machinery.

docs.title: Two training routes
docs.text: Computer vision LLM / VLM Input dataset COCO / YOLO / ImageNet version LLM-SFT / sharegpt JSONL (+ images/ for VLM) Base model YOLO / RT-DETR / timm checkpoint Qwen / LLaMA-family pretrained model from the base-model pool Trainer Ultralytics / timm template (train.py) LLaMA-Factory (NVIDIA, AMD) or native transformers + PEFT (Intel) Method Full training / fine-tuning SFT with LoRA / QLoRA adapters (or merged checkpoint) Outputs .pt + .onnx, metrics adapter / tokenizer / processor, history.jsonl, metrics Accelerators CPU, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel NVIDIA, AMD, Intel (QLoRA), CPU fallback

docs.title: Accelerators: one form, vendor-specific images
docs.text:
Forge uses an accelerator profile abstraction: you pick the target on the form (only resources the cluster reports as allocatable are offered), and the platform selects the matching trainer image variant, Kubernetes resource and PyTorch backend:

Vendor K8s resource Image suffix Backend NVIDIA nvidia.com/gpu -cu CUDA PyTorch / LLaMA-Factory AMD (RDNA) amd.com/gpu -rocm ROCm / HIP, LLaMA-Factory Intel Arc gpu.intel.com/xe -xpu native torch.xpu + PEFT CPU — default CPU image

Support is honestly graded and depends on your hardware:

  • Certified — end-to-end training verified on real devices (for example Intel Arc is certified for CV, LLM QLoRA and SmolVLM VLM-LoRA on the reference node).
  • Compatible / build-only — the image exists but CV or full E2E is not yet certified on that silicon.
  • When the cluster has no matching device, the job cannot be scheduled there; pick an available accelerator or CPU rather than assuming a GPU is present.

docs.title: Create a training job
docs.text:
1. Open the Training page and choose the task type (CV detection / segmentation / classification, or LLM / VLM).
  2. Select the dataset version (an annotation export or an LLM-SFT corpus).
  3. Select a base model from the pool.
  4. Set hyperparameters; the CV defaults are a safe starting point:
Parameter CV default Notes epochs 100 LLM/VLM fine-tuning typically uses 1–5 epochs imgsz 640 Inference/training image size batch 16 Reduce on smaller VRAM; the trainer errors clearly on OOM train/val ratio 0.8 Forge performs the split and keeps the val set for evaluation
  1. Choose the accelerator that matches your node, then submit.

For LLM/VLM jobs the form additionally exposes the fine-tuning method (full / LoRA / QLoRA), rank and LoRA hyperparameters; VLM jobs accept the vision-language base model and the sharegpt + images corpus.

docs.title: While a job runs
docs.text:
• Status & progress — the job moves through queued, running, succeeded or failed; progress reaches 100% on success.
  • Curves — the Training curves tab plots per-step/per-epoch loss and evaluation metrics (CV reads the trainer's results; LLM/VLM plots the step-level history.jsonl).
  • Logs — the log view shows the real trainer pod's standard output (loss lines, upload confirmation), falling back to pipeline-executor logs if the pod has ended.
  • Artifacts — on success the trainer uploads weights, ONNX (CV), metrics and tokenizer/processor files, and a model version is registered automatically under the job name.

Checkpoints are written during training, so an interrupted run can be resumed from its checkpoint; a failed job can also simply be restarted.

docs.title: Bring your own trainer
docs.text:
When the built-in templates cannot express a workflow, a CV/PyTorch job can use a custom image and/or a custom training script:

  • custom_image — any private registry image with Python on PATH; it becomes the trainer container.
  • custom_script_uri — an s3:// or http(s):// URL to a Python file, downloaded into the container and executed as __main__.

The script receives the standard trainer environment (INPUT_URI, OUTPUT_DIR, CONFIG_JSON, ARTIFACT_ID, S3_* credentials) and uploads its model to OUTPUT_DIR. Uploading a <artifact>.metrics.json with weights_uri/onnx_uri registers the version precisely; otherwise the worker scans the output prefix and registers the best artifact (.onnx preferred, then .pt/.pth/.safetensors). LLM/VLM jobs go through LLaMA-Factory / the XPU trainer and do not use these selectors.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Where are the curves?

On the job detail page, in the Training curves tab. They populate as the trainer writes them, not before the first epoch/step lands.

The job is stuck pending?

The requested accelerator is not allocatable. Check cluster nodes, free GPU memory and device plug-ins, then resubmit on an available profile (including CPU for a smoke test).

How is training data chosen?

You pick one immutable dataset version; Forge splits train/val at the ratio you set. The held-out val split is what Evaluation uses by default, which avoids evaluating on training images.

What if it is interrupted?

Resume from checkpoint or restart the job. Dataset and base model are fixed on the job, so a rerun is comparable.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Compress for the edge: Optimization.
  • Measure quality and latency: Evaluation.
  • Inspect, try and deploy the result: Models.

docs.title: Agbots
docs.text: An agbot (agreement bot) is the Exchange negotiation agent in NereidHorizon. It matches services and deployment policies to edge nodes and forms the agreements that cause workloads to run. Whether a node can deploy a service depends on whether an agbot has the matching pattern or policy linked.

docs.title: The detail drawer
docs.text:
Clicking an agbot opens a drawer with four tabs:

Tab Contents Patterns Patterns linked to this agbot Business Policies Business policies linked to this agbot Agreements Current agreements with status, service specs, and associated node Agbot Info ID, last heartbeat, and public key

docs.title: Link a pattern or policy
docs.text:
1. Click Link pattern or Link policy at the end of the agbot's row.
  2. Choose the pattern or policy from the popup list.

Linked items appear in the drawer's Patterns and Business Policies tabs, and resulting agreements appear under Agreements.

docs.title: Browse other organizations
docs.text: Click Authorize and provide root/root credentials, or an account with cross-organization permissions, to browse patterns and policies in other organizations. Agbots from the IBM organization are merged into the list automatically; they are visible only in the system organization.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 401 Unauthorized, or cross-organization authorization has expired 404 Pattern or policy not found 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Patterns
  • Deployment Policies
  • Edge Nodes
  • Node Registration

docs.title: Agent File Version
docs.text: The Agent File Version module in NereidHorizon manages the lists of agent software, configuration, and certificate versions. These lists guide edge nodes when they perform an agent upgrade, typically as part of an upgrade management policy.

docs.title: Edit version lists
docs.text:
Each list holds one version number per line, for example:

2.30.0

The three lists are maintained separately:

  • Software Versions — agent software versions.
  • Config Versions — agent configuration versions.
  • Cert Versions — agent certificate versions.

docs.title: Unsupported Exchange versions
docs.text: If the connected Exchange does not support this feature, the page shows an empty state. Horizon treats the backend's 400 response as a graceful degradation, so an unsupported Agent File Version capability does not affect any other function.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 400 The current Exchange version does not support AgentFileVersion — graceful degradation, other functions are unaffected 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Management Policies
  • Edge Nodes

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text: API keys in NereidHorizon let partners read their own organization's data through the read-only Partner API (GET /api/v1/{org}/...) without signing in to the console. Use a key when another system needs to pull service, pattern, policy, or node information from your organization programmatically.

docs.title: Key format and storage
docs.text:
• Keys use the nk_live_<random> or nk_test_<random> format.
  • Horizon stores only the SHA-256 hash of each key. The plaintext key is shown exactly once, when the key is created.

docs.title: Who can manage keys
docs.text: Role Can Partner Create and revoke keys for the partner's own organization only; no access to other organizations Platform Create and delete keys for any organization

docs.title: Create a key
docs.text:
1. Open the API Keys page.
  2. Provide a label describing the key's purpose.
  3. Set an expiry in days, or choose for the key never to expire.
  4. Copy the plaintext key from the creation dialog immediately.

docs.title: Revoke or delete a key
docs.text:
A revoked key becomes invalid immediately; calls made with it to the Partner API return 401. Delete a key to remove it entirely.

Handle the secret carefully

The plaintext key is displayed only once in the creation dialog. Copy and save it immediately, and revoke it at once if it is ever leaked.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• BFF Users — console login accounts and roles.
  • Users — Exchange users and their keys.
  • Audit Log

docs.title: Audit Log
docs.text: The Audit Log module in NereidHorizon records operations and backend calls for security auditing and troubleshooting. Two views are available: the system log and the audit log.

docs.title: System log
docs.text:
The system log records:

  • Every API request from the front end to the backend — method, path, status code, duration, user, and organization.
  • Every call the backend makes to the Exchange — method, URL, status code, and duration.
  • Node registration events (node_register) and service startup events.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text: The audit log records only mutating operations — POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE — and is intended for operation audit.

docs.title: Search the logs
docs.text:
Filter entries by keywords such as user, path, or status code. The view is paginated for browsing long histories.

The log files live in the backend container as system.log and audit.log, written in JSON-lines format.

docs.title: Log fields
docs.text: Field Meaning t Timestamp in ISO format type api, exchange, or event m HTTP method p / url Request path / Exchange URL s HTTP status code ms Duration in milliseconds u User (org/username) o Organization

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Dashboard
  • Node Registration
  • BFF Users

docs.title: BFF Users
docs.text: The BFF Users module manages local login accounts for the NereidHorizon console — platform administrators and partners. These accounts authenticate people into the console itself; they are not Exchange users. Exchange users are managed on the Users page.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Role Capabilities Platform Create and manage all BFF users, including platform administrators and partners; operate across organizations Partner Bound to one Exchange organization; after sign-in can operate only on resources inside that organization

docs.title: Create a partner account
docs.text: Every partner account must be bound to an Exchange organization (org). If the specified organization does not exist when the partner is created, Horizon creates it automatically.

docs.title: Password and deletion rules
docs.text:
• A platform account can change any user's password; a non-platform user can only change their own.
  • You cannot delete the account you are currently signed in with.

docs.title: Choosing the right account type
docs.text:
• Use a BFF user for a person who signs in to the console.
  • Use an Exchange user for an identity that exists inside the hub, such as a node account.
  • Use an API key for a system that calls the read-only Partner API without a console sign-in.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Users
  • Organizations
  • API Keys

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text: The Catalog in NereidHorizon is a read-only browser for public services and patterns. It shows content published by the Hub and by remote organizations, so you can reference and reuse definitions across organization boundaries without leaving the console.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Browse the public services and patterns offered by the Hub and other organizations.
  • Click any item to open its details, which are shown as JSON.

The Catalog is a read-only view: it exists for discovery and reference. To create or change a service or pattern, use the Services and Patterns modules, or import a definition there after reviewing it in the Catalog.

docs.title: Browse the catalog
docs.text:
1. Open the Catalog page.
  2. Locate the public service or pattern you want to inspect.
  3. Click the item to view its full JSON definition.

docs.title: Access errors
docs.text:
Code Meaning and action 402 / 401 You do not have permission to access that organization's catalog; the required authorization must be granted first.

For cross-organization work that requires elevated credentials, use the Authorize action as described on the Agbots page.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Services
  • Patterns
  • Organizations
  • Agbots

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: The Dashboard is the default landing page after you sign in to NereidHorizon. It gives an at-a-glance view of the overall system status so you can confirm the hub is healthy and jump straight into daily operations. Horizon renders all Dashboard data from the Exchange API and refreshes it automatically every 30 seconds.

docs.title: What the page shows
docs.text:
• System Info card — Exchange version, BFF service start time and uptime, current organization, and online node count.
  • Quick Actions — card-style shortcuts that take you directly to functional modules such as services, patterns, and nodes.
  • Recent Node Activity — the edge nodes that most recently reported a heartbeat, sorted by last heartbeat time with the newest first.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. After sign-in, confirm the System Info card shows the expected Exchange version and your current organization.
  2. Check the online node count to see whether the fleet is connected.
  3. Review Recent Node Activity to spot nodes that have stopped reporting.
  4. Use Quick Actions to open the module you need instead of navigating the sidebar.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Connection failed

If the Dashboard shows a connection failure, verify that the Exchange URL is correct, that the network from Horizon to the Exchange is reachable, and that your login credentials are valid.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Edge Nodes
  • Node Registration
  • Audit Log

docs.title: Getting Started with NereidHorizon
docs.text:
NereidHorizon (Horizon) is the edge distribution console for the Open Horizon management hub: a graphical console for defining services and rolling them out to fleets of edge nodes through patterns or policies. For a product-level overview see the NereidHorizon product page.

This guide walks a first-time operator through the core journey: sign in, connect an edge node, define a service, deploy it with a pattern or a policy, and watch the resulting agreement and rollout.

docs.title: 1. Sign in and check the dashboard
docs.text:
1. Sign in to the Horizon console with your operator account.
  2. On the Dashboard, confirm the Exchange version, current organization, and online node count.
  3. Use Quick Actions to reach the modules in the steps below.

docs.title: 2. Register and connect an edge node
docs.text:
1. Prepare a machine running the anax agent and make sure it can reach the Exchange.
  2. On the Users page, create the node account and generate its API key (shown only once).
  3. On the node, run hzn register against a pattern or policy.
  4. Confirm the node appears as online on the Edge Nodes page.

The full command sequence and verification steps are in Node Registration.

docs.title: 3. Define or import a service
docs.text:
A service definition describes the container image and its deployment settings.

  • Create one on the Services page — name, label, version, architecture, and image are required.
  • Or import an existing definition by pasting JSON or uploading a .json file.

Horizon signs the deployment automatically, so no manual signing is needed.

docs.title: 4. Deploy with a pattern or a policy
docs.text:
Choose one of the two deployment models:

  • Pattern — a fixed set of services for a class of nodes. Create it on the Patterns page with at least one service, then register nodes to it.
  • Policy — constraint-matched deployment for dynamic environments. Create a deployment policy on the Deployment Policies page that targets a service and matches node properties.

In both cases, link the pattern or policy to an agbot; the node cannot negotiate a deployment until an agbot has it linked.

docs.title: 5. Watch the agreement and rollout
docs.text:
1. Open Agbots and check the Agreements tab for the new agreement.
  2. On Edge Nodes, open the node's drawer and inspect the Agreements and Services tabs.
  3. Watch the Errors tab if the rollout stalls, and confirm the result in the Audit Log, which records the node_register event and every hub call.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Edge Nodes and Node Registration
  • Services, Patterns, Deployment Policies
  • Agbots
  • Management Policies for agent upgrades and lifecycle actions
  • Organizations, BFF Users, API Keys for multi-tenant setup

docs.title: HA Groups
docs.text: An HA (high-availability) group in NereidHorizon organizes multiple edge nodes into a high-availability cluster so that services can be deployed redundantly across the group. Use HA groups when a workload must keep running even if one member node is lost.

docs.title: Create an HA group
docs.text:
1. Open the HA Groups page and start a new group.
  2. Enter a unique group name — this is required.
  3. Optionally add a description and choose member nodes.

docs.title: Edit membership
docs.text: In the edit view, add nodes to the group or remove existing members. Each node can belong to only one HA group, so a node already in another group cannot be added until it is removed there.

docs.title: Delete an HA group
docs.text: Remove all member nodes first; a group that still has members cannot be deleted.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 400 Group name missing or invalid 409 A group with that name already exists 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Edge Nodes
  • Services

docs.title: Management Policies
docs.text: A management policy (NMP) in NereidHorizon handles node upgrade and lifecycle management — for example agent upgrades and node configuration push. Management policies target nodes by constraint, and the result of their execution is visible on each node's Mgmt Status tab.

docs.title: Create a management policy
docs.text:
Required fields:

  • Policy Name
  • Label
  • Type — upgrade or lifecycle.

Optional fields:

  • Constraints — select the target nodes.
  • Properties — payload of the policy. For an agent upgrade, supply an agentUpgradePolicy, for example:
{ "type": "agent", "version": "2.30.0" }

docs.title: Edit and import
docs.text:
• Edit — updating the policy issues a PUT that replaces its configuration.
  • Import — paste the management policy JSON.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 400 Unsupported type, or a required field is missing 409 Policy already exists 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Edge Nodes — the Mgmt Status tab shows policy execution state.
  • Agent File Version — version lists that guide agent upgrades.
  • Deployment Policies

docs.title: Node Registration
docs.text: Edge nodes — machines running the anax agent — register with the Exchange through the hzn command line. After registration they pull their pattern or policy, negotiate an agreement, and deploy services. This guide follows that flow and shows where to verify each step in NereidHorizon.

docs.title: Phase 1: Prepare the node
docs.text:
1. Install the anax agent, for example with apt install horizon, or run anax in Docker.
  2. Confirm the node can reach the Exchange URL over the network.
  3. Generate an API key for the node account on the Users page. The key is shown only once.

docs.title: Phase 2: Register the node
docs.text:
On the node, run:

hzn exchange user create -u <org>/<user>:<apikey> -o <exchange-url>

Then register with a pattern or a policy:

hzn register -o <exchange-url> -u <org>/<user>:<apikey> \
  --name <node-name> \
  -p <org>/<pattern-name>    # or --policy <policy-file>

Use -p <org>/<pattern-name> for pattern deployment, or --policy <policy-file> for policy-based deployment.

docs.title: Phase 3: Negotiation and deployment
docs.text:
1. The node sends a proposal to an agbot.
  2. The agbot matches a linked pattern or policy and returns an agreement.
  3. The node pulls the service image and starts the container.
  4. The node continues to report a heartbeat.

Make sure the pattern or policy is linked to an agbot on the Agbots page; otherwise the negotiation cannot succeed.

docs.title: Phase 4: Verify in the UI
docs.text:
• The node appears in the Edge Nodes list with status Online.
  • The node detail's Services and Agreements tabs show the deployed services and agreements.
  • The Audit Log records a node_register event.

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause and action Node does not appear Check the API key, network reachability to the Exchange, and node time synchronization Agreement timeout (reason 201) Usually the node cannot persist state, for example an anax.db permission problem After a pattern change Re-register: hzn unregister -f && hzn register ...

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Edge Nodes
  • Patterns
  • Deployment Policies
  • Agbots
  • Users

docs.title: Edge Nodes
docs.text: The Edge Nodes module is where you manage the edge nodes registered to the hub in NereidHorizon. From this page you can view and search nodes, set a deployment pattern, edit node policy, and inspect agreements, errors, and management status. For how nodes first join the hub, see Node Registration.

docs.title: Step 1: View nodes
docs.text: The table lists every node with its ID, name, type, architecture, memory, deployment method, number of deployed services, privileged flag, last heartbeat, and status. The list supports search (by name, type, pattern, or architecture) and pagination.

docs.title: Step 2: Set a pattern
docs.text:
1. Click Set Pattern at the end of the node's row.
  2. Choose a deployment pattern from the dropdown. Pattern names use the org/patternname format.
  3. Leave the selection empty to clear the pattern and deploy the node by policy instead.

Authorizing a pattern change

Changing the pattern of a registered node requires root/root authorization — click Authorize and enter the root password. After the change you must re-register the node for it to take effect; Horizon generates the command for you.

docs.title: Step 3: View details
docs.text:
Click View to open the detail drawer, which has five tabs:

Tab Contents Info Basic information and the editable node policy Services Registered and deployed services with their agreement IDs Agreements All agreements currently reached for the node Errors Node error history Mgmt Status Execution status of management policies (NMP)

docs.title: Step 4: Edit node policy
docs.text:
• System properties under openhorizon.* are read-only.
  • Add custom Properties as Name=Value pairs, for example gpu=true.
  • Add Constraints, one per line, for example openhorizon.allowPrivileged == true.
  • The allowPrivileged switch controls whether privileged containers are allowed; changes take effect automatically after about 60 seconds.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning Action 401 Unauthorized Re-login or provide root authorization 400 Bad request Fix invalid parameters, such as an incorrectly formatted pattern 502 Exchange connection failed Check the Exchange URL and network

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Node Registration
  • Patterns
  • Deployment Policies
  • Agbots

docs.title: Organizations
docs.text: An organization is the top-level isolation unit in the Exchange. In NereidHorizon each organization owns its own services, patterns, nodes, and related resources, so operations performed inside one organization do not affect the others.

docs.title: Create an organization
docs.text:
Required fields:

  • Org ID — unique identifier.
  • Label — display name.

Optional fields:

  • Description.
  • Node count limit.
  • Heartbeat interval.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
• Hub Admin users can create and delete organizations.
  • The system organization (IBM) has a global view across the hub.

When you create partner accounts under BFF Users, a partner bound to an organization can only operate on resources within that organization.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 400 Org ID missing 409 Organization already exists 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• BFF Users
  • Catalog
  • Edge Nodes

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text: A deployment pattern in NereidHorizon defines the deployment topology and version strategy for a set of services. A node registered to a pattern automatically pulls up the services the pattern contains. Use patterns when the same fixed set of services should run together on a class of nodes; for attribute-matched deployment, see Deployment Policies instead.

docs.title: Create a pattern
docs.text:
Required fields:

  • Pattern Name — for example my-pattern.
  • Label — display name.
  • Services — select at least one service from the checkbox list.

A description is optional. For each selected service Horizon generates the serviceOrgid, serviceArch, serviceVersions (default version), and nodeHealth entries automatically, with a default ping_interval of 60.

docs.title: Edit a pattern
docs.text: Editing replaces all service references in the pattern. You can edit the JSON directly or select services with the checkboxes in the UI.

docs.title: Import and inspect
docs.text:
• Import — paste the pattern JSON.
  • Detail drawer — two tabs: Info shows the pattern JSON, and Node Health shows the health of associated nodes.

docs.title: Associate the pattern with an agbot
docs.text:
Required after creating a pattern

A pattern only reaches nodes after it is linked to an agreement bot. On the Agbots page, associate the new pattern with the corresponding agbot so nodes can negotiate it.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 400 No service selected — at least one is required 409 Pattern already exists 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Services
  • Deployment Policies
  • Agbots
  • Node Registration

docs.title: Deployment Policies
docs.text: A deployment policy (business policy) in NereidHorizon is an automatic service-deployment rule based on properties and constraints. Policies suit flexible deployments that do not depend on a fixed pattern: the agbot matches the policy against each eligible node instead of the node joining a fixed service set.

docs.title: Create a policy
docs.text:
Required fields:

  • Policy Name
  • Label
  • Target Service — the URL of the service to deploy.

Optional fields:

  • Properties — characteristics describing the service.
  • Constraints — matching rules, for example openhorizon.allowPrivileged == true.
  • Service Org, Service Arch, and the service version range.

docs.title: Import a policy
docs.text: Paste the policy JSON into the importer. The JSON must include the businessPolicy wrapper.

docs.title: Policy versus pattern
docs.text: A pattern is a fixed set of services: every node registered to the pattern runs the same set. A policy is constraint-matched deployment, which fits dynamic environments where different nodes run a service depending on their attributes. After creating a policy, link it to an agbot on the Agbots page so it can be negotiated.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 400 Missing target service, or invalid constraint format 409 Policy already exists 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Patterns
  • Services
  • Agbots
  • Edge Nodes

docs.title: Services
docs.text: The Services module manages service definitions in NereidHorizon. A service definition describes the container image, deployment configuration, and resource limits that an edge node needs to run a workload. You can create, edit, import, and export definitions here.

docs.title: Create a service
docs.text:
In the Basic Info panel, the following fields are required:

Field Description Example Service Name Unique identifier myweather Label Display name My Weather Service Version Semantic version 1.0.0 Architecture Target architecture amd64, arm64, arm Image name Container image in name:tag form openhorizon/example:1.0.0

Optional settings include the service URL, HA mode, shared block device, privileged mode, memory/CPU limits, ports, health check, network, storage, environment variables, and secrets.

A minimal service definition looks like this:

{
  "label": "My Service",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "arch": "amd64",
  "deployment": {
    "services": {
      "myorg/myservice": { "image": "myorg/myservice:1.0.0" }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Edit a service
docs.text: Editing offers two modes: a JSON editor and a UI form. The two are synchronized automatically when you switch tabs. When you change the deployment in UI mode, Horizon re-signs the deployment automatically.

docs.title: Import and inspect
docs.text:
• Import — paste service JSON directly or upload a .json file.
  • Detail drawer — three tabs: Info, Keys, and Docker Auths. Keys manages the service public key; Docker Auths manages credentials for private registries.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text: Horizon signs the deployment automatically with RSA-PSS SHA-256, so there is no manual signing step.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 400 Malformed JSON, or a required field is missing (label/version/arch/image) 409 A service with the same name and version already exists 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Patterns
  • Deployment Policies
  • Node Registration

docs.title: Users
docs.text: The Users module manages Exchange users in NereidHorizon: creating users, changing passwords, and managing their API keys. These are identities inside the Exchange — for example node accounts used during node registration. Console login accounts (platform administrators and partners) are managed separately under BFF Users.

docs.title: Create a user
docs.text:
Required fields:

  • Username — unique identifier, for example alice.
  • Password — must be set at creation time.

Optional fields:

  • Email
  • Admin — whether the user is an administrator.

docs.title: Change a password
docs.text: Click Change Password next to the username and enter the new password.

docs.title: Manage API keys
docs.text: Generate a key from the user's detail view. The key is shown only once when it is created — save it immediately. Administrators can manage other users' keys. Node registration uses such a key for the node account's credentials.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 400 Username or password missing 409 User already exists 502 Exchange unreachable

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• BFF Users — local console login accounts.
  • API Keys — partner API keys for the read-only Partner API.
  • Node Registration
  • Organizations

docs.title: Getting Started with NereidIdentity
docs.text:
NereidIdentity is the suite-wide identity plane: the shared, replaceable single sign-on (SSO) and access-control centre behind Sphere, Link, Horizon and Forge. The current engine is Keycloak 26 with a dedicated PostgreSQL, using the nereidai realm. The engine is an implementation detail behind a standard OIDC/OAuth2 contract, not a portal that users open directly.

You rarely touch Identity directly

Identity is a backend service. In the default integration only Sphere speaks OIDC to it: users sign in through Sphere, and administrators manage accounts from Sphere's account console. A product deployed without the suite may instead register its own OIDC client.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A deployed, reachable Identity instance (its issuer URL) and a Sphere portal configured against it.
  • To sign in: an account in the suite realm, assigned by an administrator.
  • To administer accounts: the suite Administrator role in Sphere.

docs.title: 1. Understand where Identity fits
docs.text:
• Identity is the single source of truth for accounts, roles and tokens.
  • Sphere is the only mandatory OIDC relying party: it drives the browser login (authorization-code + PKCE) and hands identity to integrated products, by default through a one-time sealed ticket.
  • Products keep their own authorization. RBAC, tenancy and feature permissions live inside each product; a suite identity proves who you are, and per-product assignment groups grant entry.

See SSO & OIDC for the full model.

docs.title: 2. Sign in as a user
docs.text:
1. Open the Sphere portal and click Sign in with NereidIdentity.
  2. Enter your credentials on the Identity login page, or choose a brokered organization provider (such as Entra ID or Okta) if one is configured.
  3. You return to Sphere with a suite session and can open every product you are assigned to, without signing in again.

Suite users never sign in to the Keycloak administration console.

docs.title: 3. Manage users as an administrator
docs.text:
1. In Sphere, open the user menu and choose Accounts.
  2. Create users, reset passwords, enable or disable accounts, and assign suite roles and per-product tenant/role memberships.
  3. Accounts provisioned from an external identity provider are tagged as external and are read-only here — manage their lifecycle in that provider.

Sphere performs these operations through a service-account client against the Identity Admin REST API, so administrators do not need the engine's master credentials.

docs.title: 4. Operate the service
docs.text:
Identity ships as a container image with a Helm chart for the central deployment and a Docker Compose stack for development. Realms, clients and the admin service-account grant are provisioned declaratively from the Identity repository; customer identity systems are always connected behind Identity through identity brokering, never directly to Sphere or a product.

Where the operational detail lives

Realm provisioning, client registration, brokered-IdP setup and operational runbooks are documented in the NereidIdentity repository (NereidAI), not in this operator guide.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• SSO & OIDC — modes, tickets and federation.
  • RBAC — suite roles and product-local authorization.
  • NereidIdentity product page.

docs.title: Account Security
docs.text: The Account Security page (under the account menu) protects your own login identity. It manages two-factor authentication and lists active login sessions.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication (TOTP)
docs.text:
• When TOTP is disabled, choose Enable and scan the QR code with an authenticator app (or copy the secret manually).
  • Enter the six-digit code the app shows to finish enrollment. NereidLink then displays a set of recovery codes. Save them somewhere safe: each code lets you log in once if you lose the authenticator. Recovery codes are shown only once.
  • While TOTP is enabled, every login requires both your password and a current code.
  • Choose Disable to remove the second factor.

docs.title: Login sessions
docs.text:
The session list shows every session created with your credentials: client user agent, source IP address, creation time, expiry time, and whether the session is currently active.

  • Your current session is marked and cannot be revoked from this page.
  • Revoke any other session to sign that client out immediately. Revoking a session does not change your password; if you suspect account compromise, revoke the unfamiliar sessions and change your password as well.

Session management applies to your identity across every tenant you belong to; an administrator cannot enable TOTP on your behalf.

docs.title: Single sign-on (SSO / OIDC)
docs.text:
When an external identity provider (such as Keycloak, Authing or Entra ID) is configured by the operator, the login page shows a Sign in with SSO button alongside the email/password form.

  • Clicking it redirects you to your identity provider. After you approve, you return automatically and are signed in; you do not create a password in NereidLink.
  • Your account is created on first login and assigned a role from the identity-provider group your administrator configured. If your groups are not mapped to a role, sign-in is refused; ask your administrator.
  • Sign-out and session/recovery behavior on this page apply to SSO sessions too. MFA for SSO users is enforced by the identity provider, not here.

docs.title: Suite single sign-on (NereidSphere ticket)
docs.text:
When the deployment is joined to a NereidSphere (NS) suite portal, the normal entry point is the portal: open the product there, and NS redirects you back with a one-time ticket that is exchanged automatically. If you land on the NereidLink login page directly, it shows a Sign in with NereidSphere button that returns you to the portal.

  • The ticket is single-use and expires in 30 seconds. Using the browser Back button or refreshing the callback page fails with an "expired or already used" message; start again from the portal.
  • Your identity, roles and email verification come from the identity plane through NS; you still get an ordinary NereidLink session afterwards.
  • The suite administrator assigns you one role per tenant. Those assignments take effect on every login and are reconciled automatically: if an assignment is removed in the suite console, your access to that tenant is removed on your next login. Locally managed customer-level access is not affected.
  • If your email matches the platform administrator account, you sign in as that administrator; otherwise a tenant account is provisioned on first login.

docs.title: NereidLink Adapter SDK for Go
docs.text:
The Adapter SDK lets developers add a new southbound wire protocol to NereidLink as a separate project or repository. An adapter translates one wire protocol into platform contracts; it owns no command state machine and stores no authoritative state.

This is different from the Device SDK: the Device SDK is used inside device/gateway firmware, while the Adapter SDK is used to build a new ingress connector that runs with or alongside the platform.

Developer documentation

This page introduces the model and lifecycle. The package API and the complete reference adapters live in the NereidLink repository under sdk/ and adapters/ — see NereidAI.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Package Purpose sdk/adapter Lifecycle: config loading, enrollment, heartbeats, presence client, command dispatcher, request-based sessions / mailbox relay sdk/contract Stable wire contract: dispatch/event subject prefixes, command statuses, interaction modes, lifecycle Event sdk/telemetry Telemetry uplink: JSON frame → typed points → one Envelope per point → JetStream partition; stream ensuring; binary media offload via an injectable MediaStore (blob:// references) sdk/registry Registry gRPC client for device authentication sdk/profile Optional profile-descriptor resolution (PostgreSQL-backed, cached) and raw-to-engineering conversion sdk/partition Immutable partition topology used by the uplink sdk/scriptruntime JavaScript runtime used by expression descriptors api/gen/nereidlink/v1 Generated protobuf message types

The SDK has no dependency on the server's internal/ tree. Breaking changes to SDK packages follow semantic versioning; internal packages may change at any time.

docs.title: Adapter lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Load the shared config and connect to NATS (Core + JetStream).
  2. Optionally ensure telemetry streams with telemetry.EnsureStreams.
  3. adapter.Enroll(...) with the module type, ingress ID, and version.
  4. Start presence (Run) and subscribe to command dispatch.
  5. Translate protocol traffic into telemetry.Publish calls; translate dispatched commands into protocol writes; reply through the command handler. When the protocol carries binary payloads, implement telemetry.MediaStore against your storage and pass telemetry.WithMediaStore(...); frame data fields stay base64 and published points reference the object as blob://<key>.
  6. On graceful shutdown, disconnect sessions and let heartbeats stop.

A complete annotated skeleton is provided by adapters/template; the built-in CoAP adapter (adapters/coap) is a full reference implementation.

docs.title: Starting an external project
docs.text:
mkdir myadapter && cd myadapter
go mod init github.com/example/myadapter
go get github.com/nereidai/nereidlink@v0.0.1

Copy adapters/template/main.go as your main.go. Only the SDK packages listed above are needed — never import internal/ from an external module (Go forbids it).

docs.title: Shared configuration
docs.text:
core:
  nats_url: nats://127.0.0.1:4222
  nats_user: module
  nats_password: module-password
  registry_grpc: 127.0.0.1:19090
  registry_token: dev-module-token
  management_url: http://127.0.0.1:8080
  postgres_dsn: ""            # optional; enables descriptor resolution
module:
  enrollment_token: my-enrollment-token
  heartbeat_interval: 10s

Protocol-specific configuration is the adapter's responsibility: parse the same YAML file with an additional wrapper struct.

docs.title: Contract invariants
docs.text:
• Arrays in API responses are always [], never null.
  • The platform never invents semantics (for example units) — they come only from user-defined descriptors.
  • Keep processing-plane logic off the connection plane, and keep business logic out of the adapter: tenants define rules in the platform.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Device SDK (Go) — embed the client in device/gateway firmware.
  • Integrate a gateway and the connector glossary — how adapters surface as connectors managed from the console.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.text: The Alarms page is the alarm lifecycle and audit center.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
• Live — alarms currently ACTIVE or ACK.
  • Individual states: ACTIVE, ACK or CLEARED.
  • Optionally filter by device, severity (CRITICAL, MAJOR, MINOR, WARNING), alarm type and assignee (including Unassigned).
  • All active filters are reflected in the URL so the filtered view can be bookmarked or shared.

docs.title: Acknowledging
docs.text: Select Ack on a live alarm to mark it acknowledged. Acknowledging records the acknowledgment time; acknowledged alarms remain live until cleared. Acknowledging an already-ACK alarm is a no-op.

docs.title: How alarms are created
docs.text: Alarms are opened by the Create Alarm node in a rule chain. Repeated events with the same dedupe key update the open alarm instead of creating duplicates; clearing requires the Clear Alarm node.

docs.title: Command Center
docs.text: The Command Center tracks commands across every device in the tenant.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
• Search by command name or a partial device name or alias.
  • State filter: choose one lifecycle state, or In flight for every non-terminal state (PENDING, CLAIMED, QUEUED).

docs.title: Lifecycle states
docs.text:
• PENDING / QUEUED — waiting for delivery.
  • CLAIMED — an ingress has taken responsibility for delivery.
  • DELIVERED — sent to the connected device.
  • SUCCEEDED — the device returned a successful response.
  • FAILED / TIMEOUT / NOT_CONNECTED / EXPIRED — terminal failure reasons.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text: Each row shows the creation time (formatted per the selected console language), device canonical name with its alias shown beneath (linked to its detail page), command name, interaction mode (one-way or request-response), timeliness (realtime or persistent) and current state.

docs.title: Batch command form
docs.text:
• Target — a device group (select from the group list) or explicit devices; the explicit list is a searchable dropdown populated with device names, not a free-form UUID field.
  • Timeout — prefilled with a 30-second reference value; override as needed.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text: The Connectors tab is available on gateway devices. It manages protocol connector instances running on that gateway using a declarative desired/reported model (ADR-0026).

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• NereidLink is the system of record. You declare a desired spec, and the edge gateway reports back what it has actually applied.
  • A desired spec is {connector_type, type_version, config, mappings}.
  • connector_type — the connector plugin type, for example modbus-tcp. New connector types are registered by the edge; the kernel never interprets protocol details.
  • type_version — plugin version; leave empty to use the highest registered version.
  • config — a JSON object validated against the edge-registered schema for the connector type.
  • mappings — a JSON array of objects; every object must contain a non-empty string key naming the telemetry point the connector maps to. The editor suggests that key (and each EdgeX auto event's source name) from the bound profile's descriptor measurement keys; you can still type any value. Additional properties are connector-specific (register address, source name, and so on).
  • Two-level configuration: a profile stores the reusable template / point table, and a connector instance stores per-device connection parameters. At dispatch the instance overrides are merged over the profile template. A connector can therefore be created without a profile by filling config and mappings directly.
  • A connector is either gateway-level (no bound device) or bound to one of the gateway's managed sub-devices.

docs.title: Built-in type: nereid-edge
docs.text:
nereid-edge is always present in the type picker, even before any gateway registers a schema. It identifies the built-in NereidEdge runtime (the EdgeX App Service), whose behavior is hard-wired, so its config and mappings are usually left as the defaults — {} and []. Other types (for example modbus-tcp, onvif, mqtt-remote) only appear once a connected gateway registers them, but you may still type any custom value.

For EdgeX-family connector types (nereid-edge and the edge-connector/edgex-* aliases) the structured editor renders the standard EdgeX device fields (the v4 device contract NereidEdge applies to core-metadata): device service name (ds_name), EdgeX profile name, device name, description, labels, protocols and auto events (advanced fields such as tags and properties remain editable in the JSON tab). On a gateway, the EdgeX profile name is a searchable pick-and-type box populated from the profiles that gateway has reported (v1/gateway/profiles); pick one and each auto event's source name is then offered from that profile's device resources. You can always type a value that was not reported. Protocols are one card per EdgeX protocol key. When the bound profile (or the profile-template selection) declares a known protocol family, the card offers structured connection fields and a transport selector (for Modbus: modbus-tcp/modbus-rtu/modbus-ascii with Address/Port/UnitID, serial BaudRate/DataBits/StopBits/Parity on RTU/ASCII, and timeout fields); the same dictionary also renders ONVIF (Onvif: Address/Port/MACAddress/FriendlyName/EndpointRefAddress), MQTT (mqtt: CommandTopic), REST (REST: Host/Port/Path/urlRawQuery), device-virtual (other: Address/Port), SNMP (TCP: Address/Port), BACnet (BACnet-IP/BACnet-MSTP: DeviceInstance/Port/MAC) and CoAP (COAP: ED_ADDR/ED_SecurityMode/ED_PskKey); extra keys stay editable as typed pairs. For an unknown family you pick modbus-tcp/opcua/mqtt/… or type a custom key, and every property value is typed as string, number or boolean. Auto events cover the full EdgeX AutoEvent shape: interval (e.g. 10s), source name, an onChange switch that reveals its threshold, and an advanced retention section (maxCap, minCap, duration). When an instance targets one bound sub-device and the EdgeX device name is left blank, the console fills it on save with that sub-device's NL name (canonical_name). On a bulk create over several sub-devices (multi-select or Select all in device scope), a blank device name is filled per device: every created connector gets its own sub-device's NL name, so each edge device is named correctly. The name is sanitized to EdgeX-legal characters (alphanumerics, _, -); characters such as the / in an auto-provisioned name like <gateway>/<local_id> become -. Typing an explicit device name always overrides this default.

docs.title: Writing config and mappings
docs.text:
Each JSON field opens in a split editor: structured inputs on the left and a read-only live JSON document on the right. A JSON mode remains the escape hatch for keys no structured field covers; switching back requires the text to parse and satisfy the entry contract (object vs array, and the edge-registered JSON Schema when available).

For a connector instance bound to a profile template, the structured side edits only this instance's overrides, while the right pane previews the effective document — the profile template deep-merged with the override, exactly as it will be dispatched (objects merge key by key; arrays and scalars replace; a non-empty instance mappings array replaces the template list).

config is a JSON object; mappings is a JSON array whose items are objects that each carry a non-empty string key. The exact other keys depend on the connector type and are validated by the edge against the schema it registered — the platform does not interpret them.

Built-in nereid-edge (config/mappings can stay default):

{ }

[ ]

A typical Modbus TCP connector:

{ "host": "192.168.1.10", "port": 502, "unit_id": 1, "byte_order": "BIG" }

[
  { "register": "40001", "key": "voltage" },
  { "register": "40002", "key": "current" }
]

With two-level configuration, put the common part (bus settings, point table) in the profile template and only the per-device differences (this PLC's host/port) in the instance config; objects are deep-merged and a non-empty instance mappings array replaces the template array.

docs.title: Lifecycle state
docs.text: PENDING → DISPATCHED → CREATING → APPLIED, with FAILED or DEGRADED as terminal/degraded outcomes. Desired specs are never dropped: the edge retries on reconnect, and dispatch is idempotent. Hover a state tag to see the reported reason.

docs.title: Reconciliation
docs.text:
The gateway periodically sends a manifest listing the connector instances it actually runs. The tab compares that reported set against the desired set and classifies each spec:

  • In sync — desired and reported match.
  • Missing — desired but not present on the gateway.
  • Stale — the reported revision is behind the desired revision.
  • Drifted — present, but its reported config differs from desired.
  • Extra — running on the gateway but not declared in NereidLink.

By default drift only raises an alert; in strict reconcile mode the desired spec overrides the edge. Until the gateway sends its first manifest there is no watermark, so classification shows as unknown and an informational banner is displayed. The tab has no refresh button: it stays live over the WebSocket connector stream, re-fetching the list and reconcile view whenever the gateway reports a desired/status/manifest change.

The Device profile / protocol column names the device profile behind the connector (the bound profile template, falling back to the bound sub-device's profile) with a link to its detail page, and its protocol family underneath when known; it shows - when no profile resolves.

The Bound sub-device column links to the bound device with its alias underneath; gateway-level instances show a gateway-level tag instead.

docs.title: Filtering and searching
docs.text:
The toolbar above the table is right-aligned and filters locally over the gateway's connector set:

  • Connector type, reported state, reconcile state and target (gateway-level vs bound sub-device) dropdowns.
  • A search box matching connector type, type version, profile name/protocol and bound sub-device name (case-insensitive, partial).

Filtering never changes the data; clear a dropdown or the search box to return to the full list.
