docs.title: Working with connectors
docs.text:
1. Open a gateway device and select the Connectors tab.
  2. Click Add, choose (or type) the connector type, and optionally a type version.
  3. Optionally pick a profile template — only profiles carrying a connector template are listed — and/or a bound sub-device.
  4. Edit the config object and point mappings using the structured Form tab (or raw JSON tab); the save button stays disabled until both are valid, then save.
  5. Edit or delete a row as needed; after deletion the edge removes the instance on the next manifest reconciliation.

To define a reusable connector template, edit a device profile and fill its connector template fields; see the Device Profiles help topic.

docs.title: Liveness probe (health check)
docs.text:
A connector bound to one sub-device can run an application-layer liveness probe. Enable Liveness probe in the connector drawer and fill:

  • Probe resource — the south read resource/command name to ping.
  • Interval — probe cadence in milliseconds (default 30000).
  • Read timeout — per-probe timeout in milliseconds; must stay below the interval (default 5000).
  • Fail threshold — consecutive failures that mark the bound device offline (default 3); the next successful probe marks it online again.

The gateway periodically reads the resource and discards the value — a probe never produces telemetry or shadow data. Connect/disconnect is asserted by the gateway itself, exactly like an operator observing the field bus. The policy lives on the connector instance (not on the profile template) because probing is a per-device operational choice; disable the switch to stop probing.

docs.title: Device Credentials
docs.text: The Credentials tab manages how a device proves its identity. A device cannot connect until it holds at least one valid credential.

docs.title: Credential types
docs.text:
Each type proves possession in a different way, and the type is fixed at creation:

Type How possession is proven Typical use TOKEN A random shared secret, compared in constant time. Simulators and simple scripts. PASSWORD A password stored as an argon2id hash. Devices that already speak username/password. JWT A signed JSON Web Token; issuer, subject and audience are enforced on every connection. Fleets that already have an identity provider. X509 A client certificate at the mTLS layer; the registered certificate must be exactly the presented leaf. Production devices with a certificate from your own CA.

Secrets are write-only. A newly created secret is shown exactly once and cannot be recovered afterwards — a stored password is an argon2id hash, so the plaintext is unrecoverable by design. Copy and store it securely at creation time.

docs.title: Credential ID
docs.text: When you add a credential, the Credential ID is pre-filled from the device's technical canonical name and the credential type: <canonical_name>_token, _password, _cert or _jwt (for example dev-a3f9k2x7_token). Switching the type re-derives the ID until you edit the field by hand; after that your value is kept. You can always replace it with any non-empty ID that is unique on the device (it is also globally unique across the platform). For X.509 credentials the ID doubles as the MQTT username and the certificate common name.

docs.title: Validity window
docs.text:
Every credential carries an effective time and an optional expiry. It only authenticates when it is ACTIVE and inside its window and the device and tenant are themselves active. Leave the window empty for a credential that is effective immediately and never expires.

A background scanner raises escalating warnings as a credential approaches expiry, tied to a single stable alarm per credential rather than one alarm per threshold.

docs.title: Rotation with overlap
docs.text:
Rotation replaces a secret without dropping the device offline:

  1. Create the new credential — the old one is still valid.
  2. Move the device to the new secret.
  3. Disable or delete the old credential.

Because both are valid during the overlap, the device never has to reconnect mid-rotation.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• Enable / Disable — toggles whether the credential may authenticate. Disabling does not delete it.
  • Rotate — issue a new secret for an existing credential. Leave the secret field empty to keep the current secret and only change the validity window.
  • Revoke all — disables every credential of this device and ends its live session. Use this to cut off a device you no longer trust.
  • Delete — removes a single credential.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A revoked or expired credential fails closed: no fallback to another credential is attempted.
  • Disabling a credential ends nothing by itself; use Revoke all when you also want the live session dropped.

docs.title: Customers and device groups
docs.text: Customers and device groups organize devices inside one tenant.

docs.title: Hierarchy
docs.text: Tenant → Customers → Devices. Device groups are optional containers under the tenant or a customer.

docs.title: Customers
docs.text:
A customer is an organization (for example a client company), with optional contact name, contact email and external ID.

  • Assign a device to a customer when creating or editing it, or move it later from the device lifecycle menu (Transfer).
  • Click a customer name on this page to list its devices.
  • Members with the CUSTOMER_USER role only see devices of the customer they belong to.

docs.title: Device groups
docs.text:
A group is a named set of devices. A group may be anchored to a customer and may have a parent group, forming a tree; cycles are rejected.

  • Assign devices to a group in the device form.
  • Click a group name to list its devices.
  • Groups are used for filtering and later batch operations.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• One device belongs to at most one customer and one group.
  • Customers or groups with assigned devices cannot be deleted; reassign the devices first.
  • Unassigned devices stay visible in the full device list.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text: A dashboard is a saved grid of widgets that reads live from the platform. Widgets pull their data over the same WebSocket connection as the rest of the console — there is no polling.

docs.title: Manage dashboards
docs.text:
Each row shows the name, the widget count and the actions.

  • New dashboard — create an empty dashboard.
  • Edit layout — open the layout editor: add widgets, move and resize them, then save. The saved layout is stored with the dashboard.
  • Rename — change the display name. The name must be unique in the tenant.
  • Delete — remove the dashboard and its layout.

docs.title: Widget types
docs.text:
• Timeseries chart — plots one measurement key of one device (or the aggregate across devices) over a chosen time window.
  • Latest value — shows the most recent value of a measurement key as a single number.
  • Alarm list — lists recent alarms so an operator sees incidents without leaving the dashboard.

docs.title: Configure a widget
docs.text:
Every widget takes a title, and the data widgets additionally take a device (unbound means all devices), a measurement key and, for charts, a time window. A widget whose measurement has no data renders empty rather than failing.

Dashboards are pushed to every connected session, so an edit is visible without a reload.

docs.title: Data Quality
docs.text: Every telemetry point carries a quality marker. It answers a different question than the device's connection state: connection state tells you whether the device is online, while quality tells you whether an individual value that arrived is trustworthy.

docs.title: The three markers
docs.text: Marker Meaning When it is produced GOOD Valid, in range, converted successfully. The default for every accepted point. UNCERTAIN Questionable but still usable. Never assigned by the platform — only a tenant's storage hook or script can set it. BAD Invalid or unusable. Set when a descriptor transform fails, or when the converted value falls outside the descriptor's valid range.

docs.title: How a point is marked
docs.text:
• A well-formed boolean, string or number is GOOD by default.
  • A number with no matching profile descriptor is stored unconverted and stays GOOD — the platform does not guess.
  • When a profile descriptor applies a transform (linear, lookup table, expression, enum, identity):
  • if the transform raises an error, the point is BAD;
  • if the resulting engineering value is outside the descriptor's valid_min/valid_max (when set), the point is BAD;
  • otherwise it is GOOD.
  • Text results (for example an enum label) always count as in range; only numeric results are range-checked.
  • A tenant can rewrite the marker in a storage hook script by returning a quality field.

The marker is stored with the point, returned by telemetry queries, exposed to rule chains as metadata.quality, and shown as a colored tag in a device's All measurements table (GOOD green, otherwise red).

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A device can be perfectly online and still report a value you should not act on — a failed sensor, a value outside its physical range, or a broken calibration expression. Quality lets dashboards, alarms and rule chains tell "a number arrived" apart from "the number is sound", so a faulty reading can be stored for diagnosis without driving an alert.

docs.title: Device Detail
docs.text: The device detail page shows everything known about one device.

docs.title: Header
docs.text:
• Canonical name, device ID, profile ID and current connection state. When the device has an alias, the header subtitle shows the alias instead of the ID.
  • The summary panel shows every binding of the device:
  • Customer — the owning customer; empty means unassigned. The name links to the Customers page.
  • Device group — the one device group this device belongs to (groups form a tree and may be anchored to a customer); links to the device list filtered to that group.
  • Rule chain — the chain group that actually applies to this device, resolved by priority: device binding, then profile binding, then the tenant default group. A tag states the binding source; the version tag shows the active version, or a No active version warning when the resolved group has no active chain. The name opens the chain editor.
  • Profile ID — links to the bound profile. Use the Edit button in the header to change any of these bindings in the device form drawer.
  • The summary panel also shows additional information, plus created at and last activity (the latest telemetry or presence boundary, whichever is newer). The alias is shown only in the header subtitle, not repeated in the panel.
  • A sub-device summary includes a Connector line: its one bound connector instance with reported apply state, linking to the owning gateway's Connectors tab; a gateway shows the count badge of its gateway-level connector instances.
  • The status badge reflects the latest presence event (online/offline/unknown).

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Real-time telemetry pushed over the WebSocket. Select a measurement key to follow one measurement. Historical values load through the telemetry history query. The All measurements table shows each value's quality marker (GOOD, UNCERTAIN or BAD); see the Data Quality help topic under Configuration for what they mean.

A string value shaped blob://... references a media object the device uploaded (see direct-device integration). The table renders it by the object's declared type: an image thumbnail (click to enlarge), a play button that opens a video player, a text viewer for text/JSON/XML (first 256 KiB inline), or a download button for other binaries. Each object is reached through a short-lived signed URL; if the object was deleted, the cell shows an "object no longer exists" note.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attributes are relatively static per-device key/value metadata, suited to install location, business grouping, sampling interval, feature flags and similar small configuration. They differ from high-frequency telemetry and from the versioned desired/reported shadow: the platform only stores and synchronizes the values, while NereidEdge/firmware decides how an attribute is consumed.

The three scopes are:

  • CLIENT: device-owned data written by the device or rule chains. It is shown read-only in the console and cannot be added, edited or deleted here.
  • SHARED_SCOPE: written by the platform and pushed over MQTT to an online device/gateway; devices also pull it after reconnecting. Configuration that the edge must read and apply belongs in this scope.
  • SERVER_SCOPE: platform-side attributes written by the platform.

Current scope semantics: this NereidLink version currently delivers both SERVER_SCOPE and SHARED_SCOPE to devices — via live attributes/down|push and the post-reconnect attributes/get. This differs from the classic ThingsBoard model, where SERVER_SCOPE is platform-private and only SHARED_SCOPE is visible to devices. Do not treat SERVER_SCOPE as device-invisible private data today; use SHARED_SCOPE for configuration the edge should consume. For gateway-attached sub-devices, platform attributes are also mirrored into EdgeX device Tags; when the same key exists in both scopes, the SHARED_SCOPE value wins.

Add or edit SERVER_SCOPE/SHARED_SCOPE attributes with any valid JSON value. The actions column offers edit and delete; deleting removes the row immediately and pushes a JSON null change to a connected edge, which evicts the local cache key. The table updates live over the WebSocket: edits/deletes from another operator session and device-reported CLIENT values appear immediately without refreshing.

docs.title: Shadow
docs.text: Desired versus reported state for this device, with a write path for desired state. The view updates live over the WebSocket: desired changes from another operator session and device-reported state appear immediately without refreshing. See the Device Shadow help topic under Devices.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text: Every credential this device holds, its type, validity window and status, plus create, rotate, disable and revoke actions. See the Device Credentials help topic under Devices.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: The device command catalog (whitelist) and command history. Only declared commands can be sent — an undeclared name is rejected. Each catalog entry records its interaction (one-way/request-response), timeliness, default timeout, enabled switch and the allowed direction(s) (read/write); entries tagged auto are materialized from the bound profile's points and become manual once edited. When sending, pick the command (bound profile points are shown with their read/write mask), choose read or write (the choice is limited by the catalog mask), and always review the JSON parameters box ({} by default; reads may carry query parameters). Profile points without a catalog entry can be declared inline from the send drawer. History shows direction and state; open a row to inspect parameters, response and error.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.text: Alarm audit rows for this device with type, severity, state and timestamps.

docs.title: Connector & secrets (sub-device only)
docs.text: A read-only view for a gateway-managed sub-device of the two platform surfaces its connection depends on. Bound connector shows the single connector instance bound to this sub-device (matched from the owning gateway's connector set): type and version, reported apply state (hover for the reason), desired/reported revision and last report time. Secret delivery lists every secret binding the owning gateway holds — secret, type, target selectors and status — with a note that selectors are open {kind, value} pairs interpreted by the edge, so a binding may or may not apply to this device. Both sections link to the owning gateway's Connectors and Secrets tabs, where delivery is actually managed. This tab is shown only for sub-devices; see the Connectors and Edge secrets help topics under Devices.

docs.title: Firmware OTA (direct devices only)
docs.text: Shown only for a directly connected device (not a gateway and not a gateway-managed sub-device). It lists every firmware rollout that targeted this device, newest first: target version, the device's current phase, progress bar, the parent rollout's aggregate state and creation time. Open Timeline to see the append-only phase history with the structured result code and who reported each phase. Upgrade this device starts a single-device rollout — the target is locked to this device; pick a platform-hosted package or supply an external URL, and a success policy. Direct devices discover the job by polling an authenticated endpoint and download the bytes through the authorized relay. Fleet-wide rollouts and task-level pause/cancel live on the Upgrade Tasks page; see the OTA tasks help topic under Operations.

docs.title: Managed devices (gateway only)
docs.text: Sub-devices whose presence is declared by this gateway. This tab is shown only for gateway devices. Each row links to the sub-device and shows its alias beneath the name, its profile (links to the profile), the bound connector (links to this gateway's Connectors tab), the connection status (hover for last activity), and the lifecycle state. The search box matches name, alias or device id.

docs.title: Connectors (gateway only)
docs.text: Protocol connector instances running on this gateway, managed as desired/reported specs with drift reconciliation. This tab is shown only for gateway devices; see the Connectors help topic under Devices.

docs.title: Link health (gateway only)
docs.text: The history of this gateway's link outages rendered as time intervals — when each drop started, how long it lasted and whether the lease detector or the edge watchdog detected it. This tab is shown only for gateway devices; see the Link health help topic.

docs.title: Secrets (gateway only)
docs.text: The edge secrets (vault references) delivered to this gateway and their per-binding delivery status, including the secret types the edge registers. This tab is shown only for gateway devices; see the Edge secrets and Edge secret types help topics.

docs.title: Edge profiles (gateway only)
docs.text: The device profiles this gateway has reported over MQTT, cached per gateway, with content/inspect and adopt-or-sync-into-library actions. This tab is shown only for gateway devices; see the Edge profiles help topic.

docs.title: Operations (gateway only)
docs.text: The remote operations this gateway's firmware advertised in its last hello (plus tenant-defined descriptors), invoked from here with schema-driven parameters, risk gating and per-invocation history. This tab is shown only for gateway devices; see the Gateway operations help topic.

docs.title: Quarantine
docs.text: Quarantined devices show a QUARANTINED badge with the quarantine time and reason, and offer a release action. See the Quarantine help topic under Devices.

docs.title: NereidLink Device SDK for Go
docs.text:
The Device SDK is for device and gateway firmware that connects to NereidLink from the southbound side. It is a thin protocol library: typed frames, credentials, topic bindings, and MQTT/HTTP transport helpers. It runs no background goroutines or loops and makes no policy decisions — your firmware keeps full control of poll cadence, reconnection, hello negotiation, and manifest timing.

  • Module: github.com/nereidai/nereidlink/sdk/device/go
  • Independent of the server: it does not pull NATS, database drivers, or any other server dependency.
  • Reference programs: examples/simple (a direct device) and examples/gateway (a full gateway) ship in the module.

Developer documentation

This page is a hands-on introduction. The full package API, constants, and runnable examples live in the NereidLink repository under sdk/device/go/ — see NereidAI.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: go get github.com/nereidai/nereidlink/sdk/device/go@latest

docs.title: Packages
docs.text: Package Purpose device Credentials (token / id+secret / X.509); frame models for telemetry, commands, shadow, attributes, events, OTA, hello/manifest/connector/discovery/probe; topic constants devicehttp HTTP ingress client: telemetry, long-poll commands, command response, shadow, OTA list / range download / progress devicemqtt MQTT ingress client (Eclipse Paho): connect, LWT, telemetry, attributes, events, command/shadow/attribute subscriptions gateway The gateway surface on top of devicemqtt: hello, heartbeat/goodbye, sub-devices, manifest, batched telemetry, relayed commands, connectors, discovery, probe, OTA, whole-gateway operations

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Every client starts from one credential:

device.Token("device-access-token")        // MQTT username = token, empty password
device.Basic("edge-001", "credential-secret") // username / password
device.ClientCert(tlsCert)                 // mutual TLS (X.509)

A device cannot connect until an operator has created it and granted it at least one valid credential — see Credentials and Integrate a direct device.

docs.title: Direct device over MQTT
docs.text:
client, _ := devicemqtt.Connect(ctx, devicemqtt.Options{
    BrokerURL:  "tcp://nereidlink.example:1883", // or tls://...:8883
    Credential: device.Token("device-access-token"),
    ClientID:   "sensor-001",
})
defer client.Disconnect(200)

// Downlink v1/me/cmd/<name>; reply on v1/me/cmdres/<id>.
_ = client.SubscribeCommands(ctx, 1, func(cmd device.Command) {
    _ = client.RespondCommand(ctx, cmd.ID, map[string]any{"ok": true}, 1)
})

_ = client.PublishTelemetry(ctx,
    device.NewFrame().SetFloat("temperature", 21.5).SetBool("online", true), 1)

The MQTT client bypasses HTTP/SOCKS proxies because field brokers are reached directly; TLS still verifies the broker certificate unless you explicitly opt out.

docs.title: Direct device over HTTP
docs.text:
httpClient, _ := devicehttp.New(devicehttp.Options{
    BaseURL:    "https://nereidlink.example",
    Credential: device.Token("device-access-token"),
})

_, _ = httpClient.PublishTelemetry(ctx,
    device.NewFrame().SetFloat("temperature", 21.5))

for {
    cmd, _ := httpClient.PollCommands(ctx) // one long poll; firmware loops
    if cmd != nil {
        _ = httpClient.RespondCommand(ctx, cmd.ID, map[string]any{"ok": true})
    }
}

Frame rule: a telemetry frame is a flat JSON object of numbers, booleans, and strings. null and nested objects/arrays are rejected locally before upload; the server turns each key into one Envelope. Units are never guessed — they come from the bound device profile descriptors.

docs.title: OTA on a direct device
docs.text:
The SDK streams bytes but never flashes or verifies firmware — that is the firmware's job.

list, _ := httpClient.ListOTAAssignments(ctx)
for _, job := range list.Assignments {
    var f *os.File // firmware decides where bytes go
    res, _ := httpClient.DownloadOTAPackage(ctx, job.TaskID,
        devicehttp.DownloadOptions{Destination: f}) // Range resume supported
    // Verify res.SHA256 (the X-Firmware-Sha256 value) before applying.
    _ = httpClient.ReportOTAProgress(ctx, job.TaskID,
        device.OTAProgress{State: device.OTAStateDownloading, ProgressPct: 50, Bytes: res.Written})
}

Drive the ordered state machine yourself: initiated → downloading → downloaded → verified → updating → updated → rebooting → confirmed/succeeded/failed. See OTA tasks and Firmware for the operator side.

docs.title: Gateways
docs.text:
A gateway is a device with the gateway capability. It uses the device topics and, after one hello per connection, the v1/gateway/* topics.

mq, _ := devicemqtt.Connect(ctx, devicemqtt.Options{
    BrokerURL: *broker, Credential: device.Basic(id, secret),
    ClientID: edgeID, Will: devicemqtt.GoodbyeWill("transport_down"),
})
gw := gateway.Wrap(mq)

_ = gw.SubscribeConnectors(ctx, 0, func(push device.ConnectorPush) { /* apply */ })
_ = gw.SubscribeProbes(ctx, 0, func(req device.ProbeRequest) { /* answer per device */ })
_ = gw.SubscribeOTATasks(ctx, 0, func(task device.GatewayOTATask) { /* download */ })

ack, err := gw.NegotiateHello(ctx, device.Hello{
    EdgeID: edgeID, AgentVersion: "2.3.1",
    Proto:  device.ProtoRange{Min: "1.0", Max: "1.4"},
    Features: device.FeatureSet{
        Required: []string{device.FeatureTelemetry, device.FeaturePresence},
    },
}, 10*time.Second)

_ = gw.ConnectDevices(ctx, []string{subDeviceUUID}, 1)
_ = gw.PublishTelemetry(ctx, device.GatewayFrame{
    DeviceID: subDeviceUUID, TS: time.Now().UnixMilli(),
    Measurements: device.NewFrame().SetFloat("temperature", 21.5),
})
// gw.Heartbeat(...) on ack.Limits.HeartbeatS; gw.SendManifest(...) periodically.

The firmware — not the SDK — owns these responsibilities:

  • Re-run hello after every reconnect; server state resets to unidentified and frames sent before the ack are discarded.
  • Heartbeat on the negotiated interval; the LWT fires on crash, and a planned Goodbye is sent on graceful shutdown.
  • Run a local link watchdog and report each unplanned down/up interval with ReportLinkEpisode; backlog replay is oldest-first, the platform de-duplicates.
  • Send a full-state Manifest at the aligned cadence (explicitly include an empty connectors segment when reporting zero connectors).
  • De-duplicate connector pushes by (spec_id, revision); the full desired set is re-sent after every hello.

See the gateway glossary, Integrate a gateway, and Gateway operations.

docs.title: Whole-gateway operations
docs.text:
Whole-gateway, menu-driven RPC (ping/reboot/…) is distinct from sub-device commands. The platform ships no operation names — firmware advertises a catalog in hello and executes only what it advertised:

  • Subscribe before hello (gw.SubscribeOperations), advertise entries in Hello.Operations with bilingual display names, interaction (request-response/one-way), timeout, risk (read/normal/dangerous), and inline JSON schemas.
  • The hello ack reports accepted/reason per entry; one bad entry never fails the handshake. Use namespaces diag.* / sys.* / service.* and vendor.<vendor>.*; a breaking change needs a new key or type_version.
  • Answer request-response invocations within inv.TimeoutMs with gw.RespondOperation; secret:// parameters arrive as plaintext at the last mile and must never be logged.

docs.title: Current gaps
docs.text:
The SDK tracks implemented server behavior; a few edges are intentionally not yet exposed:

  • Edge → platform object-storage blob relay is deferred.
  • Gateway-published domain events are not implemented server-side.
  • Hello resume.last_cursor is accepted but no cursor replay exists; desired state is full-state and idempotently re-driven.
  • Downlink MQTT frames are QoS 0, non-retained; choose QoS 1 for uplink.

docs.title: Device Services
docs.text: The Device Services page is the visible, editable catalog of the protocol families and reference EdgeX device services NereidLink knows how to render structured forms for.

docs.title: What the catalog is
docs.text:
Each catalog entry (a protocol family) records:

  • Family key — the open-vocabulary protocol family stored on a device profile, e.g. s7, modbus.
  • Display name and service name — the reference EdgeX device service (e.g. device-s7) used to seed a blank connector template's ds_name.
  • Protocol key / transports — the concrete keys that may appear under an EdgeX device's protocols map (e.g. s7, modbus-tcp).
  • Connection parameters — structured fields rendered in the profile/device connector editor and emitted verbatim into the protocol property map.
  • Point address parameters — structured fields rendered per point descriptor and emitted into the point address object.
  • Default point address — the initial address object prefilled when a new point is created (e.g. {"NodeName": "DB4.DBX0.0"}). Leave it empty to derive defaults from each parameter's own default value.
  • A link to the official documentation.

The catalog is global: the same vendor facts apply to every tenant. The platform kernel itself parses no protocol; the catalog only drives UI forms and suggestions. Ingestion and parsing stay transport-independent.

docs.title: Built-in vs custom
docs.text:
• The fourteen device services listed by the EdgeX 4.0.2 device-service index are seeded as Official entries: Modbus, ONVIF camera, MQTT, REST, device-virtual, SNMP, BACnet, CoAP, GPIO, OPC-UA, RFID LLRP, S7, UART and USB camera.
  • Official entries can be edited (to correct a label, add a field) but cannot be deleted.
  • Use Add device service to define a custom family; custom entries can be edited and deleted.

docs.title: How it relates to device profiles
docs.text: Selecting a profile's protocol family unlocks that family's structured connection parameters (on the connector template and gateway connector instance) and point-address fields (on each descriptor). Families with no fixed properties, or families not in the catalog, fall back to free JSON editing; unknown content is never rejected.

docs.title: S7 notes
docs.text:
• device-s7 speaks ISO-on-TCP. Connection properties are Host, Port (102), Rack, Slot and Timeout/IdleTimeout as integer seconds (not duration strings).
  • A point address uses a single attribute NodeName, e.g. DB4.DBX0.0, DB4.DBD4.
  • A pasted EdgeX device profile whose resources carry NodeName is auto-tagged family s7. A gateway-reported minimal frame that omits attributes cannot be auto-tagged until the edge includes them.

docs.title: Device Shadow
docs.text: The Device shadow tab of a device shows its desired and reported state side by side, and lets you write desired state.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Device shadow separates what you want from what the device says it has:

  • Desired — state the platform wants the device to reach. The platform and rule chains write it; an operator edits it from this tab.
  • Reported — state the device last published about itself. Only the device writes this.

The two are separate documents, so a command can be issued without waiting for the device to answer.

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text:
The table lists the union of keys from both sides. For each key it shows the desired value, the reported value, and a status tag:

  • Synced (green) — the desired and reported values for that key are identical.
  • Pending (orange) — they differ; the device has not yet caught up.

A summary banner shows the overall shadow state (in sync or out of sync) together with the desired and reported version numbers. The version increments on every write and is how concurrent edits are detected.

docs.title: Writing desired state
docs.text:
1. Click the edit action.
  2. Common keys — when the device's profile declares writable points (read_write W/RW), pick one from the top selector. It adds a fixed-key row with a typed control: a switch for booleans, a bounded number input (the profile's engineering range and unit are applied) or a text input. Remove a row to delete that key.
  3. Custom keys — add a free key/value row when you need a key the profile does not declare, choosing boolean, number, string, object or array.
  4. Additional keys (JSON) — for composite or bulk values, paste an extra JSON object; its keys are merged with the rows above.
  5. Save. The result is merged into the existing desired document — keys you neither edit nor remove are left untouched; removing a previously present key sends a JSON null that deletes it.
  6. The write uses optimistic concurrency: the version you loaded is sent as an If-Match ETag. If someone else changed the shadow in the meantime, the write is rejected instead of silently overwriting their change; reload and retry.

A device whose profile declares no writable points offers only the custom rows and the JSON box. Desired state is a target, not a command. Reaching it is the device's job — usually via a rule chain that watches the shadow and issues the actual command.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Values are arbitrary JSON; the platform does not interpret them.
  • Writing desired state does not itself change device state or connection state.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text: The Devices page lists every registered device in the tenant and its connection state. Devices are never physically deleted — see Decommissioning below.

docs.title: Finding devices
docs.text:
• Type in the search box to filter by canonical name or alias (filtering is server-side).
  • Use the selectors to narrow the list in the same order as the table columns: type (gateway / sub-device / standalone Device), device profile, customer, device group, lifecycle and connection (Online / Offline / Unknown). Each selector is also type-to-search, so a long list of profiles/customers/groups can be filtered by typing inside the dropdown without scrolling. The group selector has no matching column but stays because Customers & Groups pages deep-link into the device list with a group preselected, and it also lets you clear that preselection.
  • Rows are ordered newest first (device creation time, descending). The Created column shows that creation time; hover the Connection badge to see the device's last activity time (latest telemetry or presence boundary, whichever is newer; it falls back to the last connection-change time when a device has no telemetry yet). An alias, when set, is shown under the canonical name.
  • The Connector column shows the edge connector situation: a sub-device row shows its one bound connector instance, with the tag color encoding the reported apply state (applied / creating / dispatched / degraded / failed); hover for the state text and click the tag to jump straight to the owning gateway's Connectors tab. A gateway row shows a numeric badge with the number of gateway-level (non-sub-device-bound) connector instances on that gateway, also linking to the gateway Connectors tab. Rows with no binding show "-". The type and state refresh live from edge status frames.
  • The lifecycle state selector opens on Active devices. Choose a specific state to narrow further, or clear the selector to list everything — including decommissioned and archived devices, which are tombstone rows the default views hide.
  • The connection selector filters by the live connection state, independent of lifecycle state. Unknown means the device has never produced a presence boundary.

docs.title: Creating a device
docs.text:
1. Click Create device.
  2. The Canonical name is generated for you as a technical identifier (dev-a3f9k2x7, or gw-k2x7a3f9 for a gateway): a dev-/gw- prefix plus a random letter/digit suffix, unique within the tenant. Click the reload button to regenerate it. The field is read-only here; it stays the stable identity used to cross-check names against the edge side.
  3. Optionally select a device profile. A device without a profile stores values without descriptor transformation.
  4. Optionally set an alias (a human-friendly display name shown under the canonical name) and additional information (free-form notes, up to 4096 characters). Neither field carries platform semantics; the canonical name remains the device identity.
  5. After creation, open the device and add credentials; a device cannot connect until it has at least one valid credential.

docs.title: Bulk import
docs.text:
Import many devices at once from a spreadsheet.

  1. Download the XLSX or CSV template — both contain the same columns.
  2. Fill in one row per device. Each row must carry a canonical_name that is unique within the tenant (the bulk template does not auto-generate names; only the Create-device form does). Only the measurement/profile columns vary per row; a blank state uses the platform default.
  3. Drop the file onto the import drawer (or click it to browse) and confirm.

Up to 1000 rows and 4 MiB per file. The import is reported per row: successfully created devices and a list of failures with their reasons. A bad row does not abort the whole file.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text: • The edit form changes the profile and the optional alias / additional information. The canonical name is a generated technical identifier and cannot be edited. Saving with a blank alias or notes clears the stored value.

docs.title: Decommissioning instead of deleting
docs.text:
Deleting a device never removes it. The delete action is an alias for decommission, which:

  • disables the device's credentials instead of deleting them,
  • keeps all telemetry, attributes, commands and alarms,
  • evicts presence and disconnects the live session, so the device can no longer connect,
  • starts a recall window (90 days by default) during which the device can be reactivated and its credentials re-issued.

When the recall window expires, a background sweep moves the device to the archived state. Archiving is the end of the lifecycle, not a deletion.

Select several rows and use Decommission selected to apply the same operation in bulk.

docs.title: Quarantine
docs.text: Quarantine is a separate, reversible incident-response lock — see the Quarantine help topic under Devices.

docs.title: Dead Letter Queue
docs.text: The Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) collects telemetry points rejected by a failing storage hook whose failure policy is dlq.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
• Time — when the point was received.
  • Device — originating device ID.
  • Key — measurement key.
  • Hook — the hook that rejected the point.
  • Reason — failure detail.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Select one or more rows, then:

  • Replay — re-inserts the points into telemetry, bypassing hooks, so they are processed and stored.
  • Delete — removes the rows permanently.

Replaying is useful after fixing a hook or its downstream service. Regularly review the queue so device data is not silently lost.

docs.title: Edge profiles
docs.text: The Edge profiles tab is available on gateway devices. It lists the device profiles the gateway has reported to NereidLink over MQTT (v1/gateway/profiles) and lets you inspect them. NereidLink accepts a vendor-neutral point model as well as the EdgeX profile shape.

docs.title: Profiles enter the library automatically
docs.text:
• Every connector the edge applies can reference a profile. After the gateway completes its hello handshake (and on each reconnect), it reports those profiles automatically.
  • A reported profile is auto-ingested on first sight into the tenant profile library (visible on the Profiles page, source Edge); there is no longer a separate adopt step required before it can be referenced.
  • Each row here is the per-gateway raw cache (name plus deviceResource/point count, payload kept verbatim). The same name from two gateways links to one library profile; provenance is many-to-many.
  • Re-reporting an unchanged profile only refreshes the last reported time (the platform computes the content hash itself; nothing on the wire is trusted).
  • A same-name report whose content changed is drift: it is never silently overwritten. Use Adopt → update from this tab to accept this gateway's version.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text: Use the search box at the top to filter the list by profile name (case-insensitive, partial match). Filtering is local, so it covers every cached profile without a round trip.

docs.title: Viewing profile content
docs.text: Click View on a row to inspect the cached profile. The drawer lists every reported deviceResource in report order with its name, value type, units and description, and marks resources that cannot be represented as a scalar telemetry point (Binary/Object/*Array, duplicate or empty names).

docs.title: Adopt / sync
docs.text:
Adoption now resolves this gateway cache row onto the library profile:

  • A plain Adopt links/confirms the cache row against the auto-ingested library profile (idempotent).
  • Overwrite (update) accepts this gateway's reported content over a detected drift, refreshing the spec-owned point fields (type, unit, read_write, address, range/default). Operator calibration (transform, scale, enum, valid range) is never overwritten.
  • Points the edge removes are marked inactive rather than deleted, preserving history and rule references.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Listing and viewing require profile:read; adopting requires profile:write.

docs.title: Edge Secret Types
docs.text: The Edge Secret Types tab (inside the Edge Secrets page) manages the descriptors for the credentials the platform delivers to gateways (edge secrets). A descriptor only declares which fields a credential carries — the platform itself recognizes no credential protocol.

docs.title: What a descriptor contains
docs.text:
• Type key — the credential type identifier understood by the gateway.
  • Version — optional descriptor version; empty means unversioned.
  • English / Chinese name — bilingual display names.
  • Fields schema — a draft 2020-12 JSON Schema for the credential document. The console renders credential forms from it.

docs.title: Two sources
docs.text:
• Edge — the gateway advertises descriptors in hello; they are registered per tenant and marked read-only. Re-registering on every connection keeps the catalog current.
  • Manual — tenant-defined descriptors, full CRUD. Use these for gateways that do not advertise, or click Clone to manual on an edge descriptor to edit a copy.

docs.title: Authoring modes
docs.text:
• Field builder — add rows of: field key, control type (text, password, integer, number, switch, dropdown), bilingual labels, required flag and, for dropdowns, a comma-separated option list. The builder generates the JSON Schema. Editing a manual descriptor loads its saved fields back into the builder.
  • JSON Schema — paste or edit a complete schema directly.

The eye icon opens a descriptor read-only: a field overview (key, kind, required, label). For an edge descriptor use Clone to manual there to create an editable copy; for a manual descriptor click Edit in the overview to switch straight to editing. The pencil icon (manual rows only) opens it directly in edit mode.

Unregistered types are always accepted with an ad-hoc key/value form.

docs.title: Edge Secrets
docs.text: The Edge Secrets page is the tenant vault for the credentials the platform delivers to gateways (edge secrets). It has two tabs: Secrets (the vault, this page) and Types (the secret type descriptors). Values are write-only: the list and details show metadata (name, kind, type, timestamps) and never the content. The Secrets list can be searched by name or type and is paginated.

docs.title: Creating a secret
docs.text:
1. Pick a name — a stable identifier usable in secret:// references.
  2. Pick a type:
  3. one of the descriptors listed under the Types tab, which renders its typed fields; or
  4. Ad-hoc key/value, for credentials with no descriptor. Add rows of key/value and mark each row as secret. Saving the ad-hoc form with no rows asks you to add at least one row.
  5. Save. The complete document is encrypted (AES-256-GCM under a key held outside the database).

docs.title: Rotation and deletion
docs.text:
• Saving again overwrites the secret in place; no history is kept.
  • Normal deletion is protected: if any gateway still holds a non-removed copy, the delete dialog lists those gateways and blocks the hard delete.
  • Force delete & withdraw is human-only: start and verify a fresh authenticator (MFA) challenge in the dialog. The platform then withdraws every gateway copy. If a gateway is offline its binding stays Removing until it reconnects and reports Removed; the vault original is deleted only after the last reference disappears.

docs.title: Delivering to a gateway
docs.text:
Open a gateway's detail page and use its Secrets tab.

  1. Deliver secret, then choose a typed-document secret.
  2. Optionally add target selectors — open {kind, value} pairs the platform never interprets. The integration contract defines the first kind, mac: the secret is bound to the device with that MAC, and how the edge applies it is entirely the edge's decision. No selectors means the binding is gateway-wide; a binding may carry several selectors and one target may appear on several bindings.
  3. Save. The desired state is pushed immediately when the gateway is online; while offline it stays pending and the full set is re-sent idempotently on the next hello.

Each binding shows a monotonic revision and its state:

  • Pending — recorded, not yet written to the gateway.
  • Dispatching — pushed on the transport.
  • Applied — the gateway reported success.
  • Failed — hover the tag for the gateway's reason.
  • Removing / Removed — withdrawal flow.

A warning banner reads Gateway firmware does not support secret delivery when the gateway's last hello did not negotiate the secrets feature. Such bindings can be recorded now (they are not sent) and will be delivered after a firmware upgrade.

Withdraw moves the binding through Removing to Removed: the gateway erases its copy on the next sync. The platform keeps the vault original. The table updates live; no polling is needed.

A binding stuck in Pending/Dispatching raises a warning alarm after five minutes; a continuously failed binding escalates from major to critical after one hour.

docs.title: Legacy single-value secrets
docs.text: Older entries (kind: single value, created before typed documents) continue to work, including connector configs that reference them as secret://<name>. Editing such an entry keeps the single-value shape.

docs.title: Escalation Chains
docs.text: The Escalation Chains page defines who is notified when an alarm is not handled in time.

docs.title: Chain structure
docs.text:
A chain contains an ordered list of steps. Each step defines:

  • Delay (s) — seconds from the alarm start after which the step fires.
  • Notify role — the tenant role whose members are notified (TENANT_ADMIN, ENGINEER, CUSTOMER_USER, READ_ONLY).
  • Notify group — optional device group narrowing the step to role holders whose data scope covers that group's subtree. Leave empty to notify every holder of the role in the tenant.
  • Stop on ack / Stop on clear — cancel the step if the alarm is acknowledged or cleared before the delay elapses.

docs.title: How escalation fires
docs.text: A background process checks every 10 seconds. Each due step fires exactly once: it posts the configured webhook, emails the members of the target role, and records an in-app notification. When a step names a device group, only role holders whose data scope covers that group's subtree are emailed. Editing a chain does not affect steps that have already fired.

docs.title: Binding a chain
docs.text: Open the rule chain editor, select a Create Alarm node, and choose the escalation chain in its configuration. Alarms raised by that node then follow the selected chain.

docs.title: Firmware Packages
docs.text: The firmware repository stores the artifacts that Upgrade Tasks hand to devices. A package is a binary plus the metadata the platform needs to decide whether a device may receive it. Uploading a package is the only way to serve firmware from the platform itself.

docs.title: Upload a package
docs.text:
• Release name — required, human-readable title of the release (for example Gateway Sensor Firmware). It identifies the release in lists and rollouts independently of the technical version.
  • Version label — the version string shown on devices and tasks (for example 1.4.2). It is free-form and not parsed for ordering, but it must match what a device reports after applying; the platform compares it to skip devices that are already current.
  • Release notes — optional free text describing what is new, fixed or known to matter. Hover the release name in the list to read it.
  • Firmware file — the binary. Uploads are capped at 512 MiB.
  • Device model — optional. Bind the package to one device model, or leave it empty for a model-agnostic package that any model may take. A model-bound package is rejected (400) if a rollout would target another model.
  • Mark as recommended stable version — flags the package as the default recommendation. Exactly one stable package per model scope is allowed; marking a new one clears the previous star.

docs.title: Repository list
docs.text: Each row shows the release name and version (hover for release notes), the file name, the device model (or model-agnostic), the size, the SHA-256 digest and the upload time. The digest is what a device verifies after download; use it to confirm the file is the one you intended.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• Mark stable / Unmark stable — set or clear the recommended stable flag.
  • Download — fetch the stored artifact.
  • Delete — remove the package. Packages referenced by an active rollout cannot be removed while that rollout is still running.

docs.title: How packages reach devices
docs.text: Devices never receive the artifact over the management API. When a rollout targets a platform package, the platform authorizes the download and the device streams the file through the authenticated relay, verifying the SHA-256 digest before applying. If the blob store is not configured, packages cannot be uploaded and rollouts must use an external URL.

docs.title: Data Forwarders
docs.text: A data forwarder sends device data to an external system (such as a webhook or message broker) without making that system part of the telemetry path. Forwarding is fully asynchronous: a rule-chain forward node publishes the message to a bounded queue, and a worker delivers it in the background. A failing receiver never blocks ingestion or rule processing.

docs.title: Forwarders tab
docs.text:
Each row is one forwarder.

  • Name — unique display name within the tenant.
  • Sink — the delivery mechanism: HTTP webhook, MQTT broker, NATS server, RabbitMQ (AMQP), Apache Kafka, email (SMTP) or SMS (HTTP provider).
  • Target — the sink destination, for example the HTTP method and endpoint URL.
  • Max attempts — delivery retries before the message is moved to dead letters.
  • Enabled — turns delivery on or off.

Create or edit a forwarder in the drawer. Every forwarder shares the settings below; the remaining fields depend on the selected sink type.

docs.title: Common settings
docs.text:
• Sink type — chosen only when creating a forwarder. It cannot be changed afterward: the stored configuration is specific to one sink type, so create a new forwarder if you need a different delivery mechanism.
  • Max attempts — delivery retries before the message is moved to dead letters.
  • Message lifetime — how long an undelivered message is kept. Messages older than this are dropped even if the receiver is still down, so a recovered receiver is not flooded with the whole outage. The default is one hour.
  • Max buffered messages — caps the queued messages; when the queue is full the oldest messages are discarded. The default is 1000.

docs.title: HTTP webhook (http)
docs.text:
• Endpoint URL (required) — the receiver URL (http:// or https://).
  • HTTP method — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE; the body is the JSON envelope.
  • Username / password — optional HTTP basic authentication.
  • Headers (JSON) — optional headers added to every request, given as a JSON object.
  • Private CA certificate / client certificate / client key (PEM) — trust an internal CA and/or present a client certificate for mutual TLS; system roots stay valid.
  • Skip certificate verification — insecure switch; prefer a private CA certificate.
  • Success is HTTP 2xx/3xx; 408, 429 and 5xx are retried, other 4xx are terminal.

docs.title: MQTT broker (mqtt)
docs.text:
• Broker URL (required) — tcp://host:1883 for plain text, ssl://host:8883 for TLS.
  • Topic (required) — the topic each envelope is published to.
  • QoS — 0, 1 or 2.
  • Client ID — optional; generated when empty.
  • Username / password — optional broker credentials.

docs.title: NATS server (nats)
docs.text:
• Servers (required) — external NATS server URL, for example nats://host:4222.
  • Subject (required) — the subject each envelope is published to.
  • Username / password — optional user credentials.
  • Token — optional auth token (use instead of a username/password).

docs.title: RabbitMQ / AMQP (amqp)
docs.text:
• URL (required) — connection URL including vhost, for example amqp://user:pass@host:5672/vhost.
  • Exchange — optional named exchange; empty publishes to the default exchange.
  • Routing key (required) — the routing key each envelope carries.

docs.title: Apache Kafka (kafka)
docs.text:
• Bootstrap servers (required) — comma-separated host:port list.
  • Topic (required) — the topic produced to.
  • Use SASL authentication — enable to enter SASL/PLAIN credentials (SASL_PLAINTEXT, no TLS); leave off for an anonymous broker.
  • Username / password — SASL/PLAIN credentials, shown and required when the SASL switch is on.

docs.title: Email via SMTP (email)
docs.text:
• Host (required) — SMTP server host.
  • Encryption — STARTTLS (default) upgrades after EHLO and sets port 587; TLS/SSL dials implicit TLS and sets port 465; None stays plaintext and sets port 25. The port auto-fills on switch; you can still override it.
  • Port — server port, filled from the encryption mode (587/465/25).
  • From (required) — sender address.
  • Recipients (required) — comma-separated recipient addresses.
  • Subject — optional subject line; the body is the JSON envelope.
  • EHLO domain — FQDN announced in EHLO/HELO; defaults to the sender's domain (strict servers reject the client default localhost).
  • Use SMTP authentication — enable to send username/password; Username is then required. With 587 the credentials are protected by the negotiated STARTTLS session.

docs.title: SMS via HTTP provider (sms)
docs.text:
• Endpoint URL (required) — the provider's HTTP send endpoint.
  • Recipients (required) — comma-separated phone numbers.
  • Recipient JSON field / text JSON field — provider field names carrying the number (default to) and message (default text); the worker POSTs them as form/JSON parameters.
  • Headers (JSON) — optional headers (for example an API key) added to every request.
  • Success follows the provider's HTTP status, using the same retry rules as the HTTP webhook.

docs.title: How a forwarder is triggered
docs.text: A forwarder is a tenant-level resource; it does nothing until a rule chain references it. Add a forward node to a rule chain and set its forwarder_id to this forwarder. Messages reaching the node are queued for delivery. A publish failure is logged but never fails the rule chain.

docs.title: Retries and failures
docs.text:
• Network errors, timeouts, 408, 429 and 5xx responses are retried with backoff.
  • Other 4xx responses are permanent rejections.
  • Broker-style sinks (MQTT, NATS, AMQP, Kafka) treat connection or publish errors (including rejected credentials) as retryable; SMTP and the HTTP SMS provider follow the same retry policy, bounded by the same max attempts.
  • After the max attempts are exhausted, or on a permanent rejection, the message is parked in the Dead Letters tab.

docs.title: Dead letters tab
docs.text: Inspect parked envelopes with the originating forwarder, device, attempt count and last error. Use Replay to re-publish one message onto its forwarder's queue. Replay is only possible while the forwarder still exists.

docs.title: Delivery Log tab
docs.text:
Each row is one real delivery attempt, showing the time, forwarder, device, attempt number and the receiver return code:

  • Delivered — the receiver accepted the message (for example HTTP 200).
  • Retrying — a transient failure; the message will be retried.
  • Failed — a permanent rejection; the message moved to dead letters.

Because delivery happens after the forward node returns, this code is not visible in the rule-chain trace; use this tab to see it. The log is bounded: rows older than 7 days and more than 1000 rows per forwarder are removed automatically.

docs.title: Gateway Operations
docs.text: The Gateway Operations page shows the aggregate operation catalog: descriptors each gateway advertises in hello, stored per gateway, plus tenant-defined private operations. The platform ships no operation names itself, and risk is never inferred from a name — it only comes from the descriptor. Two gateways advertising the same key keep independent copies; the page groups them into one row showing how many gateways advertise it (hover for the names).

docs.title: Descriptor fields
docs.text:
• Operation — the key the gateway understands.
  • Version — optional descriptor version.
  • Interaction — request/response (waits for a result) or one-way.
  • Risk — read, normal or dangerous.
  • Timeout — execution bound, 100–60000 ms.
  • English / Chinese name and description — shown in the operator's UI language, falling back to English and then the operation key.
  • Parameters / result JSON Schemas — the console renders parameter forms and result views from them at invocation time. The parameter schema can be built field-by-field (name, type, required flag, description) or edited directly with Advanced JSON; schemas using constructs the builder cannot represent stay in JSON mode.

docs.title: Managing the catalog
docs.text:
• Use the eye icon on any row to open its read-only detail: key, version, risk, interaction, timeout, source, bilingual names/descriptions and the full parameter/result JSON Schemas.
  • Advertised operations (source: advertised) are read-only; from the detail view use Clone to private to edit a copy, or use the enable switch to disable them.
  • Private operations can be viewed, edited and deleted.
  • The enable switch disables an operation for this tenant; disabled keys stay visible so they can be re-enabled.

docs.title: Finding operations
docs.text:
• Use the search box (matches name, key, version and description) and the source/risk filters; the table pages locally.
  • A red Contract conflict tag means the gateways advertising the same operation+version disagree on risk, timeout or a schema. Align the firmware builds, or have them advertise distinct keys; an invocation is always validated against the target gateway's own copy.
  • A gateway's detail Operations tab is the authoritative list for that gateway and supports its own search, risk filter and pagination.

docs.title: Invoking from a gateway
docs.text:
On the gateway detail page, the Operations tab lists only operations this gateway's firmware advertised in its last hello (plus tenant-defined descriptors).

  • Fill the schema-driven parameters. The platform re-validates them against the descriptor schema before dispatch, so a console that skips validation cannot send malformed params. A parameter value may reference a key from the vault with secret://<name>; the reference is resolved at the last mile and never stored as plaintext.
  • Read actions execute immediately; normal actions require a real second confirmation (a confirmation popover after you press execute).
  • You may shorten the wait with the Timeout override (minimum 100 ms); it can never raise the descriptor default, and values are clamped to 100–60000 ms.
  • All operations are human-only: a machine (service-account) identity is refused at every risk level with OPERATION_HUMAN_ONLY. Dangerous actions additionally require a fresh authenticator (TOTP) step-up completed within the last five minutes. The modal shows a signed QR code describing the operation, gateway and expiry; verify it matches what you expect, then enter the current code. Refused dangerous attempts are recorded in the audit log even though no task is created.
  • The result is shown in the modal, and every invocation (including the failure reason) appears in the operation history table below. Results are retained 90 days; the permanent who/when/which-gateway record lives in the chained audit log.
  • An offline gateway fails immediately with Not connected; operations are never queued. Use device commands when you need delivery on reconnect.

docs.title: Getting Started with NereidLink
docs.text:
NereidLink is the privatized IoT data pipeline of the suite: multi-protocol device access, a unified message backbone, a rule engine, alerting and real-time dashboards. It ships as one codebase in two forms — an all-in-one binary or Kubernetes microservices. This guide is the operator's first-run path from an empty tenant to live telemetry on the Overview.

Runs standalone

Link is a complete product on its own. You do not need Sphere, Identity or any other product to connect devices and see data. Suite single sign-on and the portal only apply when Sphere is deployed as the entry point — see Standalone by default.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A running Link instance (the all-in-one binary or a Kubernetes deployment) and the URL of its console.
  • A console account with permission to manage profiles, devices and credentials — a Link-local account on a standalone install, or a suite account with a Link role when Sphere is present.
  • Something to connect: a device that speaks MQTT/HTTP directly, or a gateway such as Edge that fronts field sub-devices.

docs.title: 1. Sign in
docs.text: Open the Link console. On a standalone deployment you sign in with Link's own account; when the suite is used, you typically enter Link from the Sphere portal without a second login. Either way the console experience is the same.

docs.title: 2. Create a device profile
docs.text:
A device profile groups measurement descriptors — point names, value types, units and optional transforms. A profile is optional (values are still stored without one), but creating one first means units and engineering values are correct from the very first frame.

  1. Open Profiles and click Create profile.
  2. Give it a name and, if relevant, a protocol family such as modbus.
  3. Add one descriptor per measurement key the device publishes.

See Device Profiles for the full descriptor and transform options.

docs.title: 3. Register a device
docs.text:
1. Open Devices and click Create device.
  2. The canonical name (dev-xxxx, or gw-xxxx for a gateway) is generated for you and stays the stable device identity.
  3. Select the profile you created (optional) and set a human-friendly alias if you like.
  4. For a gateway deployment, create the parent as type gateway, then create each field device as a sub-device bound to that gateway. See Devices.

docs.title: 4. Add a credential
docs.text:
A device cannot connect until it holds at least one valid credential. Open the device's Credentials tab and add one: TOKEN for a simple shared secret, PASSWORD, JWT, or X509 for an mTLS client certificate.

Copy the secret now

A newly created secret is shown exactly once and cannot be recovered afterwards. Copy it to a secure store before leaving the page. See Device Credentials.

docs.title: 5. Connect the device
docs.text:
Choose the path that matches the device:

  • Direct device — firmware speaks MQTT (primary) or HTTPS long-polling itself. Point it at the Link broker with the credential and publish flat telemetry frames. See Direct Device Integration.
  • Gateway with sub-devices — one process holds a single MQTT connection and relays many field devices behind it. Register and bind the sub-devices first, then run the gateway. See Gateway Integration; Edge is the ready-made EdgeX-based gateway for this path.

docs.title: 6. See live telemetry
docs.text: Return to the Overview. The device turns Online on its first presence/telemetry, the Telemetry 1h card climbs, and the throughput panel updates live over WebSocket — there is no polling. Open the device to inspect its latest readings and charts.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Overview — KPI cards and live panels.
  • Dashboards, rule chains and alarms — visualize, process and alert on the data.
  • NereidLink product page and the suite glossary.

docs.title: Direct Device Integration
docs.text:
This guide explains how to connect a directly connected device (firmware that speaks to NereidLink itself, with no gateway in between). It is written for device/edge developers, not console operators.

  • Transport: MQTT 3.1.1 / 5.0 (primary) or HTTPS long-polling (fallback).
  • Payloads: JSON, UTF-8.
  • Official SDK: Go — github.com/nereidai/nereidlink/sdk/device/go. It is a thin framing/transport library; your firmware keeps control of cadence and reconnection. Other languages can implement the wire contract in this document directly.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites on the platform
docs.text:
Before firmware can connect, an operator must prepare the device in the console:

  1. Create the device and assign a device profile (its measurement descriptors declare point names, value types and units).
  2. Create at least one credential for the device. Three kinds exist:
  3. TOKEN — one opaque access token, sent as the MQTT username with an empty password (or HTTP Authorization header).
  4. ID + secret — sent as MQTT username/password or HTTP Basic auth.
  5. X.509 client certificate — mutual TLS.
  6. A device without a valid credential cannot establish a session.

Telemetry keys should match the measurement keys declared in the device profile. The platform never guesses units or types: only descriptor-defined points get conversions/units; unknown scalar keys are still stored but without transformation.

docs.title: 2. MQTT quick start (Go SDK)
docs.text:
go get github.com/nereidai/nereidlink/sdk/device/go@latest

package main

import (
    "context"

    "github.com/nereidai/nereidlink/sdk/device/go"
    "github.com/nereidai/nereidlink/sdk/device/go/devicemqtt"
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()

    client, err := devicemqtt.Connect(ctx, devicemqtt.Options{
        BrokerURL:  "tcp://nereidlink.example:1883", // or tls://...:8883
        Credential: device.Token("device-access-token"),
        ClientID:   "sensor-001",
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer client.Disconnect(200)

    // Receive downlink commands and answer them.
    _ = client.SubscribeCommands(ctx, 1, func(cmd device.Command) {
        // Downlink topic: v1/me/cmd/<name>; reply path uses the ID.
        _ = client.RespondCommand(ctx, cmd.ID,
            map[string]any{"ok": true}, 1)
    })

    // Publish flat scalar measurements.
    frame := device.NewFrame().
        SetFloat("temperature", 21.5).
        SetBool("online", true).
        SetString("mode", "AUTO")
    _ = client.PublishTelemetry(ctx, frame, 1)
}

device.Basic(id, secret) and device.ClientCert(...) provide the other credential kinds. A complete runnable program is in the SDK under examples/simple.

docs.title: 3. MQTT topic contract
docs.text: A directly connected device only ever uses the v1/me/* topics.

docs.title: Device → platform
docs.text: Topic Direction Payload v1/me/telemetry publish Flat JSON object of scalar measurements v1/me/events publish One domain-event object or an array v1/me/attributes publish CLIENT-scope attributes object v1/me/attributes/get publish On-demand pull of platform attributes: {"scopes":[...],"response_topic"?}; omitted scopes means SERVER_SCOPE+SHARED_SCOPE v1/me/shadow/report publish Reported-state patch: {"state":{...},"version"?:N} v1/me/cmdres/{command_id} publish Result of a request-response command

docs.title: Platform → device (subscribe)
docs.text:
Filter/topic Payload v1/me/cmd/# Command frames; the concrete topic is v1/me/cmd/<command_name> v1/me/attributes/down SERVER/SHARED attribute pushes v1/me/attributes/get/ack On-demand pull reply: {"scopes":{"SERVER_SCOPE":{...},"SHARED_SCOPE":{...}}} v1/me/shadow/desired Complete desired state: {"version":N,"desired":{...}}

Downlink frames are QoS 0 and non-retained. The firmware chooses uplink QoS; QoS 1 is recommended.

docs.title: Telemetry frame
docs.text:
{
  "ts": 1728374400000,
  "temperature": 21.5,
  "online": true,
  "mode": "AUTO"
}
  • Every value MUST be a JSON number, boolean or string. null, nested objects and arrays are rejected before upload.
  • ts is optional (epoch milliseconds). Omit it to let the platform stamp arrival time.
  • One frame produces one stored record per measurement key.

docs.title: Attributes and scopes
docs.text:
Attributes are relatively static key/value configuration or metadata, not telemetry: the device only reports the CLIENT scope via v1/me/attributes; the platform manages SERVER_SCOPE and SHARED_SCOPE.

In the current version both SERVER_SCOPE and SHARED_SCOPE are delivered to the device: while online you receive incremental pushes on v1/me/attributes/down as {"scope":"...","data":{"key":value}}; after every (re)connect you should publish v1/me/attributes/get once to recover changes missed while offline, and replace the local cache wholesale with the full key/value set returned per scope in get/ack. Note this differs from classic ThingsBoard semantics, where SERVER_SCOPE is private to the server and only SHARED_SCOPE is visible to the device; do not assume SERVER_SCOPE is private here. A JSON null value in a downlink data map means the platform deleted that key, so the device must drop the local cache entry (do not store null). Omitting scopes in the request pulls both platform scopes; requesting CLIENT or an unknown scope is rejected.

docs.title: Device shadow (desired / reported)
docs.text:
The shadow holds, per device UUID, a platform-requested desired state and the device-observed reported state, so you can tell "the state I asked for" from "the state it actually reached". Use it only for state that must be maintained and confirmed; use commands for one-shot actions and SHARED attributes for fire-and-forget configuration.

  • Desired is always full-state. On v1/me/shadow/desired you receive the complete map as {"version":N,"desired":{...}}; replace your local desired map wholesale, never patch it. The frame carries no tenant/device fields — the connection already identifies the device. Desired is re-pushed in full whenever it changes and once on each ONLINE (re)connect with desired_version > 0.
  • Reported is a patch. Publish v1/me/shadow/report with {"state":{...},"version"?:N}; state is merged per top-level key. Add version to acknowledge the desired version you just applied. A JSON null value deletes that top-level key; values may be scalars, objects or arrays.
  • The platform computes delta (desired keys whose reported value differs) and flags the shadow in_sync; read both over REST/WebSocket.

docs.title: Media: images, documents and other binaries
docs.text:
Telemetry can carry binary media — camera images, inspection photos, scanned documents — not just scalars. The bytes never enter the time-series row or the message bus: NereidLink stores them in its S3-compatible blob backend (MinIO, SeaweedFS, AWS S3, …) and the point keeps only blob://media/<tenant>/<device>/<uuid>. Two uplink forms exist:

  1. Frame marker — a {"blob":true,"content_type":…,"filename":…, "data":"<base64>"} object in place of a scalar, over MQTT (v1/me/telemetry) or HTTP (POST /v1/me/telemetry). data is base64 only; the marker can share a frame with ordinary measurements.
  2. Raw HTTP upload — POST /v1/me/blob?key=<name> streams the raw file (no base64) straight into object storage, then publishes the reference point.

Per-object size (default 10 MiB) and the content-type allowlist (default image/*, extend with e.g. application/pdf for documents) are enforced once on the server. Owners download via GET /v1/me/blob; console/API users resolve a reference via GET /v1/tenants/{tenant}/blob/sign?key=… to a short-lived signed URL.

Full media contract

The marker field specification, base64 variants, S3/local backends, configuration, error codes and console rendering are documented on a dedicated page: Binary Media and S3 Storage.

docs.title: Command frame (platform → device)
docs.text:
{
  "id": "01J8...",
  "name": "set-led",
  "direction": "write",
  "params": { "color": "green" }
}
  • The topic suffix is the command name (e.g. v1/me/cmd/set-led); the reply topic suffix is the command id (v1/me/cmdres/01J8...). Never swap them.
  • direction is read or write, the south operation to perform, and is orthogonal to whether a reply is expected. Execute the GET/write exactly as directed; do not infer it from the name. A read may still carry params (query arguments), and one-way frames never carry direction=read.
  • params is a JSON document validated against the platform catalog; it is delivered verbatim.
  • For a request-response command, publish an arbitrary JSON result to v1/me/cmdres/{id}. For a one-way command, do not reply.
  • If the command cannot be executed, still reply (request-response mode) with a JSON body describing the failure; the platform marks the command SUCCEEDED once any correlated response arrives, so include an explicit error field for business failures, e.g. {"error": "busy"}.

docs.title: Domain events
docs.text:
{
  "event_type": "door_forced",
  "severity": "warning",
  "ts_ms": 1728374400000,
  "payload": { "zone": 3 }
}

severity is one of info, warning, error, critical (default info). The platform carries no business logic: event_type and payload are tenant-defined opaque data.

docs.title: 4. HTTP transport
docs.text:
For networks that only allow HTTPS, the device channel provides:

  • POST /v1/me/telemetry — upload one flat telemetry frame (base64 media markers allowed; see the Media section).
  • POST /v1/me/blob?key=<measurement> — upload raw media bytes, and GET /v1/me/blob?key=<key> — download the device's own object (Range supported).
  • GET /v1/me/commands — one long-poll wait; returns either the next queued command or an empty envelope when the wait window expires.
  • POST /v1/me/cmdres/{command_id} — submit a command result.
  • POST /v1/me/shadow/report — report shadow state.
  • GET /v1/me/ota/tasks, GET /v1/me/ota/{task_id}/package (Range resume supported), POST /v1/me/ota/{task_id}/progress — firmware update flow.
httpClient, _ := devicehttp.New(devicehttp.Options{
    BaseURL:    "https://nereidlink.example",
    Credential: device.Token("device-access-token"),
})

_, _ = httpClient.PublishTelemetry(ctx,
    device.NewFrame().SetFloat("temperature", 21.5))

for {
    cmd, _ := httpClient.PollCommands(ctx) // one long poll; loop to re-arm
    if cmd != nil {
        _ = httpClient.RespondCommand(ctx, cmd.ID,
            map[string]any{"ok": true})
    }
}

Authentication uses the same credentials (the token goes in Authorization).

docs.title: 5. Command timeliness
docs.text:
Commands are declared in the platform's command catalog per device; undeclared command names cannot be dispatched (the platform rejects them with 404). Each declaration selects:

  • Interaction: one-way (fire-and-forget, ends DELIVERED) or request-response (waits for one correlated result, then SUCCEEDED or TIMEOUT).
  • Timeliness: realtime (an offline device immediately gets NOT_CONNECTED) or persistent (queued and delivered after reconnect; undelivered commands past TTL end EXPIRED).

Firmware does not configure these; it only observes whether a reply is expected.

docs.title: 6. Integration checklist
docs.text:
• Device created in console with a profile; credential issued and embedded in firmware.
  • Firmware connects with the correct credential and unique client ID.
  • Telemetry frames are flat scalar JSON, keys match profile descriptors, ts included when sampling time matters.
  • Binary media uses the blob path: base64 frame marker or POST /v1/me/blob; never send raw text in marker data, and verify the content type is allowed (blob.media_allowed_types).
  • Firmware subscribes to v1/me/cmd/#, distinguishes name (topic) from id (reply), and always answers request-response commands — including failure cases.
  • Reconnection is handled by firmware (the SDK offers auto-reconnect for MQTT); after reconnect, resume publishing with fresh timestamps.

docs.title: Gateway Integration
docs.text:
This guide explains how to integrate a gateway / edge node — one process that connects to NereidLink over a single MQTT connection and manages many sub-devices behind it (Modbus/ONVIF/S7 field buses, local device services, and so on). It is written for gateway developers.

  • Transport: MQTT 3.1.1 / 5.0 over TLS (mTLS optional).
  • Payloads: JSON, UTF-8.
  • Official SDK: Go — github.com/nereidai/nereidlink/sdk/device/go, package gateway. A complete reference program is in examples/gateway. Other languages can implement the wire contract in this document directly.
  • The platform does not understand any south-side protocol. Mapping between platform sub-device UUIDs and local devices is entirely the gateway's job.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites on the platform
docs.text:
1. The gateway itself is registered as a device of type gateway, with its own credential (ID + secret, token, or X.509 certificate).
  2. Each sub-device is registered in the console and bound to this gateway. A gateway can only operate sub-devices bound to it; frames for a foreign or un-attached sub-device are dropped.
  3. Sub-device profiles declare the telemetry point names; commands must be declared in the per-device command catalog before they can be dispatched.

docs.title: 2. Session lifecycle
docs.text:
State machine: UNIDENTIFIED → NEGOTIATED → CLOSED.

  1. Establish the MQTT connection; pre-register the LWT on v1/gateway/goodbye.
  2. Subscribe the hello-ack topic (or use the MQTT 5 Response Topic).
  3. Publish v1/gateway/hello; negotiation must finish within 10 seconds.
  4. Only after a successful ack may gateway data topics be used. Frames sent before the ack are discarded. Exactly one hello happens per connection.

docs.title: Hello (gateway → platform), topic v1/gateway/hello
docs.text:
{
  "v": 1,
  "edge_id": "edge-001",
  "agent_version": "2.3.1",
  "proto": {"min": "1.0", "max": "1.4"},
  "features": {
    "required": ["telemetry", "presence"],
    "optional": ["ota", "shadow", "blob-relay", "command"]
  },
  "connectors": [
    {"type": "modbus", "type_version": "2.1",
     "config_schema": {"type": "object", "required": ["host"],
       "properties": {"host": {"type": "string"}, "port": {"type": "integer"}}}}
  ],
  "client_time": 1727360000123
}
  • features.required must all be supported by the server or negotiation fails (incompatible_features); features.optional are downgraded away when unsupported. Available features: telemetry, presence, ota, shadow, blob-relay, command.
  • connectors[] optionally registers inline, self-contained JSON Schemas (draft 2020-12; no external $ref) for the connector types this gateway can run. An invalid schema never fails the handshake; its result is reported per entry in the ack.
  • agent_version is your build string and is independent of the protocol version.

docs.title: Ack (platform → gateway), topic v1/gateway/hello/ack
docs.text:
{
  "session_id": "s_...",
  "status": "ok",
  "selected": "1.4",
  "server": {"min": "1.0", "max": "2.0", "version": "nereidlink-..."},
  "features": ["telemetry", "presence", "command"],
  "limits": {"heartbeat_s": 30, "hello_timeout_s": 10,
             "upload": {"max_mb": 256, "qps": 20}},
  "time": {"server_time": 1727360000456, "offset_ms": -312, "clock_warning": false}
}

Ack statuses: ok, auth_failed, incompatible_version, incompatible_features, quota_exceeded. Use limits.heartbeat_s for the heartbeat cadence. After every reconnect the server state resets to UNIDENTIFIED: re-run hello, re-subscribe, and re-announce state.

docs.title: 3. Liveness: heartbeat, goodbye and LWT
docs.text:
• Publish a heartbeat to v1/gateway/heartbeat at the negotiated interval:
{"seq": 42, "client_time": 1727360060000}
