  • Pre-register v1/gateway/goodbye as the MQTT will at CONNECT time. On graceful shutdown publish it explicitly with planned: true:
{"reason": "upgrade", "planned": true}

The broker-delivered LWT has no planned flag, so a crash is distinguishable from planned downtime. - Missed heartbeats drive the platform watchdog (HEALTHY → SUSPECT → DOWN) and cascade attached sub-devices offline. A goodbye (planned or LWT) suppresses the suspicion timer.

docs.title: 3.1 Link episode reports (v1/gateway/linkhealth)
docs.text:
Run a local link watchdog in the gateway and report each unplanned down/up episode after re-hello succeeds (QoS1):

{
  "edge_id": "<gateway-uuid>",
  "session_id": "s_…",
  "down_at": "2026-10-10T03:12:44Z",
  "up_at": "2026-10-10T03:12:49Z",
  "reason": "transport_down"
}
  • edge_id must equal this connection's gateway id; down_at/up_at are RFC3339 (the edge clock is the ground truth) and up_at must not precede down_at; session_id is optional.
  • The platform corrects the matching lease episode or records a closed alarm-free episode for flaps shorter than the lease window, and answers on v1/gateway/linkhealth/ack: accepted / duplicate / rejected. Stop retrying on any of the three; no ack (transient server error) means retry.
  • Backlog replay is just oldest-first QoS1 frames; de-duplication is by (edge_id, down_at). Five unmatched episodes in 10 minutes raise a flapping alarm, auto-cleared after a quiet 10-minute window.

docs.title: 4. Sub-device presence
5. Sub-device telemetry
docs.text:
Publish batches to v1/gateway/telemetry. The payload is a map keyed by sub-device UUID; each value is the same flat scalar frame as a direct device reports, with an optional ts (epoch milliseconds):

{
  "07704cf9-...": {"ts": 1728374400000, "MACAddress": "AA:BB:CC:00:11:22"},
  "089fbb69-...": {"temperature": 23.1, "online": true}
}

Rules are identical to direct devices: values must be numbers/booleans/ strings (no nested objects or arrays); one storage record per key; unknown keys are stored without descriptor conversion. A value may also be a {"blob":true,...} marker (see direct-device integration): the media is stored under media/<tenant>/<sub-device>/... and the point becomes a blob:// reference.

CLIENT-scope attributes use v1/gateway/attributes with {device: {key: value}}; SERVER/SHARED pushes arrive on v1/gateway/attributes/push as {"device":"...","scope":"...","data":{...}}. After every (re)connect the gateway should publish v1/gateway/attributes/get ({"device":"...","scopes":[...],"response_topic"?}, omitted scopes means SERVER_SCOPE+SHARED_SCOPE) for each attached sub-device and replace its cache from the full per-scope set in v1/gateway/attributes/get/ack. A JSON null value in a push data map means that key was deleted; drop it locally (do not store null). In the current version both SERVER_SCOPE and SHARED_SCOPE are delivered to the device (unlike classic ThingsBoard, where SERVER_SCOPE is server-private); do not assume SERVER_SCOPE is private. The gateway's own attributes use the direct-device topics v1/me/attributes, v1/me/attributes/down, v1/me/attributes/get and v1/me/attributes/get/ack — the gateway is itself a device, and whole-gateway runtime knobs (for example log level or trace switches) are delivered there, not under v1/gateway/....

docs.title: 6. Commands to sub-devices
docs.text: Commands are declared per sub-device in the platform command catalog; the gateway merely executes them against its local bus.

docs.title: Downlink (platform → gateway), topic v1/gateway/command
docs.text:
One subscription serves every sub-device; the device field selects the target:

{
  "command_id": "01J8...",
  "device": "07704cf9-...",
  "interaction": "request-response",
  "timeliness": "realtime",
  "method": "DeviceInformation",
  "direction": "read",
  "params": {}
}
  • interaction: one-way (no reply expected) or request-response (exactly one correlated reply).
  • timeliness: realtime (fails fast when offline) or persistent (queued server-side; the gateway only ever sees live frames).
  • method is the catalog command name; params is the catalog-validated JSON delivered verbatim.
  • direction: read or write, the south-side operation (read a resource vs. write a resource), orthogonal to interaction. The gateway MUST perform the GET/write exactly as directed and MUST NOT infer direction from the method name; a read may carry params (query arguments). one-way frames never carry direction=read.

docs.title: Uplink (gateway → platform), topic v1/gateway/command/response
docs.text:
{
  "command_id": "01J8...",
  "device": "07704cf9-...",
  "data": {"manufacturer": "Acme", "model": "Cam-9", "firmware": "1.4.2"}
}
  • Echo command_id and device unchanged; data is arbitrary JSON.
  • For one-way commands send nothing.
  • On local failure (device not reachable on the field bus, read error, timeout), still answer request-response commands with the error inside data, for example {"error": "no response from field bus"}. Not answering at all causes a platform-side TIMEOUT.
  • A response is accepted only from the gateway that attached the named sub-device.

Go SDK:

_ = gw.SubscribeCommands(ctx, 1, func(cmd device.GatewayCommand) {
    if cmd.Interaction != device.InteractionRequestResponse {
        return // one-way: execute silently
    }
    result := executeOnFieldBus(cmd.Device, cmd.Method, cmd.Params)
    _ = gw.RespondCommand(ctx, cmd.CommandID, cmd.Device, result, 1)
})

docs.title: 6.1 Sub-device shadow (desired / reported)
docs.text:
A shadow is stored per device UUID, independent of transport: the gateway's own shadow is direct-device traffic on v1/me/shadow/*; the shadow of a sub-device it proxies uses the batched gateway topics below.

  • Report one or more sub-devices' reported state on v1/gateway/shadow/report. A single sub-device is a length-one batch:
{
  "reports": [
    {"device": "07704cf9-...", "state": {"led": "on", "brightness": 7}, "version": 3},
    {"device": "089fbb69-...", "state": {"rpm": 1200}}
  ]
}

state is a per-top-level-key patch (a JSON null value deletes the key); version optionally acknowledges the desired version just applied. Entries are authorized and stored independently: an empty device, a non-UUID or not-attached device, or a non-object/empty state causes that entry alone to be dropped and audited — the rest of the batch still persists. A frame whose top-level JSON cannot be parsed is dropped wholesale.

  • Subscribe once to v1/gateway/shadow/desired; demux each entry by device. Like the direct channel, desired is always full-state, not a delta — replace each named sub-device's local desired map wholesale:
{"desired": [{"device": "07704cf9-...", "version": 3, "desired": {"led": "on"}}]}

Desired is re-pushed in full when it changes and once when a sub-device becomes ONLINE with desired_version > 0, so no per-device get is needed.

Go SDK:

_ = gw.SubscribeSubdeviceShadowDesired(ctx, 1, func(frame device.GatewayShadowDesiredFrame) {
    for _, d := range frame.Desired {
        applyLocalDesired(d.Device, d.Version, d.Desired) // full replace
    }
})

_ = gw.ReportSubdeviceShadow(ctx, []device.GatewayShadowReport{
    device.NewGatewayShadowReportForVersion("07704cf9-...", map[string]any{"led": "on"}, 3),
}, 1)

docs.title: 7. Connector lifecycle (desired / reported)
docs.text:
NereidLink is the system of record for connector instances; the gateway applies desired state and reports what it actually runs.

  • Subscribe the single filter v1/gateway/connectors/#. Desired specs arrive on v1/gateway/connectors/spec (spec_id, connector_type, type_version, config, mappings, health_check, revision), removals on v1/gateway/connectors/delete.
  • After every hello the full desired set is re-sent idempotently; de-duplicate by (spec_id, revision).
  • Report state on v1/gateway/connectors/status using the state machine CREATING → APPLIED / FAILED / DEGRADED, echoing spec_id and revision.

docs.title: Instance liveness probe (health_check)
docs.text:
A spec bound to one sub-device may carry health_check:

{"resource": "camera_status", "interval_ms": 30000,
 "timeout_ms": 5000, "fail_threshold": 3}
  • Every interval_ms, READ resource once for that sub-device and discard the value: never emit telemetry, shadow updates or any Envelope uplink from a probe.
  • After fail_threshold consecutive failures/timeouts, assert the sub-device offline on v1/gateway/disconnect; the first successful probe afterwards asserts it back online on v1/gateway/connect (send state edges only).
  • Stop probing when the field disappears or the spec is deleted; the probe is independent of the MQTT transport keepalive.

The console-side workflow is documented in the Connectors help topic.

docs.title: 8. Optional capabilities
docs.text:
Capability Downlink Uplink Notes On-demand probe v1/gateway/probe v1/gateway/probe/response Reachability test per sub-device; answer per device or one responses[] batch Discovery / auto-provisioning v1/gateway/discovery/result v1/gateway/discovery Report scan candidates; platform maps local IDs to UUIDs OTA v1/gateway/ota/task v1/gateway/ota/progress External firmware URL; ordered progress states Profiles library — v1/gateway/profiles Report local device profiles for adoption in the console Attribute push v1/gateway/attributes/push, v1/gateway/attributes/get/ack v1/gateway/attributes, v1/gateway/attributes/get SERVER/SHARED delivered + CLIENT reported; null deletes; see section 5 Shadow v1/gateway/shadow/desired v1/gateway/shadow/report Desired/reported device shadow Gateway operations v1/gateway/operations/invoke v1/gateway/operations/result Synchronous whole-gateway actions; see section 9

Advertise only what you implement in the hello features list (for the session-level features) and simply do not publish the rest.

docs.title: 9. Gateway operations (whole-gateway actions)
docs.text:
Operations are immediate actions on the gateway itself (reboot, vendor maintenance routines), distinct from sub-device commands (section 6). The platform ships no operation vocabulary: advertise the operations your build implements as catalog descriptors in hello operations[] — operation key, interaction (request-response/one-way), timeout, parameter/result JSON Schemas and risk (read/normal/dangerous).

The platform stores each gateway's descriptors separately (migration 0080); two gateways advertising the same key never overwrite each other, and an invocation is validated against the TARGET gateway's own descriptor. Keep these naming/version rules so a multi-vendor fleet stays consistent:

  • operations[] is the gateway's full current set on every hello: keys absent from a later hello are reconciled away. Omit the field entirely (null) on firmware that does not speak operations; sending [] clears the set.
  • operation + type_version is the contract: same key and version across gateways MUST have identical params, result, risk and interaction.
  • Use standard namespaces for common actions — diag.* (diagnostics), sys.* (host info/maintenance), service.* (managed services); vendor actions MUST use vendor.<vendor>.* so they cannot collide.
  • A breaking contract change needs a new type_version (or a new key, e.g. diag.ping.v2) since invoke frames do not select a version; when one gateway advertises several versions the newest one is invoked.

  • The console aggregates the keys across gateways and flags a contract conflict when same-key advertisers disagree on risk/timeout/schema.

  • Subscribe v1/gateway/operations/invoke. Invoke frames carry id, operation, type_version, params (already validated) and timeout_ms; the frame value is the effective bound — the smaller of the descriptor default and any operator per-call override, clamped to 100–60000 ms. Reply on v1/gateway/operations/result with the same id, ok, and result or error.

  • Execute only operations you advertised; answer every request-response invoke within timeout_ms — no reply means a platform-side TIMEOUT. For one-way operations send nothing.
  • A parameter value of the form secret://<name> arrives already resolved to plaintext at the last mile; never log or persist it.
  • Results MUST NOT contain passwords: the platform does not inspect result content, so redaction is the gateway's responsibility.
  • Invocation is live-only: an offline gateway gets NOT_CONNECTED immediately and frames are never queued. Late/duplicate results are dropped.
_ = gw.SubscribeOperations(ctx, 1, func(inv device.OperationInvoke) {
    out := runVendorOperation(inv.Operation, inv.Params)
    _ = gw.RespondOperation(ctx, device.OperationResult{
        ID: inv.ID, OK: true, Result: out,
    }, 1)
})

docs.title: 10. Topic summary
docs.text:
Gateway → platform: v1/gateway/hello, heartbeat, goodbye, linkhealth, connect, disconnect, manifest, telemetry, attributes, shadow/report, command/response, ota/progress, probe/response, connectors/status, profiles, discovery, operations/result.

Platform → gateway: hello/ack, linkhealth/ack, command, attributes/push, shadow/desired, ota/task, probe, connectors/spec, connectors/delete, discovery/result, operations/invoke.

Uplink QoS is the gateway's choice (QoS 1 recommended); downlink frames are QoS 0 and non-retained.

docs.title: 11. Integration checklist
docs.text:
• Gateway registered with a credential; all sub-devices registered and bound to it.
  • Hello sent after every (re)connect; no gateway frames published before status: ok; feature list matches what the build implements.
  • LWT registered before CONNECT; planned goodbye on graceful shutdown; heartbeats at limits.heartbeat_s.
  • Local link watchdog episodes reported after re-hello; ack subscription registered once; stop retrying on accepted/duplicate/rejected.
  • connect/disconnect on attachment changes; full-state manifest every 5 minutes with correct connectors presence semantics.
  • Telemetry batches keyed by UUID, flat scalar values only.
  • Commands: one subscription for all sub-devices; answer every request-response command by command_id + device, including failures; never answer one-way commands.
  • Connector pushes de-duplicated by (spec_id, revision); status reported through the state machine.
  • Shadow: gateway's own shadow on v1/me/shadow/*; sub-device reports batched to v1/gateway/shadow/report and one v1/gateway/shadow/desired subscription demuxed by device; replace full desired, never patch it.
  • Operations advertised in hello operations[]; every request-response invoke answered on operations/result by id within timeout_ms; results contain no passwords.

docs.title: Link Health
docs.text: The Link health tab on a gateway detail page lists the history of the gateway's link outages as time intervals. It answers "when did the link drop, how long did each outage last, and who detected it" — questions the live presence badge cannot answer.

docs.title: What each row means
docs.text:
• Down at — the start of the outage.
  • Recovered at — the end; an Ongoing tag means the outage is still open and its duration is still growing.
  • Duration — recovered minus down, rendered compactly (45s, 12m 30s, 2h 5m).
  • Source — who detected the outage:
  • Lease detector — the platform detected it from an expired gateway lease (heartbeats stopped or the transport dropped).
  • Edge watchdog — the gateway's local watchdog reported the episode over v1/gateway/linkhealth. When an edge report matches a lease episode, the row is corrected with the edge ground truth and shown as edge-sourced; a micro-flap the lease never saw appears as an edge-only row.
  • Reason — the recorded reason text.
  • Alarm — long outages link to the gateway's Alarms tab; alarm-free sub-lease micro-flaps show none. An edge flap burst is represented by a GATEWAY_LINK_FLAPPING alarm; see the Alarms help.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
• Use the Source dropdown to show only lease-detected or edge-reported episodes.
  • Use the time-range picker to narrow to a specific window.
  • Pages load server-side; an open outage stays on the first page until it ends and the list is refetched.

docs.title: Relation to other tabs
docs.text:
• The presence badge and the Devices page show only the current online/offline state.
  • The Alarms tab tracks alarm lifecycle (open/ack/clear); an outage can exist without an alarm, and one burst can drive one alarm across multiple episodes.
  • Alarm-free micro-flaps are visible only here and, aggregated, in the tenant's daily outage digest.

docs.title: Binary Media and S3 Storage
docs.text:
Telemetry is not limited to numbers: a device can upload binary media — camera images, inspection photos, scanned documents — together with its measurements. The binary bytes never enter the database or the message bus. NereidLink streams them into S3-compatible object storage (MinIO, SeaweedFS, AWS S3, …) and the telemetry point keeps only a lightweight blob:// reference.

This works on both MQTT and HTTP, for directly connected devices and for sub-devices behind a gateway.

Developer documentation

This page covers the device-facing contract and the operator-side configuration. The storage implementation lives in the NereidLink repository under internal/blob/ and internal/ingesthttp/media.go — see NereidAI.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
device / gateway                         NereidLink                         S3-compatible store
      |                                     |                                       |
      |  telemetry frame (scalars + media)  |                                       |
      |-----------------------------------> |                                       |
      |                                     |  validate size / content type        |
      |                                     |  stream bytes (PUT object)           |
      |                                     |-------------------------------------->|
      |                                     |            object key                 |
      |                                     |<--------------------------------------|
      |                                     |  store point v_string = blob://<key> |
      |             202 accepted            |  (PostgreSQL / time-series only)     |
      |<----------------------------------- |                                       |

The stored object key is always generated by the platform and is scoped to the owner:

media/<tenant-id>/<device-id>/<uuid>

The time-series row and every Envelope carry only the string blob://media/<tenant>/<device>/<uuid>, never the bytes. Read-side consumers detect the blob:// scheme and resolve it to a short-lived signed download URL on demand.

docs.title: Option 1 — wrap media inside a telemetry frame (MQTT or HTTP)
docs.text:
One structured field shape is accepted inside an otherwise flat frame — the binary media marker. The file payload is base64-encoded (standard or URL-safe alphabet, with or without padding):

{
  "temperature": 21.5,
  "online": true,
  "snapshot": {
    "blob": true,
    "content_type": "image/jpeg",
    "filename": "inspection-01.jpg",
    "data": "/9j/4AAQSkZJRgABAQ..."
  }
}

Scalar measurements and media fields can be mixed freely in one frame. Each media field becomes one string-valued point (blob://…); every other field is processed exactly as usual.

docs.title: Marker field specification
docs.text:
This is the only structured object accepted inside a telemetry frame — null, arrays and any other nested objects are rejected. The wire shape is stable and versioned as a device-facing contract:

Field Required Specification blob yes Must be the boolean true. false or any other value rejects the field, so an unrelated object is never mistaken for media. data yes The file bytes encoded as base64 — standard or URL-safe alphabet, with or without padding. Raw plain text is not accepted: "HELLO WORLD." must be sent as "SEVMTE8gV09STGQu". Empty data is rejected. content_type no MIME type of the bytes. Omit it or send "" to let the platform sniff the type from content (the platform never guesses units, but it does store/detect a media type). filename no Original file name, display only. It never influences the stored object key.

Accepted encodings of the same payload: SEVMTE8gV09STGQu, SEVMTE8gV09STGQ, SEVMTE8gV09STGQ_ (URL-safe).

Two hard rules

  1. data is base64 only — never put plain text or a URL there. To reference an external file, upload the bytes; the platform owns the object key.
  2. Bytes are never inlined into the time-series row or the Envelope. Without a configured blob backend, the marker is rejected rather than stored inline.

docs.title: Over MQTT
docs.text:
Publish the frame to the device telemetry topic — the same path used for scalar telemetry:

PUBLISH v1/me/telemetry   (QoS 0 or 1)

A gateway relays sub-device media the same way, inside the batched v1/gateway/telemetry frame: the marker goes into the per-device values map alongside the sub-device's scalars.

With the Go Device SDK, Frame.Set accepts scalars only; build the marker as a plain map and publish it with PublishRaw:

marker := map[string]any{
    "blob": true, "content_type": "image/jpeg",
    "filename": "inspection-01.jpg", "data": base64Img,
}
frame, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
    "temperature": 21.5,
    "snapshot":    marker,
})
_ = client.PublishRaw(ctx, device.TopicTelemetry, frame, 1)

MQTT packet size

Base64 inflates payloads by roughly a third. Keep MQTT frames within your broker's maximum packet size and the platform's per-object limit (10 MiB by default). For large files use the raw HTTP upload below, which streams bytes without base64.

docs.title: Over HTTP
docs.text: The same JSON document is accepted by POST /v1/me/telemetry with the device credential.

docs.title: Option 2 — raw binary HTTP upload
docs.text:
For larger files, or to avoid base64 overhead, stream the raw bytes directly:

POST /v1/me/blob?key=snapshot HTTP/1.1
Authorization: <device credential>
Content-Type: image/jpeg

<binary body>

The body is streamed straight into object storage (it is never fully buffered), and the platform then publishes one telemetry point referencing it. The key query parameter is the measurement key (default blob; letters, digits, _, ., - only); the object key is generated server side.

202 Accepted:

{
  "published": 1,
  "key": "media/tenant-a/dev-1/8f3c2d0e-...",
  "uri": "blob://media/tenant-a/dev-1/8f3c2d0e-...",
  "size": 48213
}

If the telemetry point cannot be published after the object was stored, the object is deleted again — no orphan files.

docs.title: Accepted file types and size
docs.text:
Policy Default Configuration Max size per media object 10 MiB blob.media_max_bytes Accepted content types image/* blob.media_allowed_types Download URL lifetime 15 minutes blob.presign_ttl

An allowlist entry ending with / matches a type prefix (image/); other entries match exactly (for example application/pdf). To accept documents, extend the allowlist in the platform configuration:

blob:
  media_max_bytes: 20971520          # 20 MiB
  media_allowed_types:
    - image/                         # all images
    - application/pdf                # PDF documents
    - application/msword
    - application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document

An empty Content-Type is accepted and sniffed on the read side instead of being guessed at upload time. Firmware packages use the same object store but a separate, much larger upload limit.

docs.title: Storage backends
docs.text:
• S3-compatible (default for production): MinIO, SeaweedFS, AWS S3 — standard SigV4 path-style access, one region and bucket. Uploads use the internal cluster endpoint; signed download URLs embed the externally reachable public_endpoint.
  • Local filesystem: for small or air-gapped deployments without an object service; the platform serves files itself (HTTP Range included) and signs HMAC download links.

When no blob backend is configured, media endpoints return 503 BLOB_UNAVAILABLE and media-marker fields are rejected.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Response When 413 BLOB_TOO_LARGE Object exceeds media_max_bytes (the HTTP stream is cut off while uploading). 415 BLOB_TYPE_REJECTED Content-Type is not in media_allowed_types (HTTP upload refused before the body is read). 503 BLOB_UNAVAILABLE No blob backend configured. 502 BLOB_STORE_FAILED / BLOB_PUBLISH_FAILED Object store or telemetry publish failed; on publish failure the stored object is deleted again.

docs.title: Reading media back
docs.text:
• The owning device downloads its own objects with GET /v1/me/blob?key=<key> (HTTP Range, ETag and conditional requests supported). Only objects whose key encodes the authenticated device are served — a device cannot read another device's object by guessing its key.
  • Console and API users resolve a blob:// telemetry value through the tenant REST endpoint:
GET /v1/tenants/{tenantId}/blob/sign?key=media/<tenant>/<device>/<uuid>

It returns a short-lived presigned URL (url, size, content_type) — either a presigned S3 URL or an HMAC-signed /v1/blobs/get URL, valid for the configured presign_ttl (15 minutes by default). The key must belong to the tenant in the path, and the caller needs the device-read permission — a valid key for another tenant is rejected, so a reference cannot be turned into cross-tenant access.

The console renders the resolved media by type: images as thumbnails, video in a player, text/JSON/XML in a text viewer (the first 256 KiB inline), and everything else as a download.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Direct Device Integration and Gateway Integration
  • Telemetry glossary and Connector glossary
  • Device SDK (Go) — MQTT/HTTP clients and frames
  • Platform-side REST and the device endpoints are specified in the embedded OpenAPI document at /api/docs.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: The Notifications page is the in-app notification inbox.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
• Unread — new notifications.
  • Read — notifications already viewed.
  • All — everything.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• Mark as read — marks a single notification read.
  • Mark all read — marks every unread notification read at once.
  • View device — jumps to the originating device when the notification is device-related.

Notifications are produced by alarm events and system services, and also arrive in real time over the WebSocket. External delivery (email, webhook) is configured separately.

docs.title: Upgrade Tasks
docs.text: A firmware rollout upgrades many devices to one target version and tracks each device separately. This page is the platform-side host for firmware over the air (OTA); devices pull the package themselves, the platform never pushes.

docs.title: Package source
docs.text:
Every rollout names exactly one source:

  • Platform package — an artifact uploaded to the Firmware Packages page. The version label is taken from the package.
  • External URL — a legacy firmware location. You supply the version label, an https download URL, the SHA-256 digest (64 hex characters) and the size in bytes. The device fetches from that URL directly.

A platform package can target gateway sub-devices; their gateway relays the progress frames, so the per-device view looks the same for both kinds.

docs.title: Target selection
docs.text:
Choose targets in one of two ways:

  • Choose devices — an explicit list. The membership is fixed at creation.
  • Fleet selector — pick any combination of device model, device group and customer; set dimensions are AND-combined. The fleet is resolved once when the rollout is created and snapshotted, so devices added to or removed from the selection afterwards do not move a running rollout. The selector is capped at 1000 devices; the form shows how many active devices currently match before you submit.

A platform package bound to one model can only target that model; selecting an incompatible device (or a selector covering another model) is rejected. Devices already reporting the target version are never reflashed: they are created as skipped / already_current.

docs.title: Canary batching and safety policy
docs.text:
The advanced section opens a rollout gradually:

  • All at once (default) — every target opens immediately, matching the historical single-batch behaviour.
  • Percent per batch or devices per batch — the first batch opens at creation; the next batch opens only after the previous one settles plus the observation pause. Later batches are held back server-side and are not downloadable until they open.
  • Observation pause — seconds to watch settled results before opening the next batch.

Safety tripwires auto-abort a rollout and stop further batches:

  • failure rate reaching abort threshold (default 20% of settled devices),
  • consecutive failures (default 5),
  • the download stall watchdog (default 30 minutes without progress),
  • the reboot confirmation watchdog (default 2 hours).

Devices already applying when an abort trips finish undisturbed; their results are still collected while the rollout stays aborted, and the abort reason is shown at the top of the drawer. Leave a field empty to inherit the platform default.

Offline gateways no longer fail a rollout: their devices stay pending and the platform dispatches them when the gateway reconnects.

docs.title: Success criterion
docs.text:
The success criterion decides when a device counts as succeeded. It is set once per rollout and applies to every device in it.

  • Success on device report (default) — the device reports a successful apply, the rollout finalizes immediately.
  • Confirm after reboot — the device must reconnect and report the running version after rebooting. Only then is the rollout marked successful. If the device reports a different version the rollout fails with version_mismatch; if the device never reboots it fails with reboot_timeout.

Pick Success on device report when the devices already report their running version after every apply. Pick Confirm after reboot only when a rollout must not be called successful until the new image has actually booted.

docs.title: List
docs.text: Each row shows the target version, the aggregate state, progress, the device counts (total, succeeded, failed, canceled, skipped) and the creation time. A Fleet selector tag marks selector-snapshot rollouts. Open a rollout to see its per-device progress, the currently open batch (for canary rollouts) and any abort reason. The state filter narrows the list to one aggregate state, including paused and aborted.

docs.title: Per-device progress
docs.text: The drawer lists every targeted device with its gateway (for sub-devices), the current phase, progress percentage, message and last update. Expanding a device shows its event timeline: every phase boundary is recorded, so you can see when it accepted, started downloading, verified, applied and confirmed — plus the result code and who reported it (platform, device or gateway).

docs.title: Device phases
docs.text:
pending → initiated → downloading → downloaded → verified → updating → updated (applied, awaiting reboot) → rebooting → confirmed. The terminal states are succeeded, failed, canceled and skipped.

High-frequency progress (percentage, bytes) updates the live row but is not written to the timeline; only phase changes and the final outcome are.

docs.title: Pause and resume
docs.text: Use Pause to hold a running rollout: no new batch opens and reconnecting gateways do not receive new devices, but devices already applying finish undisturbed. Resume re-dispatches the currently open batch. A paused rollout can also be canceled. Pausing a rollout that is already terminal is rejected.

docs.title: Cancel a rollout
docs.text:
Cancel affects devices by how far they have progressed:

  • pending devices are skipped — they never start.
  • Devices still downloading or waiting to apply are canceled; a gateway stops relaying the download for them.
  • Devices already updating, updated or rebooting finish undisturbed. Their result is still recorded, but the rollout stays canceled.

Canceling is final and idempotent — canceling an already canceled rollout succeeds without changing anything. Other terminal states reject the request.

docs.title: Result codes
docs.text: A failed device carries a machine-readable result code, such as integrity_check_failed, out_of_ram, flash_full, model_mismatch, version_mismatch, reboot_timeout or download_no_progress. The code tells you why a device failed without reading its log.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Overview is the tenant operational dashboard. It answers "what is happening right now?" at a glance.

docs.title: KPI cards
docs.text:
• Devices — total registered devices, with online/offline split. Click the card to open the device list.
  • Live alarms — alarms in ACTIVE or ACK state. Click to open the alarm center filtered to live alarms.
  • Pending commands — commands not yet in a terminal state (PENDING, CLAIMED, QUEUED).
  • Unread notifications — in-app notifications you have not marked as read.
  • Telemetry 1h — points received in the last hour; the helper line shows the 24-hour total.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
• Telemetry throughput — point count in 5-minute buckets.
  • Live alarms by severity — current alarm distribution.
  • Recent live alarms / presence / notifications — the newest events.

docs.title: How updates work
docs.text: The first load is a single REST snapshot. After that, values update through one wildcard WebSocket subscription per resource — there is no polling. Panels can be dragged by their title bar and resized from the bottom-right corner; the layout is stored locally in your browser.

docs.title: Gateway Probes
docs.text: A probe is an on-demand reachability check: you ask a gateway to verify, right now, whether a set of its bound sub-devices answers on the field bus. The platform itself cannot see the field bus, so it groups the chosen devices by gateway, relays one aggregated request to each online gateway, and presents each gateway's per-device answers.

docs.title: Probe vs command vs liveness probe
docs.text:
These three are related but not interchangeable:

  • Probe — answers only "is the device reachable, and what is the round-trip time". It carries no command name and requires no command catalog entry; the platform never interprets the result content. A failed probe changes no device state.
  • Command — performs an actual read or write against a device (set a point, trigger an action). Commands must be declared in the command catalog and return business data; persistent commands are queued while the device is offline.
  • Liveness probe (health_check) — a periodic, always-on probe configured on a connector instance that automatically drives the bound device's online/offline state. An on-demand probe is a single, manual batch check with no automatic state effect.

Probes for an offline gateway are not queued: those devices fail immediately with a not-connected error.

docs.title: Creating a probe
docs.text:
1. Open Gateway Probes and click New probe.
  2. Pick the gateway that manages the devices. Gateways are listed with their live presence.
  3. Select one or more sub-devices (up to 100 per task). Only ACTIVE sub-devices managed by the selected gateway are shown.
  4. Choose a mode. The platform only relays this value; its exact behavior is defined by the gateway implementation:
  5. Cached — the gateway may answer from a recent check.
  6. Fresh (default) — the gateway performs a new check.
  7. Strict — the gateway applies its strictest checking rules.
  8. Set the per-device timeout in milliseconds (default 10000), then send.

docs.title: Filtering and searching
docs.text:
The toolbar above the table filters on the server:

  • State — one aggregate state (pending, running, completed, partial, failed).
  • Mode — cached, fresh or strict.
  • A search box matching the gateway or probed device's name/alias (case-insensitive partial).

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text:
The task table shows each probe's creation time (formatted per the selected console language), the gateway it was created against (canonical name with alias beneath, linked to the gateway's detail page), mode, the per-device timeout, a live progress bar, succeeded/total counts and aggregate state:

  • Running — still waiting for gateway answers.
  • Completed — every device answered successfully.
  • Partial — some devices failed or timed out.
  • Failed — the task finished without success (for example every gateway involved was offline).

Click a row (or View) to open the result drawer: each row names the device (with its name and alias, linked to its detail page), per-device state, Reachable with round-trip time when the gateway reports it, and the failure error otherwise (timeout, no response, gateway not connected). Progress updates live over WebSocket while the task runs; task results are retained for 24 hours.

docs.title: Device Profiles
docs.text: A device profile groups measurement descriptors: how raw device values map to engineering values.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Descriptor — one measurement key with unit, precision and a value transform.
  • Transform types:
  • identity — stored as published.
  • linear — scale * raw + offset.
  • table — piecewise linear breakpoints between raw keys.
  • expression — a JavaScript expression, for example point.v_double * 9 / 5 + 32.
  • enum — raw value mapped to a text label.
  • Descriptors are versioned; recalibration never changes already-stored history.
  • A profile may bind a rule chain; devices using the profile run it unless they set their own binding.
  • A profile may optionally carry a connector template (ADR-0026 two-level configuration) so it can be reused by gateway connectors.
  • A protocol family (open vocabulary, e.g. modbus, onvif) unlocks structured connection and point-address fields. It is editable on every source, including edge/import profiles: a discovery frame commonly omits the family, so the operator fills it in by hand. The vendor-owned point specification (data type, access, range) remains source-owned on edge/import.

docs.title: Protocol family and point specification
docs.text:
The protocol family is vendor-neutral assistance, not platform logic: NereidLink still stores everything opaquely. A known family (the built-in dictionary covers the current official EdgeX device services — Modbus, ONVIF, MQTT, REST, device-virtual, SNMP, BACnet, CoAP) replaces free-form JSON with structured inputs.

  • On each measurement descriptor, the Point specification section carries the vendor-neutral fields data type (bool/int/uint/float/string/binary), access (R/W/RW), reported default and engineering min/max, plus the protocol-specific address.
  • For Modbus the address fields are primaryTable (COILS, DISCRETE_INPUTS, DISCRETES_INPUT, HOLDING_REGISTERS, INPUT_REGISTERS), startingAddress, isByteSwap, isWordSwap, optional rawType and stringRegisterSize. Any non-dictionary address keys you previously had remain editable as extra JSON.
  • Families whose points use free-form attributes (ONVIF {service, function}, MQTT, REST, virtual, SNMP, BACnet, CoAP) and any unknown family keep the address as one raw JSON object (e.g. an OPC-UA { "nodeId": "..." }).
  • The data type / access / default / range fields are editable only on manual profiles and stay source-owned on edge/import profiles. The protocol family and every point's address are editable on all sources (manual, edge and import), because a discovery/import frame frequently omits both; the calibration fields (transform/scale/offset/enum/valid range) always remain editable. An accepted edge report adopts only the values the frame actually fills, so a minimal replay never wipes an address or family you entered.

docs.title: Profile detail page
docs.text:
A profile is opened by clicking its name in the Profiles list, which navigates to its own page (/profiles/<id>). The page presents three read-first sections, each edited independently with its own Edit/Save — there is no long tabbed dialog:

  • Basic information — name, protocol family and rule chain.
  • Connection parameters — the connector template below.
  • Point descriptors (n) — the point list.

Creating a profile only asks for a name (and optionally the protocol family); after creation you land on the detail page to fill in the connector and points. Each section saves the whole profile server-side, so saving one section never changes the others.

docs.title: Connector template (optional)
docs.text:
The Connection parameters section of the detail page carries an optional reusable connector template:

  • Connector type — the connector plugin type. The built-in nereid-edge (the hard-wired NereidEdge runtime) is always listed; other types are autocompleted from those registered by connected gateways, and you may type any custom value.
  • Type version — the plugin version. Leave empty to select the highest registered version at dispatch time.
  • Config (JSON) — a JSON object holding the shared template configuration. With nereid-edge selected it opens in a split view: a structured EdgeX device form on the left and a live JSON document on the right (a raw-JSON tab remains as an escape hatch).
  • Point mappings (JSON) — a JSON array of objects, each carrying a non-empty string key plus connector-specific properties.

When the EdgeX form first opens on an empty config it is pre-filled once with convenience defaults, and any existing value is never overwritten:

  • Device service name (ds_name) — the family's official EdgeX device-service name (Modbus → device-modbus, ONVIF → device-onvif-camera); filled once the protocol family is known.
  • Profile name — derived from the profile name with EdgeX-legal characters (alphanumerics, _, -). It is a starting point for the template. The device name is not template-seeded: it is per-device and the connector-instance editor injects it from the bound sub-device's NL name (canonical_name, sanitized) when left blank. Clearing a pre-filled field keeps it cleared.
  • Auto-event source name and point-mapping key offer searchable suggestions built from this profile's descriptor measurement keys (equivalently EdgeX device resource names), while staying free text.

Example config and mappings (see the Connectors help topic for the built-in nereid-edge defaults and a full Modbus example):

{ "port": 502, "byte_order": "BIG" }

[ { "register": "40001", "key": "voltage" } ]

Leave the connector type empty to keep a telemetry-only profile. The kernel never interprets the config or mappings; the edge validates them against the schema registered for the connector type. Only profiles that carry a connector type are listed in the Profile template selector of a gateway's Connectors tab. See the Connectors help topic for the desired/reported lifecycle and reconciliation.

docs.title: Creating a profile
docs.text:
1. Click Create profile and give it a name.
  2. Add descriptors with the key exactly as the device publishes it.
  3. Configure the transform and, for table/enum types, the breakpoints or entries.
  4. Optionally bind a rule chain; leave it empty to use the tenant default chain.
  5. Optionally fill in a connector template (type, version, config, mappings) to make the profile reusable by gateway connectors.
  6. Assign the profile to devices from the device editor.

Devices without a profile keep working; their values are stored untransformed.

docs.title: Online-but-silent detection
docs.text:
Each point descriptor has an optional Expected period (seconds) and a Silence tolerance multiplier (default 3). Set the period for points that must report on a schedule, such as a meter reading every 60 seconds.

  • A device using the profile is considered silent when it is connected but no telemetry arrives within expected period × tolerance of the most recent reading. The platform then raises an ONLINE_BUT_SILENT warning alarm.
  • Leave the period empty to exclude a point from this check. The shortest expected period among the profile's monitored points sets the device's deadline.
  • The alarm clears automatically when telemetry resumes or the device goes offline; it is distinct from an OFFLINE presence state.

docs.title: Quarantine
docs.text: Quarantine is a reversible incident-response lock on a single device. Use it when a device is suspected to be compromised, stolen, flooding, or behaving anomalously — and you need to stop it now without destroying its history.

docs.title: What quarantine does
docs.text:
• Sets the device to the QUARANTINED lifecycle state.
  • Evicts presence and disconnects the live session immediately.
  • Makes further authentication fail: the device cannot reconnect, send telemetry, or receive commands, even though its credentials are still on record.
  • Raises a CRITICAL alarm.
  • Records who quarantined it, when, and why.

Quarantine is not decommissioning. Identity, ownership, telemetry and history are all preserved, and the device can be released back to service without re-provisioning.

docs.title: Reason codes
docs.text:
A quarantine requires a structured reason code plus a free-text note:

Code Use when credential-compromise A credential is suspected leaked or misused. device-stolen The device is believed to be in hostile hands. burst-flood The device exceeds its declared rate or burst budget. firmware-anomaly Suspicious device behaviour. other Catch-all. A note is mandatory here, so the code alone never carries the whole story.

docs.title: Releasing a device
docs.text:
There are two paths, both of which clear the CRITICAL alarm and record an audit event:

  • Direct release — a platform administrator releases the device from the Devices page, providing a resolution note explaining why it is safe to restore. Use this when the incident is understood and closed.
  • Dual-control release — the release is opened as an operation order from the CLI by a platform operator and confirmed by the super administrator in the web console. Use this when the decision needs separation of duties. See Operations Orders under System administration.

Either way, the device returns to its previous active state and its existing credentials work again — no re-issuance is required.

docs.title: Seeing quarantined devices
docs.text: Quarantined devices appear in the default device list with a QUARANTINED badge, the quarantine timestamp and the reason. They are deliberately not hidden: an incident nobody can see is not being handled.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A quarantined device is excluded from telemetry writes and command dispatch, not merely disconnected.
  • Releasing does not restore anything that was deleted; quarantine deletes nothing.

docs.title: Rule Chain Editor
docs.text: The rule chain editor is a visual canvas for message routing.

docs.title: Building a chain
docs.text:
1. Drag nodes from the left palette onto the canvas.
  2. Drag from a node's output handle to another node to create an edge.
  3. Click a node to configure it in the right drawer.

docs.title: Node types
docs.text:
• Script Filter — passes the message when the JavaScript condition returns true, for example return msg.temperature > 30.
  • Switch — routes to named relations from a list of cases; unmatched messages follow the default relation.
  • Transform Script — replaces the message with the returned object.
  • Save Attributes — stores attributes returned by the script in the chosen scope.
  • Create Alarm / Clear Alarm — opens or clears an alarm with type, severity and optional dedupe key.
  • Send Command — publishes a command with parameters returned by the script.
  • Forward — queues the message for a tenant data forwarder; delivery is asynchronous.
  • Log — emits a log line.

docs.title: JavaScript rules
docs.text: Scripts run in an embedded JavaScript engine. You must explicitly return a value. The incoming message is available as msg and metadata as metadata.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Enter a JSON test payload and click Test delivery. The chain executes without saving; visited nodes are highlighted, and failed nodes show the error. This lets you validate logic before committing a version.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
• Save new version — stores the current graph as a new draft.
  • Save & activate — saves and immediately makes it live; the previous active version is archived.

docs.title: Live trace
docs.text:
Use Live trace to watch real telemetry flow through the active version. It opens a bottom console:

  1. Turn on Capture real messages. Tracing only applies to the currently active version; activate the chain first if it has never been activated.
  2. Send real device data (for example with the device simulator).
  3. Each message appears in the left list with its time, node count and error count. Select one to see the ordered node path on the right.
  4. Every node step shows its type, execution time and the relations it took; a failed step shows the error in red. The visited path is highlighted on the canvas.
  5. Click a step's node name to center that node.

The console refreshes automatically while capturing. Closing the console does not stop tracing; turn the switch off to stop collecting.

docs.title: Rule Chains
docs.text: Rule chains route device messages and execute tenant-defined actions. The platform itself carries no business logic — this is where your logic lives.

docs.title: Chain groups
docs.text:
A "rule chain" is a chain group holding multiple immutable versions. Device profiles and devices bind to the group, so activating a new version never changes a binding.

Each tenant has exactly one default group, used as the fallback when nothing is explicitly bound.

docs.title: Bindings and resolution order
docs.text:
For every message the executed chain is resolved by priority:

  1. Device binding — a chain set on one device fully replaces its profile chain.
  2. Profile binding — devices sharing a profile share one chain.
  3. Tenant default group — used when neither level is bound.

Bindings are configured in the device form (device level) and the profile form (profile level).

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Every chain is immutable per version:

  • DRAFT — a saved, editable candidate.
  • ACTIVE — the single version currently processing messages.
  • ARCHIVED — superseded or retired versions.

Editing never modifies a version; saving creates a new draft. Activating a version atomically archives the previous active version of the same group.

docs.title: Working with chains
docs.text:
• Click New chain to create a group; the editor opens automatically to build the graph.
  • When the latest version of a group is a draft, use Activate to make it live. The active version is marked in the list.

docs.title: Deleting chains
docs.text:
A chain group can be deleted only when it is neither the tenant default nor bound to any device or profile. The delete button is disabled otherwise; hover it to see the current device/profile binding counts. Before deleting, unbind the referencing devices or profiles (with no explicit binding they fall back through the resolution order). Deleting permanently removes every version of the group.

See the Rule Chain Editor help for how to build graphs.

docs.title: Statistics Center
docs.text: The Statistics Center provides detailed numbers beyond the Overview KPIs. It has two tabs.

docs.title: System tab
docs.text:
Point-in-time infrastructure metrics:

  • Go runtime — uptime, goroutines, heap, GC cycles and pause.
  • PostgreSQL — server connections, application pool state, transaction totals, buffer hit ratio, deadlocks.
  • NATS — messages and bytes in both directions, client reconnects.
  • JetStream streams — stored messages, sequence ranges and per-consumer backlog (pending, redelivered, ack floor).
  • MQTT broker — type and number of connected clients.

docs.title: Business tab
docs.text:
Tenant-wide activity for a chosen time range (last 1 hour, 24 hours or 7 days):

  • Fleet totals and devices by profile.
  • Telemetry volume timeline.
  • Alarms by state and severity; commands by current state.
  • Count of active rule chains.

docs.title: Refresh
docs.text: Both tabs refresh automatically every 30 seconds. Use the pause button to stop auto-refresh, or the reload button to refresh immediately.

docs.title: For monitoring systems
docs.text: The same metrics are exposed in Prometheus format at /metrics. Point Prometheus at that endpoint and import the Grafana dashboard from deploy/monitoring/.

docs.title: Storage Hooks
docs.text: Storage hooks run before telemetry is written to the database. They implement validation, enrichment and forwarding.

docs.title: Hook types
docs.text:
• expression — a JavaScript script that mutates the incoming point.
  • webhook — the point is sent to an HTTP URL.
  • wasm — a WebAssembly module (WASI) executed in-process in a sandbox.

docs.title: Common fields
docs.text:
• Order — hooks run in ascending order.
  • Measurement keys — comma-separated keys the hook applies to; empty means every key.
  • Timeout (ms) — maximum execution time.
  • Failure policy — what happens when the hook fails:
  • passthrough — store the original point anyway.
  • abort — do not store the point.
  • dlq — move the point to the Dead Letter Queue.

docs.title: Expression example
docs.text: point.v_double = point.v_double * 2

docs.title: WASM hooks
docs.text:
A wasm hook runs a sandboxed WebAssembly module (WASI) with no network or filesystem access. The incoming point is passed to the module's stdin as one JSON object; the module prints one JSON object to stdout that overlays the point using the same contract as an expression hook:

  • {"v_double": 42, "unit": "C"} overlays fields;
  • {"drop": true} aborts the point;
  • empty stdout leaves the point unchanged.

Hard budgets: 16 MiB memory, 64 KiB output and the configured per-hook timeout (an infinite loop is killed). Upload a .wasm file or paste standard base64 (config.module_b64) in the hook editor; modules default to a 2 MiB cap (operator-configurable). When editing, leave the module field empty to keep the stored binary. Modules are validated (compiled) on save, so an invalid binary is rejected immediately.

Use the Dead Letter Queue page to inspect and replay points rejected under the dlq policy.

docs.title: Audit Chain (Platform)
docs.text: The Audit page shows the tamper-evident audit log. It is only available to platform administrators.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Audit events record security-relevant actions across the platform. Each row is part of a hash chain: every event's hash is computed from the previous event's hash plus the event's canonical content. Because each row commits to the one before it, altering or removing any row breaks every hash after it.

Each event carries a sequence number, timestamp, actor, event type, action, target resource, source IP, and a per-row prev_hash/hash pair.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text: Use the filters to narrow the log: - Event type — the category of the recorded action - Tenant — limit to one tenant's events - Actor — limit to events performed by a specific user

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Click Verify to run a full integrity check on the chain. The verifier: 1. Reads every event in sequence order and checks the sequence numbers have no gaps. 2. Recomputes each row's hash from the previous hash and the row content, comparing against the stored hash. 3. Checks the daily hash seals.

The result reports the number of events checked, whether the chain is intact, and — if not — the sequence number where the break was detected and why.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The audit chain gives evidence that log history has not been rewritten. A successful verify means the log is internally consistent; a failure pinpoints the first altered row. Because each row commits to its predecessor, an attacker cannot silently edit a past event without detection.

docs.title: Device CAs (Platform)
docs.text: The Device CAs page is the platform trust-anchor console for device mTLS. It manages which certificate authorities the platform trusts when validating device client certificates. Only platform administrators can use it; the TLS handshake pool picks up changes live, without a restart.

docs.title: What a trust anchor is
docs.text: A trust anchor is a CA certificate the platform accepts when a device presents an X.509 client certificate. For a device certificate to validate, its chain must lead back to one of the enabled anchors listed here. This is the platform-wide trust root for device mTLS — separate from any certificate a tenant issues.

docs.title: Built-in vs imported
docs.text:
• Built-in — the CA created with the platform installation (nereidlink pki init). It cannot be deleted, because every device certificate issued by it would stop validating.
  • Imported — third-party CAs you add so devices carrying certificates from your own CA can connect.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Each anchor shows its Subject, Issuer, SHA-256 Fingerprint, trust Status and Expires date. The expiry cell also carries a validity tag:

  • Valid — more than 30 days remain.
  • Expires in Nd (warning) — the anchor expires within 30 days.
  • Expired (error) — the certificate is past its NotAfter.

Expiry is parsed from the stored certificate, so it reflects the CA itself regardless of whether the anchor is currently enabled or disabled.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• Import — upload a third-party CA. Provide a label and paste the PEM certificate.
  • Enable / Disable — toggle whether the platform trusts this anchor. Disabling takes effect immediately: new device handshakes signed by that CA will fail.
  • Download — export the PEM certificate of an anchor.
  • Delete — remove an imported anchor. Built-in anchors cannot be deleted.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Changes are read live by the TLS handshake pool; no restart is required.
  • The device-facing CA bundle is served from an unauthenticated endpoint so that provisioning tools and device bootstrap code can fetch the public certificates without a login.
  • Disabling an anchor can lock out devices whose certificates chain to it — verify before disabling.

docs.title: Deployment License
docs.text: The deployment license is an offline, vendor-signed file that caps what this platform may host. It is signed with Ed25519; the platform verifies the signature against its configured public key and never trusts the file's contents on its own.

docs.title: Install a license
docs.text: Choose the vendor .json file (or paste its contents) and install. The file carries a base64 payload and its detached Ed25519 signature. Installing replaces the current license immediately; the same file is accepted by the nereidlink license command line, so a deployment can be licensed without a running console. A license that fails signature verification is rejected and the current license is kept.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• Status — Installed, or Not installed.
  • Customer — the licensed customer.
  • Tenant limit / Current tenants — how many tenants may exist. Unlimited means no cap.
  • Issued at / Expires at — the validity window.
  • Features — the licensed feature set; empty means no feature restriction.

docs.title: Read-only degradation
docs.text:
When the license is missing, expired, over the tenant or device cap, or the rollback clock detects tampering, the deployment degrades to read-only instead of stopping:

  • no new tenants and no new devices can be created;
  • no new device connections are accepted;
  • existing devices keep reporting, and existing data stays readable and queryable.

A banner on this page shows when the deployment is currently read-only. Import a valid license to restore full operation; nothing has to be recreated.

docs.title: Operations Orders (Platform)
docs.text: The Operations Orders page is the super administrator's confirmation queue for destructive operations. Only the single super administrator can see and act on this queue.

docs.title: Why it is a queue and not a form
docs.text:
Destructive operations (bulk deletion, quarantine release, data retention changes) cannot be started from the web. Instead:

  1. A platform operator opens an order from the CLI, which records the operator name, the exact action, and a payload.
  2. The order lands here as PENDING.
  3. The super administrator reviews the full payload and content hash, then confirms or refuses it.

This separation of duties means no single person can both request and authorize a destructive action.

docs.title: Order lifecycle
docs.text:
• PENDING — awaiting the super administrator's decision
  • APPROVED — confirmed; the action ran and the result was recorded
  • EXECUTED — same as approved, kept as the final executed state
  • REJECTED — refused by the super administrator, with a reason
  • EXPIRED — not confirmed before its deadline; it can no longer be run
  • CANCELLED — withdrawn before confirmation

docs.title: Reviewing an order
docs.text:
• View — open the order to see the action, the full JSON payload, the initiator, the content hash, and — for finished orders — the execution result.
  • Approve — confirm and run the action immediately. A decision reason is recorded.
  • Reject — refuse the order. A reason is required so the operator knows why.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The content hash shown in the review view lets you confirm the payload has not changed since it was opened.
  • Expired and cancelled orders stay in the list for the audit trail, but can no longer be approved.

docs.title: Tenants (Platform)
docs.text: The Tenants page is the platform administration console for creating and managing tenants. It is only available to platform administrators. Tenants represent isolated customer environments; each has its own users, devices, rule chains, and data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A tenant provisioning task tracks progress through states: - PROVISIONING — the platform is creating the tenant's backing resources - ACTIVE — the tenant is fully provisioned and usable - SUSPENDED — the tenant was suspended by a platform administrator - FAILED — provisioning failed; the last error is shown

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• Create tenant — provision a new tenant. You must supply a unique tenant name. The platform records who created it and when.
  • Retry — retry a failed provisioning task. Useful after fixing an external dependency.
  • Suspend — suspend an ACTIVE tenant. Suspended tenants cannot log in or perform most operations until resumed.
  • Resume — return a SUSPENDED tenant to ACTIVE.
  • Members — manage each tenant's administrator/member accounts (roles, enable/disable, password rotation).

docs.title: Members drawer
docs.text:
• Add members by email/name and assign roles.
  • Generated passwords are shown exactly once and must be copied immediately.
  • Disable/enable members and edit their roles without deleting their audit history.
  • Password rotation creates a new password (shown once) or rebinds validity as needed.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Suspension is a platform-level administrative control; it does not delete any data. Data retention rules still apply.
  • Provisioning is tracked in the tenant provisioning table with attempt counts and last error details for troubleshooting.
  • Audit events are written for all tenant lifecycle actions (creation, suspend, resume, member changes).

docs.title: Users & Roles
docs.text:
This page manages the tenant's member accounts: create users, assign roles, reset credentials, enable or disable accounts, and remove them. A platform administrator may open it for any tenant; a tenant administrator manages the members of their own tenant only. Engineer, customer and read-only accounts see an authorization notice.

Each member is one login identity plus exactly one membership in this tenant. Removing a member removes their access to the tenant; the login account is deleted only when it has no membership left in any tenant (a suite SSO user with assignments elsewhere keeps their account and other access).

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Roles are fixed and case-sensitive. A member may hold more than one; the effective permissions are the union of the roles' permission points.

  • Tenant Admin — full read/write inside the tenant, including user management. Can read all customer data and is auditable.
  • Engineer — device configuration and commands, profiles, rule chains, alarms, dashboards, escalation chains, probes and edge connectors. No user management.
  • Customer User — view and command the devices in scope, acknowledge alarms, read notifications and dashboards. No configuration rights.
  • Read-only — read access across devices, profiles, rule chains, alarms, hooks, dashboards and statistics. Nothing can be changed.

Permissions are evaluated as point × resource × data scope. A role grants the point; the membership's data scope narrows which devices the point applies to. A Customer User with device:read and a CUSTOMER scope sees only their own customer's devices, not the whole tenant.

docs.title: Data scope
docs.text:
Every membership carries one data scope, editable under Data scope in the row actions and settable when a member is created:

  • Whole tenant — no narrowing; every device of the tenant is reachable.
  • One customer — only the devices of the chosen customer. Choose the customer in the Scope anchor picker.
  • One device group — only the devices of the chosen group and every group beneath it, so a scope on a parent stays correct as subgroups are added.

The anchor picker switches with the level, because a customer id is not a valid group id. A Whole tenant scope carries no anchor.

SELF (resources owned by the user personally) is not offered. No resource in the current data model is owned by a user, so the scope cannot be honored; offering it would let you build a request that can only fail.

Widening a scope from a customer or group to the whole tenant grants reach over every device, so it is treated as a permission change: the previous and new scope are both written to the audit trail.

A device that belongs to neither a customer nor a group is visible only to a Whole tenant scope.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• New member — creates the login and its membership. Enter an email, an optional display name, an optional password and the roles. Leave the password empty to have the platform generate one; it is shown exactly once.
  • Set roles — replaces the member's role set. At least one role is required.
  • Data scope — replaces the member's data scope and its anchor.
  • Reset password — sets a new password (generated if you leave it empty) and clears the login lock state. The plaintext is shown once.
  • Enable / Disable — a disabled account cannot log in; its sessions stop working. Disabling is reversible.
  • Remove — deletes this tenant's membership; the login account is also deleted only when it has no membership left in any tenant.

docs.title: Protected accounts
docs.text:
Platform administrator accounts cannot be modified here — not their roles, data scope, enabled state, password or membership. The protection matters now that member administration is delegated to tenant administrators: a tenant admin must never be able to seize a platform admin account.

Every action on this page (create, set roles, set data scope, reset password, enable/disable, remove) is written to the audit trail.

docs.title: Live updates
docs.text: The member list updates live over the WebSocket member stream: when another platform administrator creates a member, changes roles or data scope, enables or disables an account, or removes one, the table refreshes itself — there is no refresh button. The member list inside a tenant's drawer in platform administration updates the same way, including when the tenant being viewed is not the administrator's own. Password resets do not change the list and are not pushed. After a reconnect the list is re-fetched to cover frames missed while offline. A tenant administrator receives only the frames for their own tenant.

docs.title: Connector
docs.text:
A connector is a protocol-connector instance running on a gateway and managed through the platform. It is the concrete realization of a connector type on one gateway.

  • A connector is either gateway-level (not bound to a device) or bound to exactly one managed sub-device.
  • The platform is the system of record: you declare a desired spec {connector_type, type_version, config, mappings}, and the gateway reports the state it actually applied (CREATED, DISPATCHED, APPLIED, DEGRADED, FAILED).
  • A connector's config and mappings are interpreted only by the edge; the platform never understands protocol details.

The bound device profile supplies the reusable point table; instance overrides are merged over it at dispatch. Health checks (health_check) are available only on connectors bound to a device.

See the Connectors page guide for full operations.

docs.title: Edge Secret
docs.text:
An edge secret is a credential — for example a username/password pair for a third-party system — that the platform delivers to a gateway for it to store and use. It is distinct from the device credentials that authenticate the gateway to the platform.

  • The platform is the system of record: the secret is stored centrally (encrypted), and the gateway receives it with the desired-state delivery used for connectors.
  • The gateway is only a copy: on (re)connection the full set is re-delivered, so replacing a gateway restores its secrets automatically.
  • The platform never recognizes a credential protocol. A secret type descriptor declares the fields a secret carries as a JSON Schema; the gateway advertises it, or an operator defines it manually. Types with no descriptor fall back to an ad-hoc key/value form.
  • A delivered secret may carry long-lived target selectors (such as MAC addresses); the edge alone interprets what they mean.
  • A secret binding tracks one secret on one gateway with a monotonic revision: PENDING → DISPATCHED → APPLIED (or FAILED + reason), with withdrawal REMOVING → REMOVED. It is managed from the gateway's Secrets tab.

See the Edge Secret Types and Edge Secrets guides.

docs.title: Gateway Operation
docs.text:
A gateway operation is an immediate, whole-gateway action requested on demand — for example rebooting the gateway or triggering a vendor-defined maintenance routine. It is distinct from a connector desired spec (long-lived configuration) and from commands sent to a managed sub-device (ADR-0012).

  • The platform has no built-in operation vocabulary. Every operation is a descriptor: key, interaction (request-response/one-way), timeout, parameter/result JSON Schemas and risk level (read/normal/dangerous).
  • Descriptors come from a gateway's hello advertisement, are defined privately by a tenant, or are a private clone of an advertised descriptor. A tenant may disable any operation.
  • Invocation of a dangerous operation requires a fresh step-up TOTP challenge. Parameters may reference edge secrets and are resolved at the last mile.

See the Gateway Operations page guide.

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
A gateway is a device that mediates between the platform and other, non-directly-connected devices. It holds a southbound connection to its managed devices and a single northbound link to NereidLink.

  • A gateway owns its managed sub-devices and runs the connectors that talk to them.
  • It appears in the device list like any device and has a Connectors and a Managed devices tab on its detail page.
  • The platform is protocol agnostic about what runs on a gateway; any edge implementation speaking the wire contract may register devices and connectors.

Contrast with a direct device, which connects to the platform itself.

docs.title: Health check
docs.text:
A health check (health_check) is an optional probe spec on a device-bound connector. The gateway periodically reads a resource and discards the reading — a probe never produces telemetry or device shadow data.

  • Fields: resource, interval_ms (default 30000), timeout_ms (default 5000, must be shorter than the interval), and fail_threshold (default 3).
  • The gateway owns the online/offline edge: it marks reachability from consecutive probe results.

Health checks are only meaningful when the connector is bound to a sub-device; a gateway-level connector has no single resource owner to probe.

docs.title: Lifecycle state
docs.text:
A device's lifecycle state is its operational status, as opposed to its live connection state.

  • ACTIVE — in service; the default device-list view shows only active devices.
  • QUARANTINED — reversibly locked by quarantine.
  • Decommissioned/archived states are tombstones: devices are never physically deleted, so history and identity remain auditable.

Lifecycle is independent of presence: an active device may be offline, and connectivity says nothing about whether the device is in service.

docs.title: Presence
docs.text:
Presence is the platform's real-time view of whether a device is currently connected: online, offline, or unknown.

  • A presence boundary is an online/offline transition event (connect, disconnect, session eviction).
  • Connection state is derived from the latest boundary; unknown means the device has never produced one.
  • Last activity is the newer of the latest telemetry and the latest presence boundary, shown when hovering the connection badge.

Presence answers "is it connected now"; lifecycle state answers "what operational status is it in" (active, quarantined, decommissioned). The two are independent.

For a passive sub-device, presence does not prove field-bus reachability: it can stay online after the device itself drops off. An on-demand probe verifies that end-to-end.

docs.title: Probe
docs.text: A probe is an on-demand, one-shot reachability check of a sub-device: the platform asks its gateway to perform a real read on the field bus and report whether the device answered and the round-trip time. The platform only relays the request; it never interprets or stores the reading as business data.

docs.title: Probe vs presence
docs.text: Presence is the platform's continuous, cached connection state. For a passive sub-device it reflects only what its gateway asserts while the gateway's own platform session is alive — a device that drops off the field bus (power loss, wiring fault) can still appear online until the gateway notices via a health check. A probe instead proves end-to-end application reachability at the moment it runs and returns the measured round-trip time. It never updates presence or any other device state.

docs.title: Probe vs health check
docs.text:
• Probe — manual, one-off batch check; results are shown only to the operator.
  • Health check — a periodic probe loop configured on a connector instance that automatically drives the bound device's online/offline state.

docs.title: Probe modes
docs.text:
The platform only validates and forwards mode; its precise semantics are defined by the edge implementation.

Mode Recommended meaning cached Answer from the most recent known check; no new field-bus read is required. fresh (default) Perform a new read on the field bus now. strict Perform a new read under the strictest checking rules.

A probe targets only sub-devices bound to a gateway. Devices on an offline gateway are not queued; they fail immediately with a not-connected error.

docs.title: Device profile
docs.text:
A device profile is the reusable template describing how a class of devices maps raw values to engineering values.

  • A descriptor is one measurement-point key with unit, precision and a value transform (identity, linear, lookup table, expression, or enum).
  • The platform never guesses units: a unit exists only when the descriptor declares it.
  • Descriptors are versioned; re-calibration never rewrites stored history.
  • A profile may bind a rule chain; devices using it execute that chain unless they override the binding.

A profile is the point table; a connector instance holds the per-device connection parameters. At dispatch the instance overrides are merged over the profile template.

docs.title: Quarantine
docs.text:
Quarantine is a reversible incident-response lock on a single device. Use it when a device is suspected compromised, stolen, flooding, or behaving anomalously and must be stopped now without losing history.

Quarantine sets the device to the QUARANTINED lifecycle state, evicts its presence and live session, and makes further authentication fail — the device cannot reconnect, send telemetry, or receive commands while its credentials stay on record. Identity, ownership, telemetry and history are preserved, and releasing the device returns it to service without re-provisioning.

Quarantine is a lifecycle action, distinct from the connection state. See the Quarantine guide for reason codes and release procedure.

docs.title: Rule chain
docs.text:
A rule chain routes device messages and performs tenant-defined actions. The platform itself carries no business logic of its own — business logic lives in rule chains.

Messages (telemetry, lifecycle, alarms, …) flow through linked rule nodes (filters, transforms, enrichments, actions) and are fanned out or stopped by each node's routing. A device profile or an individual device may bind a rule chain, so all its traffic is processed by it.

The platform only supplies generic nodes and transport; tenants define every rule.

docs.title: Device shadow
docs.text:
The device shadow stores two independent documents for a device:

  • desired — the state the platform wants the device to reach, written by operators and rule chains.
  • reported — the state the device last reported itself; written only by the device.

Because the two are independent, issuing a command never blocks waiting for the device to acknowledge. Per-key status shows synced when desired equals reported and pending when the device has not caught up.

docs.title: Sub-device
docs.text:
A sub-device is a device that cannot connect to the platform on its own and is reached through a gateway. The gateway owns and manages it.

  • Its device type is "sub-device (gateway-managed)" and it has an owning gateway.
  • Telemetry, presence and commands flow via the gateway's northbound connection.
  • It may have at most one bound connector; the connector column on the device list shows its reported state.

A direct device is the opposite case: it authenticates and connects to the platform directly.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Telemetry is time-series data a device reports — sensor readings and other numeric or discrete samples.

  • A measurement point (measurement key) is one named signal; its meaning, unit and transform come from the bound device profile descriptors. The platform never invents units.
  • Samples are addressable by device, point key and time, and power dashboards, charts and rules.

Telemetry is observed data; the device shadow holds current/desired state, and attributes hold relatively static metadata.

docs.title: Getting Started with NereidMobile
docs.text:
Tech Preview

Mobile is at an early stage. The repository currently contains the Flutter app and the native WeChat Mini Program; the operator surface described here is the target, and the license is not yet declared. Treat it as a preview rather than a finished release.

NereidMobile is the operator's window into Link: a Flutter application for iOS and Android built from one Dart codebase, alongside a native WeChat Mini Program.
