It is a thin client — it owns no domain logic, reads telemetry, dashboards, charts and alerts from Link, and relies on Identity for sign-in.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A reachable Link instance with devices already sending telemetry; Mobile has nothing to show on an empty platform.
  • The suite identity flow available (Identity through Sphere SSO) and an account with access to the Link tenant. When Link runs standalone without the suite, Mobile's SSO entry does not apply — see Standalone by default.
  • The app installed on a phone, or the Mini Program opened in WeChat. Building or releasing the Mini Program additionally requires a WeChat Mini Program AppID.

docs.title: 1. Sign in
docs.text: Open the app or the Mini Program and complete the suite sign-in flow — the same identity you use for the desktop products. There is no separate mobile account. Background on the flow: SSO & OIDC.

docs.title: 2. Browse devices and telemetry
docs.text: After sign-in you see your Link devices and their live connection state. Open a device to view its latest telemetry and dashboards. This is the same data Link collects, laid out for a phone rather than the full operations console.

docs.title: 3. View time-series charts
docs.text: Open a measurement to view a lightweight time-series chart for at-a-glance analysis while on the move. Mobile is intentionally a glanceable field view, not a replacement for the desktop dashboards.

docs.title: 4. Receive alerts
docs.text: Link alerts are delivered to the phone, so field and on-call staff can react away from the console. Alert rules and escalation remain configured inside Link.

docs.title: Trying the builds (developers)
docs.text: The app is a standard Flutter project: run flutter pub get then flutter run inside app/. The Mini Program is imported into WeChat DevTools from the miniapp/ directory with your AppID. Toolchain prerequisites (Flutter SDK, Xcode for iOS, Android SDK, WeChat DevTools) and build commands are documented in the NereidMobile repository (NereidAI).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• NereidMobile product page.
  • Link Overview — the dashboards Mobile mirrors.
  • Link Getting Started — get telemetry flowing first.

docs.title: Account Management
docs.text:
The Accounts page (user menu → Accounts) manages suite accounts from NereidSphere. It is available in OIDC mode only and requires a suite role:

  • Administrator — view and manage accounts;
  • Operator — view accounts (read-only);
  • User — no access to the account console.

Administrators never sign in to the identity engine's own administration console. NereidSphere uses the nereidsphere-admin service account for the approved account lifecycle operations only.

docs.title: Search and pagination
docs.text: Use the search box to find accounts by username, display name or email. The identity service performs the search and returns one server-side page at a time. Changing the page size or page number queries the identity service again; results are not limited to the browser's currently loaded rows.

docs.title: Account operations
docs.text:
Administrators can:

  • create a local account with username, optional email, display name, initial password and suite roles;
  • edit email and display name;
  • enable or disable an account;
  • reset a password;
  • assign User, Operator or Administrator roles;
  • permanently delete an account.

By default, new and reset passwords are marked temporary. The user must change the password on the next sign-in. Disable an account when it may have audit history or ownership of business data; use permanent deletion only when the account should be purged.

Role changes take effect on the user's next token refresh. Disabling an account prevents new sign-ins.

docs.title: Product tenant and roles
docs.text:
In OIDC mode the create and edit dialogs also assign a tenant and role per suite product. Each assignment is stored as an identity-service group named /nereid{product}/{tenant}/{role} (for example /nereidlink/tenant-a/admins), so every product can map group to role with its own configuration. Products that do not follow the convention are absent from the picker.

The tenant list is loaded at runtime from each product through the gateway, so tenants stay owned by the product; you can also type a tenant id directly if a product does not expose a list. Assignment is additive and idempotent: only the groups that differ from the current state are added or removed. External accounts remain read-only.

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
NereidSphere prevents administrator lockout:

  • an administrator cannot delete or disable their own account;
  • an administrator cannot remove the administrator role from their own account;
  • the last enabled administrator cannot be disabled, deleted or demoted.

Destructive and high-impact operations require confirmation in the UI. Account deletion additionally requires typing the account username.

docs.title: Email status
docs.text: The email column shows whether the identity service marks the address as verified. NereidSphere does not guess verification status from the address format. External accounts display the verification state supplied by their identity provider.

docs.title: External accounts are read-only
docs.text:
Accounts provisioned by an external identity provider are tagged with the provider alias and shown as External account. Their password, enabled state, profile and roles must be managed in that provider. NereidSphere rejects mutation attempts with FEDERATED_READ_ONLY.

See Connection status and Identity provider.

docs.title: Connection Status
docs.text: The Connection page (admin navigation → Connection) reports how NereidSphere is wired to the identity plane. It is visible to suite operator and admin roles.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• Authentication mode
  • NereidIdentity (OIDC + PKCE) — browser login uses authorization-code with PKCE against NereidIdentity;
  • Local emergency accounts — break-glass bcrypt accounts from the deployment Secret; no identity service is contacted.
  • Identity issuer — the OIDC issuer URL (discovery is read from <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration).
  • Issuer reachable — whether the discovery endpoint answers right now. Startup never fails when the issuer is down; readiness (/readyz) and this page reflect the live state.
  • Admin REST API — whether the nereidsphere-admin service-account client is configured for user management.

docs.title: Product integration
docs.text:
Each product has one of two modes:

Mode Meaning NS ticket hub (ns) Launching the product goes through /auth/enter/{id} with a 30-second, single-use, audience-bound sealed ticket. Standalone OIDC (oidc) The product is itself a NereidIdentity OIDC client; NS redirects straight to it and the existing SSO session makes entry seamless.

If the issuer shows unreachable while the identity service is healthy, check network policy/egress and the configured issuer URL. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Getting Started with NereidSphere
docs.text:
NereidSphere is the thin suite layer: one portal, a single sign-on (SSO) entry point and a unified API gateway, with no product business logic of its own. This guide walks an operator through the first run — open the portal, sign in, enter an integrated product, manage accounts, and sign out.

Optional, not required

Every product works standalone with its own login. Sphere and Identity only come into play when you want one portal and one login across the suite. Edge is never a central portal entry — it runs independently at each edge site.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A deployed Sphere instance and its portal URL.
  • In the default OIDC mode, a reachable Identity service and an account assigned to you in the suite realm by an administrator.
  • One or more integrated products (Forge, Horizon, Link) reachable from your browser.

docs.title: 1. Open the portal and sign in
docs.text:
1. Browse to the Sphere portal; unauthenticated visitors land on the login page.
  2. In the default OIDC mode, click Sign in with NereidIdentity. Your browser is redirected to Identity over the authorization-code + PKCE flow; enter your organization credentials there. Sphere never sees the password.
  3. On return, Sphere establishes the encrypted ns_session cookie and opens the portal. On an emergency auth.mode=local deployment, use the explicitly labeled Emergency access form instead.

Full flow and error messages: Signing In.

docs.title: 2. Take the portal tour
docs.text: The product grid lists the integrated products in closed-loop order — Forge → Horizon → Link — and your display name and suite roles are shown after login. See NereidSphere Overview.

docs.title: 3. Jump into a product
docs.text:
1. Click a product card; the portal always enters through /auth/enter/{product}.
  2. In the default ticket mode (ns), Sphere mints a 30-second, single-use, audience-bound sealed ticket; the product exchanges it server to server for your verified identity and opens its own session — no second login.
  3. In direct-OIDC mode (oidc), the product is itself an Identity client and entry is seamless through the existing SSO session.

See Opening Products with SSO. Only exact, configured product origins are accepted as post-login redirects, which prevents open redirects.

docs.title: 4. Manage accounts (administrators)
docs.text: Open the user menu → Accounts (available in OIDC mode only). Administrators create accounts, reset passwords, enable or disable users, assign User/Operator/Administrator suite roles, and set each account's per-product tenant and role. Operators have read-only access; accounts federated from an external provider are read-only here and must be managed in that provider. Sphere never uses the identity engine's own master console. See Account Management.

docs.title: 5. Sign out
docs.text: Open the user menu in the header (top-right avatar) and choose Sign out. Sphere clears the session cookie and, in OIDC mode, continues to the Identity logout page before returning to the portal. Products that established their own local sessions may require a separate logout. See Session and Logout.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Login loops, rejected redirects and appearing signed out on every request are usually a Sphere/product mode mismatch, an unregistered redirect origin, or cookies being blocked. Start with Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• SSO & OIDC — the two integration modes.
  • NereidSphere product page.

docs.title: NereidSphere Overview
docs.text: NereidSphere is the thin suite layer of NereidAI: one portal, a single sign-on (SSO) entry point, and a unified API gateway. It contains no product business logic of its own.

docs.title: What you can do here
docs.text:
• Sign in once with your suite account on the NereidSphere login page.
  • Open any integrated product from the product grid without signing in again: NereidLink, NereidForge and NereidHorizon.
  • Review your identity — display name and roles are shown after login.

docs.title: The product grid
docs.text: Each card links to one product. Clicking a card while you have a valid session takes you straight into the product. See Opening products with SSO.

docs.title: Related terms
docs.text:
• Single sign-on (SSO)
  • Session
  • Gateway

docs.title: Opening Products with SSO
docs.text: After signing in to NereidSphere, you can jump to NereidForge, NereidHorizon or NereidLink without signing in again. The portal order follows the closed-loop pipeline: Forge (model factory) → Horizon (distribution to edge sites) → Link (device platform). NereidEdge is deployed independently at every edge site and is not a central portal entry.

docs.title: From the portal
docs.text:
1. Sign in to NereidSphere (the NereidIdentity login page in oidc mode, or the emergency local form).
  2. Click a product card (it always opens /auth/enter/{product}).
  3. Products in ticket mode (ns) receive a one-time, 30-second sealed NS ticket and exchange it server to server for your verified identity, then open their own session — the ticket works only once.
  4. Products in OIDC mode (oidc) are standalone NereidIdentity clients; NereidSphere redirects you straight to the product and the existing SSO session makes entry seamless.

docs.title: Arriving from a product
docs.text:
If a product does not recognize you, it may send you to

/auth/login?redirect=<product-url>

With a valid NereidSphere session you are returned to the product immediately; otherwise you first complete the identity-service login.

docs.title: Allowed destinations
docs.text:
Only exact, configured product origins (for example https://nereidlink.yiqisoft.cn) are accepted as post-login redirects, and in-product deep links are relative paths only. Unknown or tampered URLs are rejected — this prevents open redirects.

See also Single sign-on (SSO), the NS ticket and the Gateway.

docs.title: Session and Logout
docs.text: Your suite session is stored in a single encrypted, HttpOnly cookie (ns_session). It contains your identity and the upstream token data; no token is ever exposed to browser JavaScript.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: The session follows the configured lifetime (8 hours in development). When it expires you are asked to sign in again.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
1. Open the user menu in the portal header (top-right avatar).
  2. Choose Sign out.
  3. NereidSphere revokes the upstream refresh token best-effort, clears the session/CSRF cookies, and (in oidc mode) continues to the identity service logout page, which returns you to the portal afterwards.

Logging out of NereidSphere ends the suite session. Products that established their own local sessions may require their own logout.

docs.title: Cookie requirements
docs.text:
Cookies must be enabled for the NereidSphere origin. If you appear signed out on every request, see Troubleshooting.

See also Session.

docs.title: Signing In
docs.text: NereidSphere is the single sign-on entry for the suite. How you sign in depends on the configured authentication mode.

docs.title: OIDC mode (default)
docs.text:
1. Open the NereidSphere portal; unauthenticated visitors land on the login page showing Sign in with NereidIdentity.
  2. Click the button. Your browser is redirected to the NereidIdentity login page over the standard OAuth2 authorization-code + PKCE flow.
  3. Enter your organization credentials there. NereidSphere never sees or stores this password, and the browser never receives upstream tokens.
  4. You return to NereidSphere (/auth/callback), which establishes the encrypted suite session cookie and sends you to the portal.

External identity providers (Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, …), if configured, are brokered behind NereidIdentity; nothing in NereidSphere changes when one is added. See Identity provider.

docs.title: Local emergency mode
docs.text: When the deployment runs with auth.mode=local, the login page shows an Emergency access username/password form instead. These accounts are bcrypt-hashed entries from the deployment Secret and are intended only for break-glass access; regular users always sign in through NereidIdentity.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• Sign-in cancelled or rejected — the identity service denied the login; retry or use an account assigned in the suite realm.
  • Identity service unreachable — NereidIdentity may be starting or down. In an emergency ask the administrator for local access.
  • Single sign-on failed — the handshake expired or state did not match; start the login again.
  • Local mode: invalid username or password — re-check both fields; the response does not reveal which was wrong.

If sign-in repeatedly fails, see Troubleshooting.

See also Product single sign-on and Session and logout.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common sign-in and access problems in NereidSphere.

docs.title: "invalid username or password"
docs.text:
• This only applies to emergency local mode (auth.mode=local). Confirm the username and password; the error intentionally does not say which field was wrong.
  • In development use the seeded accounts (admin/admin, user/user).
  • Make sure Caps Lock is off.
  • In oidc mode credentials are entered on the NereidIdentity page; account problems there are handled by the identity service/administrator.

docs.title: SSO sign-in failed or was rejected
docs.text:
• Sign-in cancelled or rejected — the identity service denied the login; start again and use an account assigned in the suite realm.
  • Single sign-on failed — the short handshake may have expired or the state did not match; start the login again from the portal.
  • Identity service unreachable — NereidSphere itself stays up, but the identity plane may be restarting. Retry later or ask an administrator for emergency local access.

docs.title: The page keeps returning to login
docs.text:
• Cookies must be allowed for the NereidSphere origin; the session lives in the ns_session HttpOnly cookie.
  • Do not use incognito/private mode if it blocks cookies.
  • An expired session simply requires signing in again.

docs.title: A product does not open (bad gateway)
docs.text:
• The product service may be stopped or unreachable from the gateway. Check the product itself and the NereidSphere server logs.
  • Requests to products flow through the unified Gateway.

docs.title: Redirect rejected
docs.text: Post-login URLs must match a configured product origin exactly. A modified or foreign URL is refused to prevent open redirects. Open the product from the portal grid instead.

docs.title: Language did not persist
docs.text: The language choice is stored in browser localStorage under the key i18next. Clear site data or disabled storage resets it to browser-language detection.

docs.title: Still stuck
docs.text: Contact your suite administrator. See Signing in.

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
The NereidSphere unified API gateway is the single reverse-proxy entry for requests to integrated products, exposed under /p/{product}/....

It:

  • verifies the NereidSphere session;
  • forwards trusted identity headers (X-User-Id, X-User-Email, X-User-Name, X-User-Roles) to the downstream product;
  • preserves tracing headers;
  • never passes secrets or bearer tokens to the browser.

Products keep their own business logic; the gateway only authenticates and routes. An unreachable product results in a 502 Bad Gateway.

docs.title: Identity Provider
docs.text:
An identity provider (IdP) is the OpenID Connect (OIDC) service that holds users, roles and OAuth2 clients. In this suite that service is NereidIdentity (NI). NereidSphere is a pure OIDC/OAuth2 relying party: it only knows the standard connection settings (issuer, client id/secret, admin service-account client, scopes) and never bootstraps or manages the identity plane.

  • The browser is redirected to the NI-branded login page over authorization-code + PKCE; NereidSphere never sees the upstream password and the ROPC password grant is not used.
  • Customer IdPs (Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, …) are brokered behind NI; adding one requires no NereidSphere change.
  • Keycloak-compatible engines can replace the implementation, using config only.
  • auth.mode=local provides emergency bcrypt accounts without any identity service; the built-in admin console talks to NI Admin REST via a service-account client, not an admin password.

The identity service is deployed and maintained independently by the NereidIdentity repository; see Signing in for the login flow.

docs.title: NS Ticket
docs.text: An NS ticket is a short-lived, single-use sealed credential used to hand a verified identity securely from NereidSphere to a product backend when the product is integrated in ns mode. It appears only during the single redirect that takes the user from the portal into the product, so the product can learn "who you are and which tenants/roles you hold" without ever seeing the NereidSphere session cookie or talking to the identity service directly.

docs.title: Why a ticket is needed
docs.text:
Products (NereidLink, NereidForge, NereidHorizon) are independently hosted on their own domains, which gives two hard constraints:

  • When the browser jumps to a product domain it carries only that domain's cookies — it cannot read the NS session cookie, and the product is not allowed to read or validate the NS session directly.
  • The redirect is a "front-channel" path: it passes through browser history, proxy/ingress access logs and the Referer header, so real identity data must not travel through it.

The browser therefore carries only an opaque ticket string in the redirect; the user's real identity data never travels through that browser redirect — it is exchanged exclusively in a server-to-server request between the product backend and the NereidSphere backend.

docs.title: The handoff
docs.text:
1. Already signed in to NereidSphere, the user clicks a product card, opening GET /auth/enter/{product}.
  2. NS validates the session and product authorization (default-deny: a /nereid{product}/... assignment group or the suite admin role), mints the ticket and returns 302 to the product callback https://product/auth/ns-callback?ticket=….
  3. The product backend immediately calls POST /api/v1/auth/ticket/verify with its own server credentials (X-NS-Client-Id / X-NS-Client-Secret).
  4. NS validates the ticket and returns the identity snapshot (sub, username, email, suite roles, product groups); the product then establishes its own local session. The ticket is consumed at that moment.

This is the same well-established pattern family as the CAS Service Ticket, the OAuth2 authorization-code separation of front/back channels, and the SAML Artifact Binding — not a bespoke cryptographic protocol.

docs.title: What the ticket contains
docs.text:
The ticket is an AES-256-GCM authenticated-encryption envelope sealed with the 32-byte server key, containing:

  • a kind purpose marker (isolated from session cookies and login-flow cookies so ciphertext cannot be replayed across purposes);
  • a unique jti, the target product (aud), the identity snapshot, an in-product deep link (to), and issue/expiry timestamps.

The browser sees only opaque ciphertext. The ticket is stateless: the envelope carries everything, any NS replica can verify it, and minting writes nothing to a database.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Forgery/tampering: AES-256-GCM provides confidentiality and integrity together — a single flipped bit fails decryption. The sealing key lives only on the NS server side; neither products nor browsers hold it, so nobody else can mint tickets.
  • Replay: every ticket gets a random jti, consumed with an atomic claim (shared Valkey SET NX PX across replicas); a second exchange is rejected (TICKET_NOT_FOUND). When the replay store is unavailable NS fails closed (503 TICKET_STORE_UNAVAILABLE) — it would rather reject a login than risk honouring the same ticket twice.
  • Theft: the lifetime is 30 seconds and usage is one-time; the legit callback typically consumes it within a second. It travels over HTTPS, never through browser JavaScript and never into local storage. Even if a URL leaks into a log, the ticket is long expired and already consumed when found.
  • Product isolation (audience binding): one ticket is minted for exactly one product (aud). A product can only exchange tickets issued to itself using its own secret; cross-product use returns TICKET_AUDIENCE, and the ticket is burned even on an audience mismatch to stop probing products one by one with the same ticket. Per-product secrets are independent and compared in constant time; compromising one product lets an attacker neither forge tickets nor touch other products' tickets.
  • Open redirect: post-login targets and product callbacks accept only exact, configured origins; deep links inside a product must be relative paths.
  • Timely revocation: roles/groups in the ticket are a snapshot at mint time; the 30-second lifetime makes the stale-authorization window negligible, and products reconcile memberships from the latest groups on every SSO login.

docs.title: Known limits / future hardening
docs.text:
• The sealing key is currently static; automated key rotation (kid with overlapping new/old keys) is not implemented yet.
  • The server-to-server verify endpoint currently relies on HTTPS plus a per-product shared secret; mTLS on the internal path is a future defense-in-depth option.
  • Tickets currently ride in the redirect URL (the standard approach for CAS and authorization codes); a stricter baseline could switch to an auto-submitted POST form moving the ticket into the request body without changing the protocol shape.

The OIDC authorization-code + PKCE flow happens between NereidSphere and NereidIdentity and follows the generic standard; the NS ticket is the suite-level mechanism on the product-integration side. See also Single sign-on (SSO) and the Gateway.

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
A session is the server-issued record that you are authenticated. In NereidSphere it is a single cookie named ns_session:

  • Encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a server-side 32-byte key.
  • HttpOnly — browser JavaScript cannot read it, so no token is exposed to the page.
  • Stateless — there is no session database; any NereidSphere instance can decrypt the cookie with the shared secret.

The cookie carries your identity (subject, email, name, roles). Clearing the cookie or choosing Sign out ends the session.

docs.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
docs.text:
Single sign-on means a user authenticates once at NereidSphere and can then open every integrated product without signing in again.

In NereidSphere the browser is redirected from /auth/login to the NereidIdentity login page and back through /auth/callback using the OAuth2 authorization-code flow with PKCE. NereidSphere verifies the returned tokens and keeps the identity in a sealed session cookie; the upstream password and tokens never appear in the browser. Emergency local mode instead uses the break-glass username/password form backed by built-in bcrypt accounts.

When entering a product, NereidSphere either hands over a one-time sealed NS ticket (mode ns) or sends the browser to the product's own OIDC login (mode oidc).

docs.title: The NereidAI Suite
docs.text:
NereidAI is an end-to-end AIoT platform built for air-gapped and multi-vendor silicon environments. It closes the loop from edge data collection (Edge) → multi-silicon model factory (Forge) → large-scale offline edge distribution (Horizon) → inference and feedback (Link) — without mandatory cloud dependency.

NereidAI ships as a suite of focused products; each can be deployed standalone, and together they form one unified platform. A thin suite layer ties them together without absorbing their domain logic: the Sphere portal and API gateway, and the Identity single sign-on and access-control center.

docs.title: Two thin services, six domain products
docs.text:
Every domain product is a complete system that can run on its own — the suite services only federate them. Short names are used in prose and abbreviations in diagrams — see Naming & abbreviations.

Product Abbr. Role Repository NereidSphere NS Thin suite layer — a single portal and a unified API gateway, plus the closed-loop event glue between products. Holds no domain logic and delegates authentication to Identity. NereidSphere NereidIdentity NI Suite authentication and identity center — single sign-on across every product, OIDC / LDAP / SAML federation, RBAC, token issuance, and tenant-aware access governance. NereidIdentity NereidLink NL Privatized IoT data pipeline — multi-protocol device access, unified messaging, rule engine, alerting, and real-time dashboards. One codebase, two forms: an all-in-one binary or Kubernetes microservices. NereidLink NereidForge NF Model factory — dataset / annotation management, training and fine-tuning, optimization and quantization, hardware-targeted export, evaluation, and model registry. NereidForge NereidHorizon NH Edge distribution and deployment — distributes Edge itself, plus applications and models, to large numbers of remote edge nodes: policy-driven rollout, bandwidth-aware delivery, OTA lifecycle, and autonomous reconciliation while offline. NereidHorizon NereidEdge NE Southbound edge integration, delivered and kept up to date by Horizon — runs on field gateways, connects field devices into Link with zero-touch onboarding, secure mTLS links, store-and-forward buffering, local autonomy, and OTA lifecycle. NereidEdge NereidFleet NFL Robot fleet management — multi-robot task scheduling, traffic coordination, a live operations dashboard, and teleoperation, from wheeled AMRs to legged robots. NereidFleet NereidMobile NM The operator's window into Link — mobile app and WeChat Mini Program: sign in through Identity, browse device telemetry and dashboards, lightweight time-series charts, and alert delivery. NereidMobile

docs.title: Standalone by default
docs.text:
The products are loosely coupled, not a monolith. Every domain product can be deployed and used entirely on its own — its own login, its own data, its own release cycle — with no requirement to install Sphere or Identity, and no runtime dependency on the other products. You can start with a single product and add the suite layer later.

Suite-level bindings appear only when you choose Sphere as the entry point:

  • Authentication. Integrated products trust the identity Sphere hands them (sealed-ticket handoff by default, or direct OIDC). Sphere and the product must agree on the mode; a mismatch causes login loops. Without Sphere, a product uses its own direct OIDC client or local accounts. See SSO & OIDC.
  • Navigation / jump. The portal's single sign-on enter product redirect goes through Sphere; standalone you open the product's own URL.
  • Cross-product event glue. The optional closed-loop events (for example Forge → Horizon → Edge) flow through the suite layer; they are opt-in, not a startup requirement.

Nothing else couples the products. NereidEdge is not a central portal entry at all: it runs independently at each edge site.

    MOBILE -->|telemetry · charts · alerts| LINK

Each product owns its domain end to end — its own UI, APIs, and release cycle. The suite layer is deliberately thin: Sphere provides the common portal, API gateway, and cross-product event glue, while Identity owns authentication and access control. Neither duplicates a product's features, and both are optional for single-product deployments.

docs.title: Platform invariants
docs.text:
• Private by design: all products support fully air-gapped operation with no mandatory call-home and no internet dependency at runtime.
  • Product autonomy: each product owns its domain end to end; Sphere and Mobile are thin layers that never duplicate or absorb another product's features or business logic.
  • Neutral contracts: southbound / wire contracts and platform APIs stay protocol-, stack-, and vendor-agnostic.
  • Multi-silicon via the factory: vendor-specific acceleration, images, and toolchains are isolated inside Forge pipelines — every other product consumes versioned artifacts, never vendor tooling.

docs.title: NereidEdge
docs.text: Edge is the edge agent that connects field devices to Link; it runs on field gateways and is delivered and kept current by Horizon.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
• Field devices and sensors speak many southbound protocols; Edge brings them into Link without per-device cloud integration.
  • Edge sites sit behind flaky or absent WAN links; local buffering and autonomy keep data and control working while the platform is unreachable.
  • Onboarding large numbers of gateways must be repeatable and secure; gateways link to Link over a secure connection driven by declarative configuration from the platform.
  • Keeping the edge runtime and its configuration consistent across a fleet is an operations problem; Horizon owns distribution and update, while Edge reconciles its declared state.
  • Operators need visibility of gateways and their attached devices; Edge reports presence, device state, and a periodic manifest.

docs.title: Core capabilities
docs.text:
Device integration

  • Telemetry bridge: turns field events and readings into Link's gateway telemetry.
  • Device mapping: relates field device names to Link sub-devices.
  • Lifecycle management: attaches devices on first telemetry, detaches them on shutdown, and sends a full device manifest at a regular interval.
  • Runs alongside an EdgeX Foundry edge stack on the gateway.

Gateway behaviour

  • Mandatory handshake and feature negotiation at connect time.
  • Periodic heartbeat, aligned with the limits agreed during negotiation.
  • Platform-managed device attributes cached locally and refreshed on every reconnect, with deletions honoured.
  • Device shadow: reports the gateway's real runtime state on connect and on change.
  • Gateway-level settings applied live from the platform.

Declarative connectors

  • Connector definitions are pushed by the platform; Edge applies, updates, and deletes them, reports status, and self-heals removed devices.
  • New connector types are added without changing the platform or the wire protocol; a node-level export connector is on the roadmap.

Resilience

  • Secure MQTT transport to Link over plain or TLS connections.
  • Designed for disconnected operation: store-and-forward buffering and cursor-based resume so an intermittent WAN does not lose data.
  • Health and observability built in.

docs.title: How it fits in the suite
docs.text:
Edge is the southbound edge hop of the closed loop, between the field devices and Link, and it is deployed by Horizon.

  • Devices → Edge: the edge gateway collects event and reading streams from southbound device services.
  • Edge → Link: telemetry, presence, attributes, and shadow flow up; commands and connector definitions flow down.
  • Horizon → Edge: the distribution hop. Horizon publishes the service definitions and policies that run Edge on the gateway; Edge does not carry its own firmware-update mechanism.
  • Forge: the models and applications Edge runs on site are produced by the model factory and distributed through Horizon.

Developer documentation

The authoritative, detailed developer documentation for Edge lives in its own repository — see NereidAI.

docs.title: NereidFleet
docs.text:
Fleet is a management, control, and collaboration platform for embodied-AI robot fleets — wheeled, quadruped, humanoid, and balancing robots — built on an open stack of ROS 2, Eclipse Zenoh, Open-RMF, and EdgeX Foundry.

Tech Preview

Fleet is at an early design stage (v0.1 draft). The repository is currently design documents and research; the implementation follows the phased PoC route below. Treat these capabilities as the target design, not shipped features.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
• Closed fleet platforms lock operators into one vendor and one robot shape; Fleet aims to unify management, control, and collaboration over an open stack instead.
  • Heterogeneous robots (wheeled AMRs, quadrupeds, humanoids, balancing vehicles) expose different control surfaces; Fleet abstracts them behind a single unified fleet, robot, task, and capability model.
  • Mixing real-time control with platform traffic is a source of jitter and fragility; Fleet separates the real-time control domain from the management and telemetry domain.
  • Sites lose connectivity; edge autonomy must let robots and the edge tier keep operating safely while the platform is unreachable.
  • Adopting a platform must not force replacing vehicle-side middleware; Fleet bridges existing ROS 2 robots rather than intruding on them.

docs.title: Core capabilities
docs.text:
Management

  • Asset ledger, fleet grouping, and edge-node management.
  • Maps, permissions, and audit.

Control

  • Single-robot teleoperation and emergency stop.
  • Safety-mode switching.
  • Real-time state and telemetry.

Collaboration

  • Multi-robot task orchestration.
  • Traffic control and conflict resolution.
  • Cross-robot cooperation.

Architecture approach

  • Data/control separation: vehicle-local control loops stay in the real-time domain for low latency and safety, while platform observation, management, and tasks ride on a separate data bus across network segments.
  • Heterogeneous abstraction: a fleet-adapter layer hides locomotion differences behind the unified model.
  • Bridge, not invade: existing ROS 2 robots join the platform rather than having their middleware replaced.
  • Edge autonomy and heterogeneous sensor intake through EdgeX Foundry.
  • An industry northbound protocol (VDA5050 over MQTT) is under pre-research for cloud-master scenarios.

docs.title: How it fits in the suite
docs.text:
Fleet lives in the site/field plane of the suite, alongside Edge and the robots themselves, on the local LAN rather than in the central platform.

  • Fleet → robots: the platform schedules tasks and issues telecommands, while robots report state and telemetry back to the platform.
  • Open-RMF: owns global task allocation, traffic negotiation, and resource conflict resolution.
  • EdgeX Foundry: owns heterogeneous sensor access and edge autonomy, the same edge framework Edge builds on.
  • Closed-loop integration is future: Fleet is not yet wired into the Edge → Forge → Horizon → Link loop; it is an early stage addition to the suite. See the suite overview.

Developer documentation

The authoritative, detailed developer documentation for Fleet lives in its own repository — see NereidAI.

docs.title: NereidForge
docs.text: Forge is a privatized model factory: an on-premises platform that turns business data — datasets, images and video — into models that run on field devices, covering data and annotation management, training and fine-tuning, optimization and quantization, hardware-targeted export, evaluation and a model registry.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
• Data cannot leave the organisation. Industrial, government and security data is constrained by regulation; the whole factory runs inside the customer's own environment and works fully offline, with base models shipped rather than downloaded.
  • AI projects are hand-crafted. Data preparation, annotation, training, evaluation and deployment are stitched together by a few experts across many separate tools; Forge turns that into one repeatable production line.
  • Capability lives in individuals, not the organisation. Data, models and evaluation reports are registered and versioned, so knowledge outlives staff turnover.
  • Lab models do not reach the field. Field devices have limited compute and many silicon variants; one training run produces models targeted at multiple hardware routes.
  • Vendor and cloud lock-in. The platform is privatized and open in its data and format choices, so today's investment does not become tomorrow's island.

docs.title: Core capabilities
docs.text:
Data and annotation

  • Dataset management with versions and traceable provenance, including draft-to-final workflows.
  • Multi-format import — object detection, classification, segmentation and instruction formats — with a canonical, split-preserving layout.
  • Annotation through integrated Label Studio and CVAT studios, covering images and video.
  • Machine pre-annotation: a model proposes boxes so annotators review and correct rather than draw from scratch; video annotators label key frames and the platform tracks the frames between.
  • Per-project assignees and collaborative review.

Training and fine-tuning

  • A standardized pipeline an ordinary engineer can operate, from dataset to trained model.
  • Support for computer-vision models and for language / vision-language models, with fine-tuning on organisation data.
  • Per-vendor training images keep vendor-specific acceleration and toolchains isolated; there is never a single catch-all image.

Optimization, export and evaluation

  • Optimization and quantization plugins (compile / quantize) applied before a model is released.
  • Multi-framework export to a portable runtime format, with automatic detection of the source framework family.
  • Hardware-targeted export, including NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and domestic silicon routes, so hardware procurement keeps its options.
  • Automated evaluation before release, with the report kept alongside the model version.

Registry, serving and verification

  • A model registry that answers, for any version, what data trained it, how it scored and where it is deployed.
  • Model serving with on-demand loading of uploaded weights.
  • "Try with image" verification of any model artifact without deploying first, with a visualization of what the model attends to.

Delivery

  • Fully privatized delivery: images come from an internal registry and the stack runs in an offline machine room.
  • Declarative deployment and upgrade on Kubernetes.

docs.title: How it fits in the suite
docs.text:
Forge is the model-factory stage of the closed loop. It consumes data collected at the edge — the telemetry Link lands — and produces the models and applications that Horizon distributes to edge nodes. Per the suite's design, vendor-specific acceleration, images and toolchains are isolated inside Forge pipelines; every other product consumes versioned artifacts, never vendor tooling.

flowchart LR
    LINK["NL"] -->|telemetry data| FORGE["NF"]
    FORGE -->|models / apps| HORIZON["NH"]
    HORIZON -->|OTA| EDGE["NE"]
    EDGE -->|data| LINK

docs.title: NereidHorizon
docs.text: Horizon is the operations console for the Open Horizon Management Hub: the place where the suite defines, signs, and rolls out the edge services, patterns, and policies that deliver Edge — and the applications and models built by Forge — to fleets of remote edge nodes.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
• Managing Open Horizon edge resources (nodes, services, patterns, policies, AgBots, HA groups) by hand against the management hub's raw APIs is slow and error-prone; Horizon gives operators one graphical console.
  • Open Horizon requires every service deployment configuration to be signed; Horizon signs it automatically, so operators never handle signing material per service.
  • Third parties and sub-organizations need access to edge resources without sharing the hub-level credentials; Horizon issues organization-scoped, read-only API keys instead.
  • Regulated environments need a tamper-evident record of every action against the hub; Horizon keeps an append-only audit trail.
  • Deployment often happens in air-gapped networks where the console cannot reach the internet; Horizon is delivered for offline installation.

docs.title: Core capabilities
docs.text:
Hub resource management

  • Manage edge nodes, service definitions, deployment patterns, deployment policies, management policies, Agreement Bots (AgBots), organizations, and hub users from one interface.
  • High-availability (HA) node groups: configure, manage, and monitor groups, memberships, and network configuration.
  • Browse public services and patterns across organizations.
  • Import services, patterns, and policies from JSON, with interactive handling of template variables.

Deployment and rollout

  • Sign service deployment configurations automatically on create and update.
  • Follow assignments through, from services and patterns to the nodes that run them, and manage node-side environment variables in place.

Access and identity

  • Two-layer authentication: local console accounts plus a single, system-level connection to the hub shared by all operations.
  • Role-based access: a cross-organization administrator role and an organization-bound partner role.
  • Single sign-on through the suite identity center (Sphere / Identity) or a direct OIDC provider.
  • Organization-scoped, read-only API keys for third-party integration.

Operations and security

  • Server-side sessions with credentials encrypted at rest.
  • Append-only audit log of every console and API-key action, including the actual hub endpoint reached.
  • Hardened TLS and security response headers.
  • Offline, air-gapped installation from prebuilt images.

docs.title: How it fits in the suite
docs.text:
Horizon occupies the distribution hop of the closed loop. Forge produces versioned models and applications; Horizon publishes them — together with Edge itself — as Open Horizon service definitions, patterns, and policies, and the hub's agents roll them out to field nodes. Edge then runs on those nodes and feeds data back to Link.

  • Forge → Horizon: versioned artifacts become distributable services.
  • Horizon → Edge: policy-driven rollout of the edge runtime and the workloads it hosts. See the edge delivery guide.
  • Sphere / Identity: in a full suite deployment, operators sign in once through Sphere and reach Horizon from the common portal. See SSO & OIDC.
  • Standalone: Horizon can also run on its own as the hub console.

Developer documentation

The authoritative, detailed developer documentation for Horizon lives in its own repository — see NereidAI.

docs.title: NereidIdentity
docs.text: Identity is the suite-wide identity plane for NereidAI: the shared, replaceable single sign-on and access-control centre behind Sphere, Link, Horizon and Forge.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
• Many products, one identity. Users and administrators get a single shared account across the suite instead of a separate login per product.
  • Duplicated authentication work. In the default integration, products do not implement identity protocols at all; they trust the suite's one-time handoff from Sphere.
  • Customer identity sprawl. Customer identity systems connect once, behind the identity plane, instead of being wired into every product.
  • Engine lock-in. The identity engine is an implementation detail: another standards-compliant engine can replace it with connection-settings changes in the relying party.
  • Unsafe legacy flows. Password-grant (ROPC) authentication is excluded everywhere, in line with current OAuth 2.0 best practice.

docs.title: Core capabilities
docs.text:
Single sign-on across the suite

  • Standard OIDC/OAuth2 single sign-on with authorization-code + PKCE, refresh tokens and single logout; relying parties verify tokens against the published identity metadata.
  • Sphere is the single mandatory relying party in the default integration; the suite session it holds then reaches every product without a second login.

Integration modes

  • Suite-federated (default): products trust a one-time handoff from Sphere and need no identity configuration of their own. Account governance is fully available.
  • Direct OIDC (optional, per product): a product registers as a standard OIDC client of the identity plane and still participates in suite SSO.
  • Standalone customer IdP: used only when a single product is delivered without the suite; it is explicitly outside suite governance.
  • Mixed deployments are first-class: for example one product on direct OIDC and the rest on the suite-federated handoff.

Identity federation

  • External customer identity providers (for example Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, Authing, AD FS) are brokered behind the identity plane, over OIDC or SAML 2.0.
  • Adding, swapping, or disabling a customer provider requires no change and no restart in Sphere or the products.
  • Group/claim-to-role mapping happens in one place, so every product receives the same suite roles from the same upstream identity.

Roles and account governance

  • A small, stable suite vocabulary — user, operator, admin — with fine-grained authorization kept inside each product.
  • Account administration is centralized: create, enable/disable, reset passwords and assign roles in one console; disabling an account takes effect across the suite.
  • Accounts federated from a customer provider stay read-only in the suite console; their lifecycle is owned by the customer.
  • A built-in local administrator remains available as a break-glass path when the identity service is unreachable.

Private by design

  • Fully air-gapped operation with no call-home and no external runtime dependency; internal certificate authorities are supported.

docs.title: How it fits in the suite
docs.text:
Identity is the identity source of truth that Sphere talks to and that account governance is driven from. In the default handoff integration it is invisible to the domain products; when a product runs direct OIDC it becomes the product's own identity provider.

docs.title: NereidLink
docs.text: Link is a privatized IoT data pipeline platform for on-premises enterprise deployment: multi-protocol device access, a unified messaging pipeline, a rule engine, alarm notifications and real-time visualization.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
• Protocol and device fragmentation. Many protocols, one common device contract.
  • Polling and stale data. All changes are pushed live; no periodic polls.
  • On-premises, regulated operations. Data never leaves the customer's site.
  • Multi-tenant governance. Isolated data, fine-grained permissions, metering.

docs.title: Core capabilities
docs.text:
Real-time communication

  • All data changes are pushed over WebSocket — telemetry, presence, attributes, device shadow, domain events, alarms, command progress, connector status and OTA progress; polling is not used.
  • One connection carries multiple subscriptions with server push, reconnect and session resume; push is tenant-isolated and bound to access-control data scopes.

Device access and management

  • Four credential types (token, password, JWT, mutual-TLS X.509) with a full lifecycle: validity windows, enable/disable, in-place and overlap-window rotation, and expiry warnings.
  • Lifecycle: pre-registration with single-use claim tokens, transfer between customers and groups, non-destructive decommission with a recall window, reactivation and archival.
  • Simple gateway / sub-device containment, bulk CSV/XLSX import with a validation preview, and display aliases and notes.

Commands and remote control

  • Synchronous request-response commands; offline devices fail immediately rather than queue behind a false promise of success.
  • A command catalog is the security boundary, with enable switches, timeouts and read/write masks; batch commands cover a device-group subtree or an explicit list with live aggregate progress, and gateway-relayed commands reach sub-devices. Whole-gateway operations carry risk levels, and probes can be run on demand.

Telemetry, storage and state

  • A unified uplink across the MQTT, HTTP and CoAP ingresses, with typed points (number / boolean / string) and user-defined descriptors; protocol-agnostic and free of business logic.
  • Ingest rate limiting, optional message compression, asynchronous forwarding with per-destination back-pressure isolation, and a dead-letter queue.
  • One data foundation for entity and time-series data, plus S3-compatible object storage for firmware, imports/exports and cold data, with tiered Hot / Warm / Cold storage, per-tenant and per-domain retention, and legal hold.
  • Device shadow with drift detection, three-scope attributes, an append-only device-event ledger, and versioned rule chains with a visual node editor and tiers of scripting.

Alarms and notifications

  • A complete raise / acknowledge / clear lifecycle with assignees, comments and escalation chains, plus multi-channel delivery (in-app inbox, webhook, SMTP email), link-down alarms, a daily per-gateway digest, and a platform-level dead-man fallback independent of tenant notifications.

Edge management and OTA

  • Edge handshake negotiation and session resume; connector lifecycle; two-level configuration with schema validation and drift reconciliation; automatic discovery and enrollment; and a link watchdog.
  • Firmware OTA from an external URL or platform-hosted packages, with phased states, structured result codes, canary rollout, circuit breakers and resumable downloads.

Security, tenancy and operations

  • A built-in certificate authority for device mutual TLS, TOTP multi-factor authentication, and step-up confirmation for dangerous actions.
  • Permissions decide what a caller can do while data scopes decide which rows they can reach, enforced for reads and writes; a tenant secret vault and a tamper-evident audit log.
  • Automated tenant provisioning, machine identities via OAuth2 service accounts, and signed licenses that degrade to read-only rather than stop reporting.
  • Prometheus and Grafana observability, ingress resource accounting, device and adapter SDKs, simulators, a vendor-neutral profile library and a catalog of official device services (Modbus, OPC-UA, ONVIF, BACnet, S7, LLRP, CoAP and more).

docs.text:
Link is the inference-and-feedback stage of the closed loop. Edge connects field devices into Link over mutually authenticated, store-and-forward links; the resulting telemetry feeds Forge as training data, and Mobile is the operator's window into it. Sign-in is federated through Identity.

    LINK -->|telemetry data| FORGE["NF"]
    MOBILE["NM"] -->|telemetry · alerts| LINK

docs.title: NereidMobile
docs.text:
Mobile is the operator's window into Link, delivered as a mobile application for iOS and Android alongside a WeChat Mini Program.

Tech Preview

Mobile is at an early stage. The repository currently contains the mobile app and the WeChat Mini Program; treat the surface described here as the target rather than a finished product. The license is not yet declared.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
• Operators need to see device telemetry and alerts away from a desktop console; Mobile puts that view in a phone app and a WeChat Mini Program.
  • Teams in the WeChat ecosystem expect a Mini Program entry point, not only a native app; Mobile ships both.
  • Field and on-call staff need lightweight, glanceable charts rather than a full operations console.
  • Sign-in should follow the suite identity model rather than a separate mobile account.

docs.title: Core capabilities
docs.text:
Mobile app

  • A single codebase targeting both iOS and Android.
  • Native iOS and Android shells for platform-specific configuration.
  • Static analysis and a test suite in the project's CI workflow.

WeChat Mini Program

  • A native WeChat Mini Program developed with WeChat DevTools.
  • A WeChat Mini Program AppID is required for development and release.

Operator surface

  • Sign in through the suite identity flow, browse Link device telemetry and dashboards, view lightweight time-series charts, and receive alerts.

docs.title: How it fits in the suite
docs.text:
Mobile is a thin client: it never owns domain logic and does not replace Link. It reads from Link and relies on the suite identity center for sign-in.

  • Mobile → Link: the app surfaces telemetry, dashboards, charts, and alerts from Link.
  • Identity: sign-in follows the suite SSO model, so operators use the same identity as the desktop products. See SSO & OIDC.
  • Product autonomy: like the other thin layers, Mobile must not duplicate Link's features or business logic — it is a view onto them.
  • See the suite overview for how the thin clients fit the closed loop.

Developer documentation

The authoritative, detailed developer documentation for Mobile lives in its own repository — see NereidAI.

docs.title: NereidSphere
docs.text: Sphere is the thin suite layer for NereidAI: one portal, single sign-on (SSO), a unified API gateway, and the closed-loop event glue between products. It holds no domain logic of its own.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
• One login for the whole suite. Without Sphere every product still authenticates and runs standalone; with it enabled, a user signs in once and opens any integrated product without re-authenticating.
  • No unified entry point. It provides a single portal that lists the central products in closed-loop order — Forge → Horizon → Link.
  • Cross-product access control. A session proves identity, not product authorization; entry is default-deny and decided by suite assignments.
  • Fragmented edge concerns. It centralizes sign-in, access control and the shared protections in front of every product, so each product does not have to solve them alone.
  • Account governance. It hosts the built-in account administration console, which manages identity-service accounts without storing a master password.

docs.title: Core capabilities
docs.text:
Suite SSO and sessions

  • A standards-based OIDC/OAuth2 relying party to Identity: users sign in on the identity provider's own login page, so Sphere never handles the upstream password.
  • A single, sealed session keeps the user signed in across the suite, with idle and absolute timeouts and transparent renewal while the session is valid.
  • Signing out clears the suite session and, where supported, ends the upstream session as well.

Cross-product entry

  • One sign-in serves every integrated product. Moving into a product is a default-deny decision: a user needs an explicit assignment for that product, with the suite administrator as the single implicit exception.
  • Product entry is handed off with a short-lived, single-use ticket that the product exchanges for the verified identity and then manages its own session.
  • Each product can integrate through the suite handoff (default) or as a standalone identity-provider client, chosen per product.
  • Multi-replica deployments share a replay store so a ticket can be consumed only once, and entry fails closed if that cannot be guaranteed.

Unified API gateway

  • One reverse proxy fronts every integrated product: it authenticates the session, discards any client-supplied identity headers, and forwards a verified identity to the product.
  • Cross-cutting protections live here in one place: an exact-origin allowlist, per-client rate limiting (with a stricter limit on sign-in), protection against cross-site request forgery, upstream timeouts and browser security headers.

Account console and emergency access

  • A built-in administration console manages identity accounts: create, enable/disable, reset passwords and assign suite roles. It uses a dedicated service account rather than a master administrator password, and protects against locking out the last administrator. Federated accounts are read-only.
  • Per-product tenant and role assignments are managed from the same console.
  • An emergency local-account mode keeps administration reachable when the identity service is unavailable; it is clearly labelled as break-glass and is not the default.

Portal and delivery

  • A bilingual portal presents the products and launches each of them.
  • Ships as a self-contained binary and container image plus a Helm chart for Kubernetes; there is no suite business database to operate.

docs.title: How it fits in the suite
docs.text:
Sphere federates the domain products without absorbing them. It is the only suite component that speaks OIDC to Identity, and it hands each product a short-lived ticket so the product can establish its own session.

flowchart LR
    USER["Browser"] -->|sign-in| NS["NS\nportal + gateway"]
    NS -->|identity| NI["NI"]
    NS -->|product entry| FORGE["NF"]
    NS -->|product entry| HORIZON["NH"]
    NS -->|product entry| LINK["NL"]

Edge runs independently at each edge site and is intentionally not a central portal entry. The identity plane is Identity; the full loop is in the architecture overview.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms used across the suite and this site. Product short names and abbreviations (NS, NF, NFL, …) are listed on Naming & abbreviations.

docs.title: Suite & products
docs.text: Term Meaning NereidAI The platform / suite and the GitHub organization; never abbreviated. Suite The eight products used together; each product still works on its own. Product suite Two thin suite services (Sphere, Identity) plus six domain products. Thin layer A component that only federates others — portal / SSO / gateway / event glue — and holds no domain logic. Applies to Sphere and Mobile. Standalone deployment Running a single product without the suite layer. It has its own login and data and does not depend on the other products. Domain product A product that owns a full domain end to end — Link, Forge, Horizon, Edge, Fleet, Mobile. Commercial solution An industry offering (NereidFactory, NereidSentinel, NereidMedical) built on the open platform and licensed separately.

docs.title: Identity & access
docs.text: Term Meaning SSO Single sign-on: sign in once, reach every integrated product. Identity (NI) The identity plane; the single source of truth for users, currently a Keycloak realm (nereidai) behind a replaceable OIDC engine. OIDC OpenID Connect; the identity protocol Sphere speaks to Identity. PKCE Proof Key for Code Exchange; used with the OAuth/OIDC authorization-code flow. Ticket (sealed ticket) In the default ns SSO mode, a short-lived, single-use, audience-bound token Sphere issues and a product exchanges server-to-server for the verified identity. ns / oidc mode The two product SSO integration modes: ticket handoff (default) or a product acting as its own direct OIDC client. Sphere and the product must agree on the mode. Break-glass (local) account A local bcrypt account in Sphere used only for emergencies when the identity plane is unreachable; never the production default. RBAC Role-based access control. Permissions decide what you may do; data scope (tenant / customer / group) decides which data you may reach. Stays inside each product. Tenant An isolated customer/partition inside a multi-tenant product. IdP Identity provider (a customer directory). External OIDC / LDAP / SAML IdPs are always connected behind Identity via brokering. Identity brokering Federating an external IdP behind Identity, so Sphere and products always see the same issuer and claims. Service account An OAuth2 client-credentials machine identity, separate from human users. mTLS Mutual TLS; both sides present certificates. Used for service-to-service and device-to-platform links.

docs.title: Security posture & delivery
docs.text: Term Meaning Air-gapped Installed and run with no internet access; all images and dependencies come from an offline bundle / internal mirror. Call-home A mandatory outbound connection to the vendor. NereidAI has none at runtime. SBOM Software Bill of Materials; a per-release inventory of components. CVE A publicly disclosed security vulnerability; enterprise contracts add a response SLA and backported fixes. LTS Long-term support with backported fixes, offered commercially. Private registry An internal container image registry (e.g. Harbor) used instead of public ones. Helm / chart The Kubernetes packaging used to deploy the products. Store-and-forward Edge buffering that keeps telemetry locally during a WAN outage and replays it when the link returns, without losing data. OTA Over-the-air delivery of Edge itself, applications, models, or firmware to remote nodes. Rollout Distributing an artifact to a set of nodes according to a policy (batches, percentage, canary). Bandwidth-aware delivery Delivery that adapts to constrained / intermittent links (resumable, chunked transfers). Agreement / agbot Open Horizon concepts: an agreement is a node's commitment to run a service; an agbot negotiates and maintains agreements.

docs.title: Link (IoT) domain
docs.text: Term Meaning Telemetry Time-series data a device reports — sensor readings and other numeric or discrete samples. Measurement point One named signal (key); its meaning, unit and transform come from the bound device profile. The platform never invents units. Device profile A reusable template describing how a class of devices maps raw values to engineering values. Descriptor One measurement-point definition with unit, precision and a value transform (identity, linear, lookup, expression, enum). Device A registered, credential-bearing entity that can connect; the platform never physically deletes one. Gateway A device that mediates between the platform and devices that cannot connect directly; one northbound link, many southbound devices. Sub-device A device reached and owned through a gateway. Standalone device A device that connects to the platform directly (MQTT / HTTP / CoAP). Connector A protocol-connector instance running on a gateway and managed through the platform; gateway-level or bound to one sub-device. Edge secret A third-party credential the platform delivers to a gateway to store and use, distinct from the gateway's own platform credentials. Credential What authenticates a device: TOKEN, PASSWORD, JWT, or X.509. Presence The real-time view of whether a device is connected: online, offline, or unknown. Lifecycle state A device's operational status (e.g. active, quarantined, decommissioned), distinct from live connection state. Quarantine A reversible incident-response lock that disconnects a device and blocks auth while preserving its identity and history. Device shadow Two independent documents per device: desired (target state) and reported (last state the device sent). Attribute Relatively static metadata in one of three scopes: client, server, or shared. Rule chain A versioned graph of rule nodes that routes messages and runs tenant-defined logic; the platform itself carries no business logic. Command A remote operation sent to a device/gateway; one-way or request-response, read or write, gated by a command catalog. Probe An on-demand, one-shot reachability check of a sub-device through its gateway; returns answered + RTT, never stored as telemetry. Health check A periodic connector read that is discarded; used by the gateway to mark a sub-device reachable/unreachable. Alarm A triggered condition with a lifecycle (active → acknowledged → cleared) and optional escalation. Escalation chain Ordered, delayed notification steps and target roles for an unhandled alarm. Forwarder An async side output that pushes data to an external system over a pluggable channel. DLQ Dead-letter queue where messages that failed processing can be inspected. Firmware A device software package delivered via OTA with staged status and structured result codes. WebSocket push The single connection over which all live updates are delivered server-side; polling is not used. NATS The message backbone (Core / JetStream / KV); the only service-to-service channel inside Link. TimescaleDB The time-series extension on PostgreSQL used for telemetry.

docs.title: Forge (model factory) domain
docs.text: Term Meaning Dataset A versioned collection of images/data in an annotation format (e.g. COCO / YOLO). Annotation / labeling Marking data (bounding boxes, masks, …), with optional VLM-assisted pre-labeling. Training / fine-tuning Producing or adapting a model on a dataset via a Kubeflow pipeline. Optimization / quantization Reducing a model's size/latency (e.g. NNCF, OpenVINO, TensorRT) without retraining from scratch. Export Producing an artifact for a target hardware/runtime. Multi-silicon / NPU The range of GPU/NPU vendors supported; vendor toolchains stay isolated inside Forge pipeline images. Evaluation Assessing model quality / benchmarking, producing dashboard metrics. Model registry The versioned store of produced models and metadata. Artifact A produced, versioned package (model or application) handed to Horizon for rollout. Kubeflow Pipelines The workflow engine that runs Forge training/optimization/evaluation.

docs.title: Edge & fleet
docs.text: Term Meaning EdgeX Foundry The open edge framework Edge is built on (an EdgeX application service), tracked upstream rather than forked. Zero-touch onboarding A field gateway comes up and registers securely with no manual per-device setup. Local autonomy The edge keeps operating and enforcing local logic while the platform link is down. Field gateway The on-site hardware running Edge and connectors to field devices. AMR Autonomous mobile robot; one class of robot Fleet schedules. Teleoperation A human driving a robot remotely; low-latency LAN path. WeChat Mini Program One of Mobile's two targets, alongside the mobile app.

docs.title: Releases & open source
docs.text: Term Meaning GA General availability; production-ready gate (frozen API, docs, signed images + SBOM). Preview Tryable but not stable; core flows work, contracts may change. Tech Preview Minimal demoable slice; no stability or upgrade promise. VERSION The per-repository file that is the single source for release and image tags. Conventional Commits Commit message convention (feat:, fix:, docs:, …). DCO Developer Certificate of Origin; commits are signed off with git commit -s.

docs.title: Naming & Abbreviations
docs.text:
Curious where the name comes from and what we are building toward? See About NereidAI.

NereidAI is a suite of eight products. To keep pages and diagrams readable, this site refers to each product three ways:

Full name (titles) Short name (prose) Abbreviation (diagrams / tables) NereidSphere Sphere NS NereidIdentity Identity NI NereidLink Link NL NereidForge Forge NF NereidHorizon Horizon NH NereidEdge Edge NE NereidFleet Fleet NFL NereidMobile Mobile NM

docs.title: How they are used
docs.text:
• Page titles and navigation always use the full name — for example NereidForge.
  • Body text uses the short name after the first mention: NereidForge (Forge) on first use, then simply Forge.
  • Diagrams and dense tables may use the abbreviation — for example the node NF in an architecture mermaid diagram means NereidForge.
  • NereidAI is the name of the platform / suite and the GitHub organization; it is never abbreviated.

docs.title: Not part of this scheme
docs.text:
• The commercial industry solutions — NereidFactory, NereidSentinel, NereidMedical — are separate commercial offerings, not members of the eight-product open-source suite, and have no short forms.
  • Edge (the product NereidEdge) is distinct from the generic word "edge"; in prose the short name is capitalized as a product name.

Standalone by default

None of these short names imply a runtime dependency. Every product can be deployed and used on its own; the short names are only a writing convention. See Standalone by default.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Security and operability are first-class concerns in NereidAI, not bolt-ons. The platform is designed to run with no internet access and to keep every byte inside the customer perimeter.

docs.title: Posture
docs.text: Capability Status Air-gapped / offline installation (full image bundles, no internet required) Available No mandatory call-home; data stays inside the customer perimeter Available mTLS service-to-service and device-to-platform links Available Unified SSO and centralized RBAC across all suite products (Identity) Available Signed release artifacts and per-release SBOM Planned Enterprise SLA on CVE response and backported fixes Commercial contract Compliance baselines (e.g. 等保 2.0) and local-OS / accelerator certifications Per-engagement roadmap

docs.title: Defense in depth
docs.text:
The suite layers several independent controls rather than relying on a single gate:

  • Network isolation. Products run with no runtime internet dependency and no mandatory call-home; a privatized build pulls only from internal mirrors and a private registry. See Air-Gapped Install.
  • Transport integrity. Service-to-service and device-to-platform traffic is protected with mTLS. Field links between edge gateways and the platform use outbound-only mTLS with store-and-forward buffering.
  • Identity. A single suite-wide identity plane is the source of truth; the portal never stores users. See SSO & OIDC.
  • Authorization. Access is default-deny: identity proves who you are, and product-local RBAC decides what you can do and which rows you can reach. See RBAC.
  • Secrets and data at rest. Tenant secrets and stored credentials are encrypted at rest under a key kept outside the database; plaintext is restored only where it is truly needed.
  • Integrity and provenance. Audit records form an append-only, tamper-evident chain; deployments published to the field are signed. Signed release artifacts and a per-release SBOM are on the roadmap.

Zero trust between services

Products never reach into one another's data stores. Products communicate over their documented APIs and a message backbone, and the suite layer carries no domain logic — so there is no shared database that would widen the blast radius.

docs.title: Identity and access
docs.text:
Two suite services own the security plane, and both are optional for a single-product deployment:

  • Identity — the suite authentication and identity center: single sign-on across every product, OIDC / LDAP / SAML federation, coarse suite roles, token issuance, and tenant-aware access governance. The identity engine is replaceable: any OIDC/OAuth2-compliant engine that satisfies the published contract can take its place.
  • Sphere — the suite portal and the only component that speaks OIDC to the identity plane. It hands verified identity to products and never sees or stores their passwords.

A detailed walkthrough of the two product integration modes is in SSO & OIDC; the role and tenant model is in RBAC.

docs.title: Product-level controls
docs.text:
Domain products contribute their own hardened controls on top of the suite baseline, for example:

  • a built-in certificate authority issuing device certificates, with mTLS and certificate-revocation checks for device authentication;
  • multi-factor authentication with recovery codes, login lockout, and per-session revocation;
  • step-up confirmation for dangerous operations, with machine identities refused;
  • device quarantine on credential compromise or anomalous traffic, preserving identity and time-series data.

Operations documentation

Deployment hardening checklists and operational security detail live in each product repository: github.com/NereidAI.

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text: NereidAI separates identity from authorization. The suite identity plane proves who a user is; each product decides what that user may do. This page describes the role-based access control model at the level the suite shares.

docs.title: Identity vs. authorization
docs.text:
• The suite supplies identity: a stable subject, email, display name, and a small, coarse set of suite roles (user, operator, admin).
  • Each product owns authorization: its roles, its permission model, and its data scopes are entirely product-local. Products do not invent new suite role names; they map the coarse suite roles onto their own fine-grained permissions.

The identity plane also stores per-user, per-product tenant and role assignments as realm groups shaped /nereid{product}/{tenant}/{role}. Products filter these groups by their own nereid{product} prefix — so one account can hold different tenants and roles in different products.

docs.title: Default-deny product access
docs.text:
Access is default-deny and gated at the suite entry point:

  • A user with no assignment group for a product cannot enter it. Having an account only enables signing in to the portal and receiving assignments.
  • Realm administrators are the exception: they implicitly administer every product, so a fresh deployment's bootstrap admin is never locked out.
  • Removing the last assignment for a product revokes access on the next login, because products reconcile their memberships from the groups on every login.
  • Products enforce the same boundary on their own callback: they consume only their own groups and refuse to issue a session when none is present.

Not every account is a product grant

The operator suite role grants access to the portal's account console but is not automatically a product grant — operators still need a product group to enter a product.

docs.title: Tenant-aware access
docs.text:
Multi-tenancy is a product concept, not a cluster boundary. Each product maps the tenant segment of an assignment group onto its own tenancy model, so access is scoped to the tenants (and, in some products, the orgs) a user is assigned to. The identity plane intentionally invents no tenant semantics of its own.

For example, Horizon binds users to Open Horizon organizations through its roles: a cross-org platform role, and a partner role bound to one org (with several partner assignments becoming switchable orgs). Other products use their own tenant shapes — the pattern is the same, the vocabulary is product-local.

docs.title: Permission points vs. data scope
docs.text:
A product's RBAC typically answers two separate questions, and enforcing both is what makes the model sound:

Question Decided by Example What may this caller do? Permission points attached to a role create a device, run a command, edit a rule Which rows may they reach? Data scopes (tenant / customer / group) only devices in their assigned group

Link is a good illustration: permissions decide what a caller can do, while data scopes decide which rows they can reach, enforced in the store layer on both reads and writes. This prevents a role that can read devices from reaching devices outside its scope, and it applies to real-time push as well — a restricted member's wildcard subscription is materialized server-side to the set of devices they are allowed to see, so pushed frames never cross tenants or exceed authorization.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text: Authorization decisions and the actions they permit are recorded. Link's audit log is an append-only, tamper-evident hash chain — each entry is linked to the previous one and anchored with daily seals, enabling online verification and tamper detection. The distribution console keeps its own append-only audit trail covering console and API activity, attributing each action to a user or an API key.

docs.title: Account governance
docs.text:
The portal's account console manages identities against the identity plane with a service-account client: create, enable/disable, reset password, and assign suite roles. Accounts federated from a brokered customer IdP are shown read-only in the console — their lifecycle (password, MFA, lockout, deprovisioning) is owned by the customer's identity system.

No universal role list

The suite shares only the coarse roles above. The concrete role lists — tenant admins, engineers, read-only users, platform/partner operators, and so on — are defined per product and documented with that product.

Operations documentation

Product-specific role definitions, permission tables, and audit retention settings live in each product repository: github.com/NereidAI.
